setting: General practice. You are the GP. Online: 6-minute history, findings on screen. Face to face: 4 + 2 + 2.
stem: Your next patient is Lily Ferrand, 45, who presents complaining of tiredness and loss of energy. There is nothing else in the stem.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient, with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Tiredness in 60 s · screen — two positives arrive together (night sweats, Cairns) · the travel box in FULL, signposted and closed (destination/duration then A B C D E F G S), undeflected by 'we were just on holiday' · come back OUT and finish the screen — that is where the cough and the two failed antibiotics surface · examination with percussion on both sides, RR and SpO2 · lay diagnosis with reasons · TWO differential groups announced as groups · doxycycline or a macrolide, 48-hour review, safety net.

back.dx: Atypical (community-acquired) pneumonia after four weeks in Far North Queensland: three weeks of dry cough, low-grade fever 37.8, night sweats, back/body aches, exhaustion; two failed beta-lactam courses (amoxicillin then amoxicillin-clavulanate — neither covers Mycoplasma, Chlamydia or Legionella); right middle-zone dullness with crackles, RR 18, SpO2 96%. Four reasons: dry cough for three weeks; low-grade rather than high fever; aches, night sweats and exhaustion; and the antibiotic failure points towards, not away from, this — plus right-sided chest signs. Differentials in two announced groups. Group 1, other causes of persistent cough: typical bacterial pneumonia (chesty cough, high fever, would have responded), tuberculosis (taken seriously — three weeks of cough with night sweats; no weight loss or haemoptysis; CXR and sputum settle it), lung cancer (CXR in any adult with cough >3 weeks, never-smoker or not). Group 2, travel-acquired infections: Q fever, leptospirosis, melioidosis, mosquito-borne viruses — Ross River fits the aches. Then the negative screen: anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, hepatitis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications, mood, OSA. Do not blame the previous doctor. Plan: CXR today, bloods, sputum, atypical PCR swab, travel serology; doxycycline 100 mg bd 5–7 days (macrolide if pregnant or <8 y); review 48 h; named red flags.
plan: Intro, consent; tiredness: low energy, weeks, constant, worse, nothing helps, impact — 60 s, not 90

Checklist: liver, endocrine, malignancy (weight, appetite, lumps, ★ night sweats → YES), infection (fever/chills, flu-like, sore throat, ★ 'have you travelled anywhere recently?' → Cairns) — take BOTH positives

★ 'I'd like to ask about that trip in some detail, because where you went and what you did there can matter a great deal.' Destination and duration → A activities · B bushwalking, bites (insect/tick) · C contacts (animals, unwell people) · D drugs · E exposures (tattoos, piercings, transfusion) · F food and water (street food, unbottled/creek/tank) · G GP before travel (vaccines, tablets) · S sex while away — ask every heading despite 'we were just on holiday'

★ 'Thank you — let me finish the rest of my checklist': PMR/headache, joints and body aches (back ache), bowels, chest pain/ankles, ★ 'any cough?' → ★ five questions: dry or chesty / duration / haemoptysis / smoking / 'has anyone treated you for it already, and did it help?' → amoxicillin then Augmentin, no help
Close: medications (ask about the antibiotics directly if not volunteered), drugs, mood, work, alcohol, smoking; 'what do you think this is?' (hidden agenda: 'something I caught in Cairns')

Examination by name: general · ★ temperature, HR, BP, ★ RR and SpO2 · thyroid, nodes, CVS briefly · full respiratory: expansion, trachea, tactile fremitus, ★ percussion on BOTH sides, air entry and added sounds, ★ vocal resonance · abdomen · office tests

★ 'A chest infection caused by an unusual group of bugs rather than the ordinary ones' — four reasons incl. ★ 'the fact those antibiotics didn't work points towards this, not away from it'; right-sided signs

★ 'I'd like to give my differentials in two groups' — cough list (typical pneumonia, TB reasoned, lung cancer → CXR), travel list (Q fever, leptospirosis, melioidosis, Ross River/arboviruses), then the negative screen · plan: CXR today, bloods, sputum, atypical swab/PCR, travel serology; doxycycline; review 48 h; ★ safety net — breathless, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, confusion/drowsiness, climbing fever → ED; someone at home?
ask: 'I'm going to run through a checklist quite quickly — most of these will be no.' / ★ 'Have you travelled anywhere recently?'

★ 'I'd like to ask about that trip in some detail, because where you went and what you did there can matter a great deal.' → 'Where, and how long? What activities? Bushwalking, insect or tick bites? Contact with animals or anyone unwell? Recreational drugs? Tattoos, piercings, transfusions? Street food or unbottled water? Did you see a GP before you went? Any sexual contact while away?'
★ 'Thank you — let me finish the rest of my checklist.'
★ 'Is it a dry cough or a chesty one — are you bringing anything up? How long? Ever coughed up blood? Do you smoke? Has anyone treated you for it already, and did it help?'
★ 'Could I have percussion on both sides, and vocal resonance?' / 'Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, please.'
★ 'A lung infection caused by an unusual group of bugs.' / ★ 'Neither antibiotic you were given works against these bugs — the fact they didn't help points towards this, not away from it.'
'So the other doctor got it wrong?' → 'No — amoxicillin was a reasonable first choice; the response tells us which group of bugs this is.'

'Is it tuberculosis? My aunt had that.' → 'A fair question and I have thought about it. TB usually causes months of cough with weight loss; yours is three weeks with none. But because of the night sweats I'm not going to guess — the chest X-ray and a sputum sample will settle it. I'd rather check than reassure you wrongly.'
★ 'I'd like to give my differentials in two groups — other causes of a persistent cough, and infections you could have picked up because of the trip.'

'Doxycycline covers these bugs; I'd like to see you again in 48 hours. Come back sooner, or go to the emergency department, if you become short of breath, get chest pain on breathing in, cough up blood, become confused or drowsy, or the fever climbs.'
pefe: Examiner: tired, not unwell; not pale/jaundiced, no rash · ★ T 37.8, HR 92, BP 118/74, RR 18, SpO2 96% · thyroid, nodes, CVS normal · expansion possibly reduced right, trachea central, ★ dullness to percussion right middle zone, crackles same zone, air entry otherwise equal, vocal resonance normal–mildly increased · no hepatosplenomegaly · office tests unremarkable

Investigations: CXR today (cough >3 weeks = CXR always), FBE, UEC, LFT, CRP, sputum MCS ± AFB ×3, nasopharyngeal/throat swab for Mycoplasma/Chlamydia/Legionella PCR, Legionella urinary antigen, serology for Q fever, leptospirosis, Ross River/Barmah Forest, ± melioidosis culture/serology; HIV if risk VERIFY

Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg bd 5–7 days, or a macrolide (azithromycin/clarithromycin); not doxycycline in pregnancy or <8 years — macrolide VERIFY; severity by CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7, RR ≥30, SBP <90/DBP ≤60, age ≥65) / SMART-COP; review 48 h; repeat film at 6 weeks if smoker, >50 or slow to clear VERIFY
Variant — overseas (SE Asia/Pacific): any fever = malaria testing regardless (thick and thin films + rapid antigen, ×3, 12–24 h apart); typhoid live
Variant — 22 weeks pregnant: macrolide, not doxycycline; CXR with abdominal shielding — not diagnosing pneumonia is the bigger risk VERIFY

Variant — deteriorates (RR 30, SpO2 90%, confused, SBP 88): severe CAP — oxygen, IV access, cultures, medical registrar for admission, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval · Variant — farm/abattoir contact: Q fever serology; ask about Q fever vaccination (needs pre-vaccination screening) ADDED · TIS 131 450
fails: A one-question travel history ('where?' and move on) ★
Never exploring the cough — 'any cough?' 'yes' next question ★
A single undifferentiated differential list instead of two announced groups ★
A third beta-lactam (cephalosporin), or 'see how you go in a month' ★
Taking only the second of two positives (dropping the night sweats from the summary and the TB reasoning)
Asking only 'any added sounds?' — never percussion on both sides, RR, SpO2
Blaming the previous doctor; dismissing TB rather than reasoning it; no 48-hour review or named red flags
numbers: Cough 3 weeks, dry · cough >3 weeks = CXR always · T 37.8 low grade (typical pneumonia 39–40 with rigors) · Cairns 4 weeks · failed amoxicillin ×2
Travel box: destination + duration, then A B C D E F G S (activities, bushwalking/bites, contacts, drugs, exposures, food/water, GP pre-travel, sex)
Doxycycline 100 mg bd 5–7 days, or macrolide VERIFY · not doxycycline in pregnancy or <8 y · review 48 h · repeat film 6 weeks if smoker/>50/slow
CURB-65: confusion · urea >7 · RR ≥30 · SBP <90 · age ≥65

setting: Regional general practice, Wallaroo, South Australia. You are the GP. Booked for routine BP monitoring with the practice nurse; nurse's note: BP 135/85, he has asked to see you because he has been feeling tired.
stem: James Corrigan, 40, has known hypertension on perindopril for six months. He attended for routine blood pressure monitoring with the practice nurse (BP 135/85 mmHg) and has asked for a consultation because he has been feeling tired lately.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
No management or investigations task — do not drift into either
time: 8 minutes, 6 + 2. Acknowledge, contract · sleepy vs low energy — get the fork right in the first minute · H to D in ~90 s · C: the heart-failure screen you must be HEARD to do (clarify the ambiguous night-waking) · O: snoring/witnessed apnoeas, the sleep probe, weight, alcohol, ★ occupation → ★ sleepy at the wheel · hidden cardiac worry · plain-English diagnosis reasoned from his answers · BP link · three reasoned differentials then the list · non-blanket driving advice, safety net.

back.dx: Obstructive sleep apnoea in a treated hypertensive commercial driver: months of worsening daytime sleepiness (nodding off at his desk), wife reports chainsaw snoring and witnessed apnoeas, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, poor morning concentration, dry mouth, 6 kg weight gain with tighter collar, 4–5 beers nightly up to bed, brief nocturnal arousals that settle in seconds (not PND), grain-haulage truck driver with one or two episodes of sleepiness at the wheel; BP 135/85 on perindopril — close to target, not 'fine'. Reasons drawn from his own answers. BP link: OSA is a recognised cause of hypertension resistant to tablets (nocturnal sympathetic surges); treating the OSA may do more than another tablet. Differentials reasoned: heart failure (no chest pain, one pillow, no oedema — the arousals settle in seconds), lymphoma/leukaemia (no weight loss, lumps, sweats), infections — EBV, COVID, hepatitis, HIV (no fever, travel, risk); then hypothyroidism, diabetes, anaemia, haemochromatosis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications/alcohol, depression, shift work. Driving: no blanket ban, no blanket reassurance — 'I am not taking anything off you today'; do not drive sleepy; sleep study; commercial standards stricter (Austroads), specialist opinion and evidence of treatment; hidden worry is his father's MI at 58.
plan: Intro, open question; ★ acknowledge ('being tired all the time is wearing'); contract; 'some will sound unrelated — I ask everyone'
★ 'Lack of energy, sleepy, or feverish?' → sleepy · months · mornings · worse · worse after beers · nodding off at his desk, stopping more when driving

H → D in 90 s: tanning/jaundice/urine · polyuria/thirst/weather · weight (gained 6 kg), appetite, lumps, sweats, cancer FHx · fever, sore throat, sexual history, travel · exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, stiffness, headaches (mornings only — 'I'll come back to that'), joints, rash · medicines incl. OTC, mood, anhedonia, stress

★ C — heard to do it: greasy stools/diarrhoea/blood · chest pain · pillows · ankle swelling · 'wake at night gasping?' → ★ clarify: 'breathless and needing to sit up, or settles in seconds?' → settles · cough · smoking (quit 8 y)

★ O — the station: 'has anyone ever told you that you snore, or that you stop breathing or gasp during sleep?' → wife: snores, stops breathing · refreshing? · morning headache · morning concentration · dry mouth · weight gain / collar tighter · ★ alcohol — how much and how close to bed · ★ 'what do you do for work?' → truck driver

★ 'Have you ever felt sleepy at the wheel, or had a near miss?' → pause → once or twice, pulled over · 'the gynaecological causes obviously do not apply' · allergies, PMH, FHx (father MI at 58) · ★ 'anything in particular you were worried this might be?' → the heart

Start with the worry ('I've asked the heart questions and they're reassuring'); ★ name OSA in plain English (throat muscles go floppy, airway closes, brief arousals dozens of times, never deep sleep); ★ reasons from his answers; ★ BP link; keep taking the tablet

★ Differentials: heart failure, blood cancers, infections reasoned; the rest listed — 'one blood test covers most' · ★ driving: not taking anything off you today; sleep study; don't drive sleepy, pull over, avoid long stretches alone; no alcohol 3–4 h before bed; weight later with permission · safety net (worse headaches, chest pain, ankle swelling, any episode at the wheel) · questions (mask? licence?) · summary
ask: 'Is it a lack of energy, feeling sleepy, or feeling feverish?' / 'I am going to run through some questions quickly to make sure I am not missing anything.'

★ 'Has anyone ever told you that you snore, or that you stop breathing or gasp during sleep?' / ★ 'When you wake up, is your sleep refreshing?' / 'Any headache in the morning? Any trouble concentrating in the morning? Dry mouth on waking?'
★ 'How much alcohol, and how close to bedtime?' / ★ 'What do you do for work?' / ★ 'Have you ever felt sleepy at the wheel, or had a near miss?'
'When you wake like that — are you breathless and having to sit up, or does it settle in seconds?'
'The gynaecological causes obviously do not apply here.' / ★ 'Was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'

★ 'The muscles at the back of your throat go floppy and the airway closes over. You stop breathing for a few seconds, your body wakes you just enough to open it again, dozens of times a night. You never remember it — but you never get deep sleep, which is why eight hours leaves you wrecked.' / ★ 'The reasons I think this are your own answers…'

★ 'Sleep apnoea is one of the known reasons a blood pressure will not settle on tablets. Your reading today is close to target — treating the sleep may do more for it than another tablet. Keep taking them.'

★ 'Because you drive for a living I need to be straight with you. I am not taking anything off you today. The test is a sleep study and I'll get that moving. Until then: do not drive if you feel sleepy, pull over and rest if you do, avoid long stretches alone.'

'Will I lose my truck licence?' → 'The rules are about sleepiness, not the label. Commercial standards are stricter and need a specialist opinion and evidence that treatment is working. Most people who are treated and controlled keep driving. What I need from you is that you do not drive while sleepy.'

'I can't afford to stop. I'll push through.' → 'I don't want you to lose your income. But if you keep driving while sleepy I have a duty I cannot ignore — in South Australia doctors are required to report a driver who is unfit. I'd much rather get you treated quickly. Can we agree you won't drive on days you haven't slept?' VERIFY the SA reporting duty before quoting

'Will I need a mask?' → 'Possibly, and they work very well. If mild, a dental splint may be enough, and weight loss helps more than anything else — could we talk about weight next visit?' Never say OSA, AHI, PSG, CPAP or BMI unexplained.
pefe: No examination task in this version. If a card is offered: BMI, neck circumference, Mallampati class, BP, nasal patency, thyroid and lymph nodes, CVS and respiratory, abdomen, office tests (BSL, dipstick)
Variant — pillows, ankle swelling, waking breathless positive: heart failure moves up — ECG, BNP, echocardiogram; consider central sleep apnoea with Cheyne–Stokes rather than purely obstructive
Variant — weight loss and night sweats mid-sweep: examine every node group and the abdomen for hepatosplenomegaly, urgent bloods — exclude a blood cancer before settling on OSA

Variant — normal BMI, no witnessed apnoeas: OSA still possible (blocked nose, small jaw, crowded airway); think harder about insufficient sleep, shift work, thyroid, anaemia, depression, narcolepsy; sleep diary

Next steps (not the task): Epworth (>10 = excessive sleepiness; 0–24 over eight situations), STOP-BANG (≥3 raises risk), sleep study (home or lab polysomnography) via sleep physician; screening bloods and ECG; alcohol 3–4 h clear of bed; 5–10% weight loss measurably lowers AHI; CPAP if moderate–severe (AHI 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe; 5–14 mild); mandibular advancement splint if mild; review BP after treatment; Austroads fitness to drive — commercial standard VERIFY
SA: PATS >100 km VERIFY · TIS 131 450 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
fails: Never asking about snoring or witnessed apnoeas ★
Never asking occupation, or hearing 'truck driver' and not asking about sleepiness at the wheel ★
Missing the malignancy or infection screen entirely ★
Imposing a blanket driving ban, or blanket reassurance about the licence ★
Prescribing a sedative ★
Seizing the ambiguous night-waking as proof of heart failure without clarifying; not being heard to do the cardiac screen
Telling him the BP is 'fine'; saying 'OSA' to the patient; a 90-second physiology lecture; reasoning no differentials (or all twelve); never eliciting the cardiac worry
numbers: BP 135/85 — close to target on treatment, not 'fine' · perindopril 6 months · weight +6 kg / 2 years · 4–5 beers nightly to bedtime
Epworth >10 = excessive daytime sleepiness (0–24, eight situations) · STOP-BANG ≥3 raises risk · AHI 5–14 mild · 15–29 moderate · ≥30 severe
5–10% weight loss measurably lowers the AHI · no alcohol 3–4 h before bed · 4 airway levels · 4 Mallampati classes
Driving: 'I am not taking anything off you today' — rules are about sleepiness, commercial standard stricter (Austroads) VERIFY; SA reporting duty VERIFY
>100 km PATS VERIFY · TIS 131 450 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: Your general practice. Face-to-face station. The role-player is in the room even though there is no history-taking task. Notice on the door: findings are given only if you ask for them specifically.
stem: Mary Whitfield, a 40-year-old woman, has presented complaining of feeling tired, weight loss over the last few months, night sweats and loss of appetite.
tasks: Ask the examiner for the findings of the physical examination you would perform
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Request your further investigations
time: 8 minutes (2 reading). Greet the patient first, then turn to the examiner. Frame the examination in one sentence · general, vitals (temperature first), hands, face/mouth · ★ all lymph node chains, then the four node characters · thyroid with the reason · bone tenderness · chest · abdomen — name splenomegaly · bedside tests · examination gate 5:10 · turn to her, warning shot, say the word lymphoma · reasons from your findings, not her stem · differentials by group · investigations in order — FBE, film, excisional biopsy, PET-CT — then the rest.

back.dx: Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) presenting with B symptoms: four months of fatigue, ~7 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats, anorexia, generalised pruritus; examination — pallor, thin and unwell, T 37.8, HR 96, scratch marks, ecchymoses, conjunctival pallor, two to three rubbery, fixed, non-tender cervical nodes (largest ~3 cm, skin normal), bone tenderness, splenomegaly 4 cm, thyroid normal, chest clear. Clubbing is present but is NOT a lymphoma sign — it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on the list (say so). Reasons to the patient led by your findings: rubbery, fixed, non-tender neck glands (infection glands are tender and mobile), enlarged spleen, scratch marks from the itch — plus her B symptoms. Differentials by group: other cancers — leukaemia (ecchymoses, bone tenderness), lung/bowel/breast; infections — TB, HIV, syphilis, EBV, CMV, toxoplasmosis (some need consent); hyperthyroidism (explains fatigue, sweats, weight loss; thyroid normal today). Investigations in order of priority: FBE, blood film today, excisional node biopsy (architecture, not FNA cells), PET-CT staging (or CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis); then LDH, ESR/CRP, HIV and syphilis serology with consent, EBV/CMV/toxoplasma serology, IGRA + CXR, TSH. Febrile neutropenia = emergency: cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour.
plan: Gel; ★ greet the patient first ('I've been asked to examine you and then talk you through what I think — give me a moment with the examiner'); ★ frame: 'a general examination with a focus on the haematological system, looking for a cause of B symptoms — general appearance, hands, face and mouth, all lymph node groups and thyroid, chest, abdomen, bedside tests'

General: cachexia, pallor, jaundice, rash · ★ vitals, temperature first, then HR, BP, RR, SpO2 · hands: clubbing, scratch marks, ecchymoses, joint swelling → ★ 'pruritus is a recognised feature of lymphoma' · ★ 'clubbing is not a lymphoma sign, so it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on my list' · face/mouth: conjunctival pallor, gum hypertrophy/bleeding, tonsils

★ 'A full lymph node examination, all chains over the whole body — cervical and supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal' → two to three cervical nodes → ★ 'consistency? mobile or fixed? tender? overlying skin? — I ask about tenderness to separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy' → rubbery, fixed, non-tender, 3 cm → 'that is a malignant pattern'; ask anyway if the examiner deflects

Thyroid with the reason (hyperthyroidism explains tiredness, sweating, weight loss): mass, size, nodularity, tenderness, retrosternal percussion · ★ bone tenderness sternum/spine/long bones · chest: air entry, added sounds, S1 S2, murmur · abdomen: inspection, tenderness, masses, ★ 'specifically hepatomegaly or splenomegaly?' → spleen 4 cm · bedside BSL, dipstick — ★ stop asking at 5:10

Turn the chair fully, lower the voice, eye contact: ★ 'I have finished examining you, and I am afraid I have found some things that concern me. Is it alright if I go through them?' [pause] ★ 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.' — say the word, stop, let it land

★ Reasons led by findings: rubbery, fixed, non-sore neck glands vs infection glands; enlarged spleen; scratch marks — then her tiredness, weight loss, sweats. 'Am I going to die?' → no number you cannot stand behind; many lymphomas respond very well; not yet a diagnosis until a gland is sampled

★ Differentials by group: other cancers (leukaemia; lung/bowel/breast less likely), infections (TB, HIV, syphilis, EBV/CMV/toxoplasma — 'some need a blood test and your permission'), overactive thyroid; 'why HIV?' answered

★ To the examiner, in order and slowly: FBE · blood film today · excisional biopsy of a cervical node ('lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture; an aspirate gives cells without architecture') · PET-CT staging (or CT N/C/A/P) · then LDH, ESR, CRP; HIV and syphilis with consent; EBV/CMV/toxoplasma; IGRA + CXR; TSH · febrile neutropenia answer if asked · safety net to Mary (fever, breathlessness, face/neck swelling, bleeding → hospital; specialist phoned; results by phone; someone with you; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20)
ask: ★ 'Examiner, a general examination with a focus on the haematological system, looking for a cause of this patient's B symptoms.' / 'Vital signs, temperature first, please.'

★ 'A full lymph node examination, all chains, over the whole body.' → ★ 'Consistency? Mobile or fixed? Tender? And the overlying skin?' / ★ 'I am asking about tenderness because I want to separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy.'
'Pruritus is a recognised feature of lymphoma.' / ★ 'Clubbing is not a lymphoma sign, so it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on my list.' CORRECTION
★ 'Specifically, is there hepatomegaly or splenomegaly?' — 'any masses?' gets 'no'
★ 'I am afraid I have found some things that concern me.' → ★ 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.'

★ 'Glands from an infection are usually tender and mobile; yours are rubbery, they do not move under my fingers, and they are not sore. I also found your spleen — an organ on the left side of your abdomen — is bigger than it should be, and I noticed the scratch marks from the itching.'
'Why HIV?' → 'Because HIV can cause swollen glands, weight loss and sweats, and it is treatable. I test for it in anyone with this picture. I'd need your consent, and the result stays confidential.'

★ 'My investigations in order of priority: one, full blood examination; two, a blood film today; three, an excisional biopsy of one of the cervical nodes — lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture, so an aspirate is not enough; four, PET-CT to stage.' Then the rest.

'If she rings tonight with a fever of 39?' → 'A medical emergency until proven otherwise — present immediately; blood cultures and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour; haematology involved; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval is needed.'
Jargon check: if she says 'sorry, what does that mean?' — translate lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, excisional on the spot
pefe: Examiner holds: pallor, thin, unwell, no jaundice/rash · T 37.8, HR 96 reg, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 98% · hands: scratch marks, clubbing, ecchymoses, no joint swelling · conjunctival pallor, no gum changes, tonsils normal · ★ 2–3 cervical nodes — rubbery, fixed, non-tender, largest ~3 cm, skin normal; no other group · thyroid normal · ★ bone tenderness present · chest clear, HS dual · ★ splenomegaly ~4 cm, no hepatomegaly, no tenderness · BSL 5.4, dipstick negative

B symptoms: unexplained fever >38°C · drenching night sweats · weight loss >10% over 6 months. Node characters: consistency, mobility/fixation, tenderness, size and overlying skin. Chains: cervical/supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal.
Variant — 50-year-old: add pelvic and breast examination (menopause, breast carcinoma on the list); 'menopause would not explain the glands or the spleen'

Variant — T 38.9, tachycardic, mucosal bleeding, gum hypertrophy, sternal tenderness: acute leukaemia with febrile neutropenia — cultures, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h, urgent FBE/film, haematology now

Variant — tender mobile nodes, age 24, sore throat, spleen just palpable: infectious mononucleosis — EBV serology, film for atypical lymphocytes, avoid amoxicillin, no contact sport while the spleen is enlarged
SA: urgent haematology referral (RAH/FMC); excision biopsy via surgical/ENT pathway; PATS; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450
fails: 'I would do a full physical examination' — the generic opening that burns thirty seconds ★
Not asking for all lymph node chains, or accepting 'enlarged cervical nodes' without the four characters ★
Not specifically naming splenomegaly ★
Euphemism instead of the word lymphoma ('a blood problem', 'something in your immune system') ★
Justifying with her stem symptoms only, not your examination findings ★
Folding clubbing into the lymphoma justification; a shotgun investigation list; FNA instead of excisional biopsy
Never greeting the patient before turning to the examiner; pushing on without pausing after the word cancer; giving a survival number
numbers: B symptoms: weight loss >10% / 6 months · fever >38°C unexplained · drenching night sweats · here: ~7 kg, T 37.8, soaked 2–3 nights/week
4 node characters: consistency, mobility, tenderness, skin (+ size) · chains: cervical, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal · largest node ~3 cm · spleen 4 cm
Examination gate: stop asking at 5:10 · first four investigations: FBE, film, excisional biopsy, PET-CT
Febrile neutropenia: antibiotics within 1 hour
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · TIS 131 450

setting: Hospital ward, evening shift. TELEPHONE station — no examiner, no role-player in the room; a card says 'please pick up the telephone'. The nurse on the line is the examiner. Your consultant is unavailable. Management is NOT a task.
stem: You are the HMO. Blood results have returned on Mr Arthur Nolan, 78, a resident of a nearby aged-care facility, currently an inpatient. Sodium 118 mmol/L (135–145), chloride low, serum osmolality low. Nothing else is given.
tasks: Report and explain the investigation results to the nurse
Take a history from the nurse
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the nurse
time: 8 minutes. Name yourself, who and where · ★ conscious state and fitting BEFORE any number · obs · report in colleague register, name what the low osmolality means · orient: admission, PMHx, ★ the whole chart including long-standing drugs, surgery · symptoms · pseudo screen (glucose, TG, protein) said out loud · three volume blocks announced · ★ ask her to EXAMINE him for fluid state · four SIADH cause groups · three-layer explanation · escalate, safety-net, offer to document.

back.dx: Drug-induced (thiazide) SIADH → euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia. Na 118, low serum osmolality = true hypotonic (not pseudo; not glucose-driven — glucose 5.4, TG and protein normal). Nurse's examination on request: moist mucosa, no postural drop, no oedema, chest clear, weight stable, fluid chart balanced ~1400/1300 → euvolaemic. Chart: hydrochlorothiazide, paracetamol, atorvastatin — nothing changed since admission (asking only 'new medications' gets 'nothing new' and you miss it). Three-layer explanation: (1) true hypotonic, euvolaemic → SIADH, most likely trigger the thiazide; (2) other SIADH causes — malignancy (lung, lymphoma), infection (pneumonia, TB, meningitis), intracranial (bleed, head injury) — clear CT, no fever/cough/weight loss make them less likely but not excluded on history; (3) outside SIADH — hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (TSH, morning cortisol), hypovolaemic group (losses, poor intake, diuretics), hypervolaemic group (heart, liver, kidney). Confirm with paired serum/urine osmolality + urine sodium. Close: discuss with medical registrar and document — do not change the thiazide over the phone; call back if drowsy, more confused, vomiting, fitting.
plan: ★ 'This is Dr [name], the HMO covering the ward tonight. Who am I speaking with, and which ward?' → Jackie, RN 4B, bed 12
★ 'Before I go through the results — is he alert and oriented, or drowsy or more confused than usual? Any fitting? Latest obs?' → alert at baseline, no fits, BP 128/76 HR 78 RR 16 SpO2 97 T 36.6

Report as a colleague: Na 118 vs 135–145, significant; chloride low tracks Na; ★ 'serum osmolality is low — this is a true hypotonic hyponatraemia, not an artefact'. If asked what osmolality means: one technical sentence, no lay translation

Orient: admitted 3 days ago after a fall, no fracture · HTN, OA, mild memory impairment · ★ 'read me the whole chart — everything, including anything started or changed in the last few weeks' → hydrochlorothiazide, paracetamol, atorvastatin · no surgery. Note the thiazide, keep going

Symptoms (confusion vs baseline, drowsiness, headache, nausea/vomiting, unsteadiness/falls) · ★ pseudo screen: glucose 5.4, TG normal, total protein normal → say aloud 'not pseudohyponatraemia, not glucose-driven — true hypotonic; next I need his fluid state'

Three volume blocks, each announced: 1 losing — vomiting, diarrhoea, intake, burns/wounds · 2 retaining — orthopnoea/pillows, ankle swelling, jaundice/dark urine/pale stools, urine output, fluid balance chart → ~1400 in/1300 out · 3 euvolaemic — cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain

★ THE DISCRIMINATING ASK: 'Can I ask you to look at him and tell me what his fluid state looks like — dry mouth/tongue, reduced turgor, postural drop; or ankle oedema, raised JVP, basal crackles? Weight on the chart?' → euvolaemic → say 'that narrows this considerably'

SIADH cause groups, one question each: drugs (have the chart) · infection — fever, cough, SOB, headache, neck stiffness, new drowsiness · malignancy — weight loss, lumps/nodes, night sweats, past cancer · brain — head strike in the fall, imaging → CT clear · 'drinking unusually large volumes?'

ask: 'Before we look at them — can I ask what prompted the test in the first place?'
'Any dizziness, confusion, memory trouble, headaches, tiredness, or any change in your walking or balance?'
★ 'Can you tell me every medicine you take — prescribed, bought over the counter, and anything herbal?'
'Your blood test shows a low sodium level. Sodium is a mineral, or a salt, that your body keeps in careful balance in the blood.'

'The most likely cause is a condition called SIADH — the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH. ADH is a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Your body makes more of it than it should, so you hold on to extra water, and that extra water dilutes the salt in your blood.'
'In your case the most likely trigger is your medication — both citalopram and carbamazepine are recognised causes, and that is a side effect rather than anything you have done wrong.'

'There are other things that can cause SIADH and I've looked for them: certain cancers, particularly of the lung, and lymphoma — your chest X-ray is normal; infections of the chest or the lining of the brain; and problems inside the head such as a bleed or an injury — your brain scan is normal.'

'Causes outside SIADH: losing fluid through vomiting, diarrhoea or not drinking enough; fluid tablets; an underactive thyroid, which your test has ruled out; and heart, liver or kidney problems, which your results and examination don't support.'

★ 'Should I stop them?' → 'Not today. We confirm it first, then I talk to whoever prescribes them — stopping an antidepressant suddenly causes withdrawal symptoms, and stopping carbamazepine suddenly can bring on seizures. We plan the change together.'
'Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you get a bad headache, become confused or unusually drowsy, start vomiting, or have any fitting.'

setting: Renal unit of a metropolitan teaching hospital; you are the resident. A 12-lead ECG is supplied with the stem — read it before you enter. Vitals available on request. Older recall adds a fourth task: outline your immediate management.
stem: Mr John Whitfield, 60, known end-stage kidney disease on maintenance haemodialysis, attends for his scheduled session. He has had several days of palpitations and diarrhoea. ECG provided: tall, narrow-based, symmetrical peaked T waves, most marked in the mid-precordial leads; QRS normal; P waves preserved.
tasks: Take a further focused history (3 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant investigations
Explain the condition to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 40 s opening · 3 min history · 45 s investigations · 2.5 min explanation · 45 s safety-net and close. back.dx: Acute kidney injury on end-stage kidney disease with hyperkalaemia (K 5.9 with ECG changes = treat as severe) — multifactorial: (1) perindopril dose increased by the GP last week (he can't say which tablet; deduce it from pharmacology — of perindopril, hydrochlorothiazide, erythropoietin, the ACE inhibitor is the one that raises potassium), (2) missed Monday's dialysis — a session's worth of potassium not removed, (3) four days of watery diarrhoea with poor intake and postural dizziness — volume depletion. eGFR 10–12 (baseline ESKD); VBG no significant acidosis → reduced clearance and retention, not a transcellular shift. 'You have hyperkalaemia' is a laboratory state, not a diagnosis — the commonest fail. Explain: 'your kidneys have taken a sudden knock on top of the long-standing damage — an acute injury on chronic kidney disease'; three reasons stacked; potassium controls the heart's electrical rhythm, hence the palpitations. Plan: cardiac monitor, dialysis brought forward to today, hold the perindopril, letter to the GP, don't stop anything else alone. Handle 'my GP did this to me' by explaining the monitoring gap (UEC 1–2 weeks after any ACE-i dose change), not the person.

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. You are the GP. Pre-operative results station; no physical examination.
stem: Mark Ellis, 50, storeman, is booked for elective open right inguinal hernia repair in 10 days and attends for his pre-operative blood results. He feels well and has no complaint. Hypertension for 6 years on a thiazide diuretic. BP 138/84, HR 78 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.7. Results: sodium 135 (135–145), potassium 3.1 (3.5–5.2), bicarbonate 30 (22–32), creatinine 82 µmol/L, eGFR >90, anion gap normal.
tasks: Explain the blood test results to the patient
Take a focused, relevant history
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes after 2 reading: results 2 min (marks earned in the first three sentences — say the kidneys are normal) · history 4 min (surgical context → ★ hypertension block incl. the dose change → intake → GI loss naming laxatives/teas → renal loss/mineralocorticoid → phaeo triad → other drugs by category, SADMA, FHx) · diagnosis + ★ four differentials aloud 2 min · plan: repeat, ECG, magnesium, replace, review the antihypertensive · answer the operation question · safety-net · summarise.

back.dx: Mild hypokalaemia (K 3.1) from thiazide-induced renal potassium wasting — the dose was doubled four weeks ago for creeping readings, which fits the timing exactly; bicarbonate 30 at the top of range is consistent. Normal renal function (say so — interpreting creatinine/eGFR is part of 'explain the results'). Four differential buckets, numbered, in plain English: (1) not enough in — restricted diet; (2) losing it through the bowel — vomiting, diarrhoea, laxatives (name tablets, powders, teas); (3) losing extra through the kidneys — a tablet like his, or 'a small gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone that dumps potassium' (primary aldosteronism: cramps, weakness, polyuria, resistant BP); (4) shift into cells — some asthma puffers, insulin, and 'a rare adrenaline-producing tumour' (phaeo triad: headache + sweating + palpitations, patients go pale, not flushed). Plan: repeat U&E to confirm, ECG today (arrhythmia is the consequence that matters 10 days from a GA), magnesium (thiazides waste Mg; low Mg makes K replacement ineffective), oral KCl supplement, review the antihypertensive for a potassium-sparing option, write to surgeon and anaesthetist, recheck in 3–7 days and again before theatre. The operation most likely proceeds — mild, asymptomatic; if it stays low a short delay is for anaesthetic safety. Never tell him to stop the antihypertensive himself. Hidden agenda: daughter's wedding in six weeks — ask an open concerns question early.

'Is that going to stop my operation?' → acknowledge, park explicitly, promise to return · ★ 'Was there anything else you were hoping to cover today?' (wedding) · permission for questions

'I'd like to repeat the test, do a heart tracing today, and check your magnesium.' / 'I'll write to your surgeon and speak to the anaesthetic team so everyone has the same information.'

I'll review it and there are options that control your pressure without stripping potassium; we'll change it properly, not suddenly.' / 'Come back straight away if you get marked weakness, palpitations or fainting.'
pefe: Role-player: Mark, 50, storeman at a rural hardware/grain depot on the Yorke Peninsula; hernia 8 months, reducible, never stuck; thiazide 6 y, dose doubled 4 weeks ago, adherent; no other meds/puffers/steroids/laxatives/herbals/liquorice; smokes 5/day cutting down, 6 drinks/weekend; meat and potatoes, banana most days; father HTN, mother stroke 70s. Pushes 'is this going to stop my operation?' at 1:30 and 4:00; tense at the word heart; hidden agenda — daughter's wedding in six weeks, walking her down the aisle (revealed if asked an open concerns question, else at ~7 min); 'should I just stop the tablet?' if you finish early

Examiner challenges: 'Why an ECG? he's asymptomatic' → 'the consequence I care about is arrhythmia, ten days from a GA; changes appear without symptoms; finding T–U fusion or ectopy changes my urgency and my discussion with the anaesthetist' · 'Why magnesium?' → 'hypomagnesaemia causes renal K wasting and makes replacement ineffective; thiazides waste both' · 'Normal K range?' → 'laboratory-dependent, commonly ~3.5–5.2; I'd use the report's range; 3.1 is mild on any' · ★ 'Does hypokalaemia raise aldosterone?' → 'No — wrong way round: potassium stimulates aldosterone, so low K suppresses it; excess aldosterone causes renal K wasting, not a shift into cells' CORRECTION

Variant B — K 2.5, BP 168/98 on two agents, calf cramps, heavy legs on stairs, nocturia ×3–4: primary aldosteronism — 'a small gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone called aldosterone, pushes BP up and potassium down; treatment is different — a particular tablet, sometimes surgery; there's a blood test (ARR — correct K first, adjust interfering antihypertensives VERIFY)'; ECG today; ★ talk to the surgical team about postponing — automatic fail if the plan is unchanged

Variant C — 34F, K 2.8, 'a herbal regularity tea most nights, that's not really a medicine': senna = laxative = real cause; how often, how long; 'some people use them to manage their weight or how they feel about their body — is any of that part of it? no judgement, I ask everyone'; no moralising; National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline (not NEDA) VERIFY current Australian service

Variant D — 68 on digoxin, K 3.2, off food, nauseated, 'the telly looks yellowish': ★ digoxin toxicity potentiated by hypokalaemia — ECG and digoxin level now, repeat UEC/K/Mg, seen today not next week; automatic fail if digoxin is on the list and you neither identify it nor escalate
SA: letter to surgeon and anaesthetist (regional hospital list); pre-anaesthetic clinic; TIS 131 450 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 (not needed here)
fails: Giving the diagnosis and stopping — no four differentials said aloud in patient language ★
No concrete plan for the operation ★
Telling him to stop his blood pressure tablet himself ★
Reassuring him before proposing a repeat test; 'it's definitely just the fluid tablet' ★
Explaining results for four minutes; skipping 'your kidneys are normal'
Asking 'what medications?' and stopping — never asking about the dose change; accepting 'no other medications' without naming laxatives, puffers, steroids, insulin
Asking about 'flushing' for phaeo; 'hyperaldosteronism' or 'transcellular shift' to the patient; 'the operation will be fine, don't worry'

Recheck U&E + Mg 3–7 days, again before theatre · timing: results 2 · history 4 · dx + DDx 2

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. No physical examination; no results provided. The examiner may ask what you would order. Six minutes of history, then explanation.
stem: James Whitfield, 45, warehouse supervisor, married with two children, not seen here for two years, no recorded chronic disease: 'I've been feeling very thirsty and I'm drinking far more water than usual.' Nurse observations: BP 128/78, HR 76 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98%, T 36.8, weight 84 kg, BMI 27; blood glucose not yet done.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain the most likely cause and the other conditions you considered
Answer his questions and outline the plan
time: 8 minutes. Elicit his worry in the first minute (diabetes — his dad) · ★ put a number on the litres · ★ 'passing more urine?' — say aloud that no polyuria lowers diabetes · six blocks: sugar · marrow · brain · thyroid · ★ drugs and SUPPLEMENTS · lifestyle · hypercalcaemia sweep · four-link explanation: vitamin D → calcium → kidneys → thirst · ★ 'I can't be certain until I check a calcium' · separate him from his mother · safety-net.

back.dx: Excessive vitamin D supplementation (4 × 1000 IU = 4000 IU/day for six weeks, started because his mother has osteoporosis with two fractures this year) → probable hypercalcaemia → polydipsia. Ten days of constant worsening thirst, 4–5 L/day up from 2, no polyuria, nocturnal drinking not voiding, bowels sluggish this last week; no weight loss, vision change, infections; no bone pain, fatigue, sweats, bruising; no headache/vision loss; no heat intolerance, loose bowels, palpitations, tremor; no stones, nausea; lifestyle unremarkable. Four-link chain in plain words: vitamin D helps you absorb calcium → too much pushes blood calcium up → high calcium makes the kidneys pass out more water → your body feels that as thirst; the word is hypercalcaemia. Differentials, each with why less likely: diabetes (no polyuria/weight loss; finger-prick today anyway), overactive thyroid, a brain problem with the water-balance hormone (DI), a bone-marrow condition that raises calcium (myeloma — asked bone pain, tiredness, infections), everyday causes (coffee, alcohol, salt, heat). Honest uncertainty: no blood test yet, so no declared 'vitamin D poisoning'. Plan: stop the capsules today, bring the bottle in, BSL now, bloods for calcium, UEC, 25-OH vitamin D, glucose, TSH; drink to thirst 2–3 L; review when results back, phone sooner if needed. Separate him from his mother: her dose was worked out for her bones and her blood test — his wasn't; do not change her treatment.
plan: WIPE, 'can I call you James?' · open · 'I can understand why that would be worrying you' · signpost groups · ★ 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' → diabetes, dad → 'I'll check your sugar before you leave either way'

Explore: duration 10 days, constant, worsening · ★ 'how much are you actually drinking — put a number on it' → 4–5 L, was 2 · better/worse (no) · night — drinking, not voiding · impact (bottle round the warehouse)

Sugar block, five questions: ★ passing more urine? (no) · hungrier? · weight loss? · blurred vision? · recurrent infections? · FHx → ★ say aloud: 'thirst without passing more urine makes diabetes a good deal less likely — I'll still check your sugar'

Marrow (bone/back pain worse at night/rest, fatigue, weight loss/sweats/infections, bruising/bleeding) · brain (morning headache, vomiting, vision) · thyroid (heat, bowels, palpitations, tremor) — four questions each, no more

★ Drugs in this order: 'regular medicines from a doctor?' (no) → 'anything you buy yourself — painkillers, herbal?' → ★ 'any vitamin D, or a multivitamin?' → 'just vitamin D, that's not really a medicine, is it?' → no change of tone: strength per capsule (1000), how many/day (4), how long (6 weeks), anything with calcium (no), ★ 'what made you start?' → mother's osteoporosis, two fractures this year → acknowledge, promise to return

Hypercalcaemia sweep: loin pain/stones, bone ache, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain/indigestion, ★ constipation (sluggish this week), mood/memory/concentration, weakness/drowsiness · lifestyle: smoking, alcohol, coffee, salt, exercise, hot workplace · PMHx, FHx

Move 1 summarise and check · Move 2 ★ the four-link chain, name 'hypercalcaemia' · Move 3 ★ 'I can't be certain until I check a calcium level' + differentials in plain English with why less likely · Move 4 ★ separate him from his mother

His questions ('I thought vitamins were safe' — stored in fat, builds up; 'have I damaged myself' — almost certainly not, bloods check the kidneys; 'should Mum stop hers' — no, her own GP; 'how long' — halves every 2–3 weeks) · plan · ★ safety-net unprompted: vomiting, bad tummy pain, bad constipation, weakness, confusion or unusual sleepiness → straight back/ED, 'you'd need a drip' · summarise, 'anything I haven't covered?'
ask: ★ 'Was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' (in the first minute)
★ 'How much are you actually drinking in a day — can you put a number on it, glasses or bottles?'
★ 'Are you passing more urine than usual?' → 'Thirst without passing more urine makes diabetes a good deal less likely, and I'll check your sugar with a finger-prick before you leave either way.'
'Any pain in your bones or your back — worse at night or at rest? Unusually tired? Weight loss, night sweats, infections you've struggled to shake? Easy bruising?' (myeloma, out loud, man over 40)

★ 'Any medicines from a doctor — and anything you buy yourself, vitamins or supplements?' / 'What does the bottle say — how many units per capsule, and how many a day? For how long? Anything with calcium in it?' / ★ 'What made you start taking it?'

★ 'Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium from your food. If you take more than you need, the calcium in your blood can drift up. High calcium makes your kidneys pass out more water, which dries you out — and what your body feels when it's drying out is thirst.'
★ 'I want to be straight with you — I can't be certain until I check a calcium level in your blood.'

★ 'Taking it because of your mum was a sensible instinct, not a silly one. The difference is that her dose was worked out for her bones and her blood test. Yours hasn't been.' / 'Please don't change your mum's treatment — that's a conversation for her own GP.'

'Am I going to end up like Mum?' → 'Osteoporosis isn't something you catch from your mother — family history is one risk among several. The right answer isn't extra vitamin D on spec; it's checking your own level, your other risks, and at the right age a bone density scan. Shall we book a longer appointment once this settles?'

★ 'Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you start being sick, get bad tummy pain or become badly constipated, feel weak, or if you or your wife notice you're confused or unusually sleepy.'
pefe: Role-player: James, 45, air-conditioned warehouse, wife Karen, two teenagers, non-smoker, 4–5 beers/week, 2 coffees, gym twice a week, no prescribed meds. Withholds the vitamin D: 'any medications?' → 'no, nothing from the doctor'; only 'things you buy yourself / vitamins / supplements' gets 'just vitamin D — that's not really a medicine, is it?' — then makes you ask strength and number separately. Fear: diabetes (dad T2DM). Hidden agenda: mum's osteoporosis, two fractures — if never asked, pushes at ~5 min 'is this going to happen to my bones like my mum?'. If blamed: 'I was only trying to look after myself', then flat single words. End question: 'should I tell Mum to stop hers?' — changing her treatment = fail

Investigations (if the examiner asks): BSL now; corrected calcium (albumin), UEC/eGFR, phosphate, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH (expect suppressed), glucose/HbA1c, TSH · corrected Ca = measured + 0.02 × (40 − albumin)

Variant B — genuine toxicity: 50 000 IU capsules DAILY for three months (label said weekly), morning nausea, constipation → 'around fifty times what most people need, for months — enough to make the calcium genuinely high; bloods TODAY not next week; stop everything with vitamin D or calcium now; if very high, or vomiting/confused → a drip in hospital for a day or two' · say the ED threshold out loud · remote: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

Variant C — 68, thirsty, worn out, 2 months of night-time mid-back ache, 5 kg loss, no supplements: 'a few conditions raise calcium; one is a condition of the bone marrow, and with your back pain and weight loss I don't want to leave that unchecked — it's on my list, not a diagnosis; this week: calcium, blood count, kidney function, specific protein tests (SPEP/free light chains), imaging of the back' — no 'wear and tear', no blunt 'cancer'

Variant D — corrected Ca 2.35 (normal): vitamin D is not the explanation; with normal glucose and true polydipsia 4–5 L → paired serum/urine osmolality for diabetes insipidus, TSH, UEC, K, drug review (lithium); dilute urine against raised serum osm → refer for water deprivation test; primary polydipsia last, diagnosis of exclusion; still advise a sensible dose but don't claim causation
SA: regional GP; pathology courier timing for same-day bloods; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval; TIS 131 450
fails: Never asking about vitamins or supplements — 'any medications?' → 'no' → station unpassable ★
Never asking whether he is passing more urine ★
No bone pain / weight loss / infection screen in a man over forty ★
Declaring vitamin D toxicity as established fact with no blood test ★
Ending without a named safety-net and a definite review ★
Leaving his worry to the last thirty seconds; accepting 'more than usual' without litres; spending three minutes on diabetes because of the family history
Reacting with alarm at the vitamin D, or hearing it and abandoning the rest of the history; implying he's been foolish; changing his mother's treatment
numbers: Thirst 10 days · 4–5 L/day (was 2) · vitamin D 4 × 1000 IU = 4000 IU/day × 6 weeks · half-life 2–3 weeks

25(OH)D: sufficient ≥50 nmol/L · insufficient 30–49 · moderate deficiency 12.5–29 · severe <12.5 · toxicity generally >10 000 IU/day sustained or 25(OH)D >250 · deficiency Rx 1000–2000 IU/day mild; 3000–5000 IU/day 6–12 weeks moderate–severe
Calcium normal 2.10–2.60 · corrected = measured + 0.02 × (40 − albumin) · mild <3.00 · moderate 3.00–3.40 · severe >3.40 or symptomatic → ED · oral fluids 2–3 L; IV 0.9% NaCl if severe
Timing: worry asked <0:45 · supplement question reached by 4:15 · history stops at 6:00

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Results-discussion station; the examiner interrupts to hand you further results after your investigation list.
stem: Ms Janine Whitfield, 45, teacher's aide, attends to discuss blood tests taken at a routine check-up two weeks ago. Hypothyroidism for eight years on levothyroxine 100 µg daily; no other regular medicines on file; non-smoker; she has no complaint and feels perfectly well. Results: TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0), free T4 14 (10–20), albumin 31 g/L (low, 35–50), total calcium 2.56 (normal, 2.10–2.60), corrected calcium 2.78 — HIGH.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Explain the blood results you already have, in plain language
Tell the examiner the further investigations you would request, in order of priority
The examiner will give you those results. Explain your diagnosis and your reasoning to the patient, including the differentials you considered
time: 8 minutes after 2 reading: history 4 · explain current results 1 · investigations 1 · diagnosis + differentials 2. Write 'corrected 2.78 · albumin low · TSH normal · PTH first' and the seven history headings before you speak. Name the abnormal result early and size it · why the test, ever told before · ≥5 hypercalcaemia symptoms · ★ full malignancy screen · supplements, antacids, thiazide/lithium by use, TB/sarcoid, phaeo, thyroid · ICE before explaining · ★ corrected not total · ★ PTH first WITH a reason · four glands, one overworking · not cancer · ≥4 differentials · plan, referral, safety-net, summary.

back.dx: Primary hyperparathyroidism (single adenoma ~85%) — PTH elevated with corrected calcium 2.78, vitamin D normal, phosphate low-normal, eGFR 88, examination normal. Total calcium 2.56 reads 'normal' only because albumin is 31: corrected = 2.56 + 0.02 × (40 − 31) = 2.74 ≈ 2.78 per report — a station-ending false reassurance if you read the total line. Calcium was 'high last year'; she was told to stop her multivitamin and cut dairy — chronicity makes malignancy less likely but does not exclude it, and diet was never the driver (correct the science kindly without attacking the colleague). Only positive symptom: 'a bit more thirsty, I keep a bottle on my desk'. Malignancy screen clean (weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, breast/mammogram clear last year, cough, smoking, haematuria); mother had breast cancer at 60 — the hidden agenda; ask ICE before you explain. Investigations ranked with BECAUSE: 1 serum PTH (commonest cause; the one test that splits the differential in two) · 2 25-OH vitamin D with phosphate (read as a set; low phosphate supports PTH) · 3 UEC/eGFR (renal function, hypercalcaemic nephropathy) · then CXR (lung Ca, TB, sarcoid), FBE/ESR/SPEP + free light chains (myeloma, lymphoma), 24-h urine calcium (exclude FHH before any surgery), full examination incl. breasts and nodes. Explain: four tiny glands behind the thyroid, different job — keep blood calcium right; one is overworking, pulling calcium from bone; the hormone is raised, which confirms it; not cancer, not the thyroid tablets, not diet. Differentials named: cancers (blood, breast, lung, kidney), vitamin D/calcium antacid excess, fluid tablets, lithium, overactive thyroid (excluded), sarcoid/TB. Refer endocrinology (age <50 → surgery will be discussed, their decision with her); hydrate; do not restrict dairy; safety-net.
plan: WIPE, identity · open question · ★ 'I can see one of the numbers, your calcium, is a little higher than we'd like. It's not an emergency, but it does need explaining. Would it be alright if I asked you some questions first?'

'What made you have the test?' · ★ 'Has anyone ever told you before that your calcium was high?' → yes, last year; multivitamin stopped, dairy cut, nothing else done · 'any further tests or treatment?'

Symptoms ≥5: nausea/vomiting · abdominal pain/constipation · bone/back pain · weakness/tiredness · thirst/polyuria/nocturia (→ 'a bit more thirsty') · stones/loin pain · mood/memory/concentration — 'these cover both the symptoms and the commonest cause'

★ Malignancy screen, full, 'questions I ask everybody with this result': weight, appetite, lumps (neck/axilla/groin), night sweats, breast lump/discharge/mammogram, cough/haemoptysis/smoking, haematuria, cancer in you or family (mother, breast, 60) · 'why are you asking all this?' → stop, turn, explain honestly

Supplements: vitamin D, multivitamin, calcium — dose, duration · antacids (Gaviscon monthly) · health-food products · prescription by USE: 'anything for blood pressure or fluid, or any tablet for your mood' · SOB/chest pain/fevers/TB contact · joint pain/rash/shin lumps · headache-sweating-flushing-palpitations, endocrine FHx · thyroid duration/adherence/tremor/heat · alcohol, smoking, PMHx · ★ ICE: 'anything worrying you about these results?' → mother's cancer

★ Explain: TSH and T4 normal → thyroxine dose right · 'calcium travels two ways — free, and carried by a protein called albumin; your albumin is a bit low so the raw number looks normal; adjusted for the protein the true level is 2.78, we'd want it under 2.60 — genuinely high, mildly' · 'calcium isn't controlled by what you eat; a hormone controls it — the question is which part of that system is out' · 'so the dairy was pointless?' → reasonable first step, but not the fix

★ To the examiner, ranked with reasons: 1 PTH because… 2 25-OH vitamin D + phosphate because… 3 UEC/eGFR because… then CXR; FBE, ESR, SPEP + FLC; 24-h urine calcium; full examination incl. breasts and nodes → PTH elevated, vit D normal, PO4 low-normal, eGFR 88, examination normal

★ 'Behind your thyroid sit four tiny glands called the parathyroid glands — different glands, different job. One appears to be overworking… today's test shows that hormone is raised, which confirms it. It's called primary hyperparathyroidism. It is not a cancer, and it is not caused by your thyroid tablets or by what you eat.' · 'is it my thyroid tablets?' answered

Differentials aloud: cancer (blood, breast, lung, kidney — why I asked, CXR and bloods still) · vitamin D/antacid excess · fluid tablets, lithium · overactive thyroid (excluded) · sarcoid/TB (other reason for CXR) · plan: endocrine referral, surgery discussed because of her age — their decision; drink plenty of water; don't cut dairy · ★ safety-net: very thirsty + lots of urine, vomiting, drowsy/confused, severe abdominal/back/loin pain → same day · review ~1 week · summarise, offer to write it down
ask: ★ 'I can see one of the numbers, your calcium, is a little higher than we'd like. It's not an emergency, but it does need explaining. Would it be alright if I asked you some questions first, so I can work out why?'
★ 'Has anyone ever told you before that your calcium was high?' / 'Did anyone do any further tests, or start any treatment for it?'

★ 'I'm going to ask some questions I ask everybody with this result, just to be thorough.' → weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats, breast/mammogram, cough/blood, smoking, urine blood, cancer in you or your family

'Why are you asking all this?' → 'A high calcium has several possible causes. Most are not serious, and the commonest by far is a small gland problem. But a few cancers can also raise calcium, so I check for them in everybody — not because I suspect it in you. Nothing you've told me so far points that way.'

'Apart from the thyroid tablet, any other regular medicine — anything for blood pressure or fluid, or any tablet for your mood?' (thiazide, lithium by use) / 'Any vitamin D, multivitamins or calcium tablets? Anything for indigestion — antacid tablets or liquid?'

★ 'Calcium travels in the blood two ways — some floats free, some is carried by a protein called albumin. Your albumin is low, so the raw number looks normal; once we adjust for it, the true level is high.' / 'Calcium isn't really controlled by what you eat — your body controls it with a hormone.'

★ 'My first priority is serum parathyroid hormone, because primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the community and PTH is the single test that splits the differential in two.' / 'Calcium, phosphate and vitamin D are read as a set.'

★ 'Behind your thyroid gland sit four tiny glands called the parathyroid glands — different glands, different job. Their only job is keeping your blood calcium right. One of them appears to be overworking, and that pulls extra calcium out of your bones into your blood.' / ★ 'It is not a cancer, and it is not caused by your thyroid tablets or by what you eat.'

'Is it cancer?' → 'On everything I have so far, no. Your hormone result points to a gland problem, not a cancer. I'm still completing a chest x-ray and a couple of blood tests so that I'm certain rather than nearly certain.' / 'Should I stop dairy?' → 'No — diet isn't the driver, and cutting calcium hard can be bad for your bones. Drink plenty of water.' / 'Will I need an operation?' → 'Possibly — the only definitive treatment, but not everyone needs one; because you're forty-five the specialist will talk it through seriously.'

★ 'If you become very thirsty and pass a lot of urine, start vomiting, feel drowsy or confused, or get severe tummy, back or loin pain, I want you seen the same day.' / 'To summarise — is there anything I've missed, or anything you'd like me to write down?'
pefe: Role-player: Janine, 45, teacher's aide 4 days/week, husband, two teenagers, 40-min drive; levothyroxine 100 µg, never misses; stopped multivitamin last year on advice; Gaviscon ~monthly; no BP/fluid/mood tablets; never smoked, 2 wines Friday; mammogram last year clear; mother breast cancer at 60, alive. Only positive: 'a bit more thirsty, I keep a bottle on my desk' — given only if asked. Brisk, impatient at first; guarded during cancer questions; after the breast question asks 'why are you asking all this?' every time; if you read the total calcium as normal: 'so there's nothing wrong then?'; asks 'is it my thyroid tablets?' and 'will I need an operation?'; if falsely reassured before tests: 'how can you be sure?'. Hidden agenda released on ICE, else volunteered at ~7 min as you summarise

Examiner returns: PTH elevated · 25-OH vitamin D normal · phosphate low-normal · eGFR 88 · full examination normal · everything else normal. Examiner challenges: 'Why not image the parathyroids?' → 'the diagnosis is biochemical; sestamibi/ultrasound are for the surgeon to localise, not to diagnose' · 'Avoid dairy?' → 'no; severe restriction can worsen bone loss; hydration matters more' · 'Frusemide?' → 'only for overload during rehydration; not a routine calcium-lowering treatment'

Version B — high-dose health-food vitamin D for 8 months + calcium antacids most nights: examiner gives PTH suppressed <1.0, 25-OH D 310, eGFR 74, PO4 normal → 'a low parathyroid hormone tells me the gland is behaving and being switched off — the extra calcium is coming from somewhere else; your vitamin D is ~4× target — the supplement, probably with the antacids (milk–alkali)' → stop both today, hydrate, recheck 2–4 weeks; ★ suppressed PTH is the MALIGNANCY arm — still complete CXR and bloods · corrected Ca 2.88

Variant C — 62, corrected Ca 3.15, 6 kg loss since Christmas, night-waking low back ache, worn out; Hb 96, creatinine 148, PTH suppressed, ESR 88 → 'myeloma until proved otherwise': SPEP, serum FLC, urine Bence-Jones, film, LDH, whole-body low-dose CT or MRI spine (not plain films); IV normal saline now; urgent haematology; ★ ask about cord compression (numbness, leg weakness, bladder/bowel) — same-day emergency; warning-shot register, 'today rather than next week'

Variant D — 58 on indapamide + lithium, corrected 2.72, asymptomatic: switch the thiazide to another antihypertensive, recheck 2–4 weeks; ★ do NOT stop lithium unilaterally — speak with the psychiatrist, decide together; check PTH (lithium can make the glands overactive) · Variant E — 28M, Ca 2.70 pre-employment, father and sister 'high calcium', PTH mildly raised: FHH — 24-h urine calcium and Ca:Cr clearance ratio (<0.01 supports), CaSR gene testing; these patients are harmed by parathyroid surgery
SA: endocrinology referral (RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin); PATS for travel; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 only if a Version B/C patient needs retrieval; TIS 131 450
fails: Saying 'your calcium is actually normal' because you read the total line ★
PTH not first in the investigation list, or a flat list with no BECAUSE ★
Never asking a single cancer question; abandoning the malignancy screen because it was 'high last year' ★
Falsely reassuring ('it's definitely nothing') before any tests; or finishing on the diagnosis with no differentials, plan or safety-net ★
Jargon: 'PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia secondary to a parathyroid adenoma'
Endorsing the dairy restriction to avoid contradicting a colleague; asking 'any other medications?' and accepting 'no' without naming thiazide and lithium by use
Skipping ICE so the mother's cancer lands at minute seven; stopping the supplement in Version B and declaring the case closed; stopping lithium unilaterally in Variant D
numbers: Corrected Ca = total + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L) · here total 2.56, albumin 31, corrected 2.78 · reference 2.10–2.60 · mild <3.0 · moderate 3.0–3.5 · severe >3.5
Top three: PTH · 25-OH vitamin D + phosphate · UEC/eGFR · causes 1 and 2: hyperparathyroidism, then malignancy · adenoma ~85% of primary disease
Surgery triggers: age <50 · Ca >0.25 above upper limit · eGFR <60 · urine Ca >10 mmol/day · stones · T-score ≤−2.5 · FHH: Ca:Cr clearance ratio <0.01 · ECG: short QT
Severe: saline 4–6 L/24 h · zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over ≥15 min after rehydration · calcitonin 4 units/kg SC/IM 12-hourly · prednisolone 20–40 mg/day if vitamin D–mediated VERIFY

Timing: 0:00 WIPE/name it · 0:30 why/before · 1:00 symptoms · 1:45 malignancy · 2:45 drugs etc + ICE · 4:15 explain · 5:15 ranked ix · 6:15 dx/DDx/plan · cut the thyroid block, never the malignancy block · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
