setting: Suburban general practice; you are the GP. Vitals (including BSL) on request. 9-minute station. RECALL NOTE: the source recording verifies the stem and history; later tasks follow the standard three-task shape.
stem: Marianne Kovac, 50, presents with two days of nausea and vomiting on a week of feeling weak, tired and lethargic. She is holding a vomit bag. Known hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Current medications: perindopril 5 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the examination findings and investigations you want
Explain the most likely diagnosis and outline your immediate management
time: 9 minutes: 40 s opening · 4 min history · 1.5 min examination/investigations · 2 min explanation · 45 s safety-net and close. The diagnosis is on the medication list — the marks are for what you ask AFTER you've worked it out: ★ obs incl. BSL · acknowledge the bag, offer water · vomit content · ★ 'when did you start the PAINKILLER, who started it' + OTC/chemist separately · ★ cardiac screen unprompted · abdomen/melaena · ★ urine output, uraemic symptoms · fluid status FIRST · investigations by analyte incl. ECG and troponin · ★ diagnosis by name · triple whammy in plain English · stop, hold, ★ transfer today, no driving · teach-back.

back.dx: Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (stage 2 — eGFR 45 → 22, creatinine roughly doubled) with hyperkalaemia (K 6.3 + peaked T waves, narrow QRS → treat as severe) and metabolic acidosis (HCO3 18) — the 'triple whammy': NSAID (constricts the afferent arteriole) + ACE inhibitor (dilates the efferent) + thiazide (lowers circulating volume), in a woman with baseline CKD. Ibuprofen 400 mg tds for three weeks for a knee — self-bought at the chemist, then scripted by a locum who didn't have her record; she doesn't call it a medication. Uraemic symptoms: much less urine, postural dizziness, metallic taste; examination — dry mucosa, postural drop 20 systolic, JVP not visible, abdomen soft, no bladder, no asterixis. BSL 5.4 removes DKA at the door; troponin normal and cardiac screen negative (nausea + lethargy without chest pain is a recognised MI presentation in women and CKD). Explain: 'your kidneys were working at about half strength and have taken a sudden extra hit — an acute injury on chronic kidney disease; waste products build up and cause the sickness and exhaustion'; mechanism of the three drugs in plain words; 'you can buy it anywhere' → 'that's exactly why it catches people out'. Plan: ibuprofen stops today and never again without checking; hold (not stop forever) perindopril and the thiazide while unwell; ★ ED today for fluids and potassium treatment — ring ahead, results with her, don't drive; repeat UEC 48–72 h; paracetamol + physiotherapy for the knee; letter to usual GP, flag on file. Hidden agenda: mother died on dialysis — 'not today, and in most cases like yours this is reversible once we take the pressure off'.
plan: ★ 'Examiner — BP, pulse, RR, saturations, temperature AND blood sugar?' → 142/86, 72 reg, 16, 98%, afebrile, BSL 5.4 → 'stable, afebrile, normal sugar — a diabetic emergency is unlikely from the outset'
WIPE, 'how would you like me to address you?' · open · ★ 'I'm sorry — that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first?' (the vomit bag is marked)

Symptom package in one block: onset (tiredness 1 week, vomiting 2 days), worse, better/worse · 'tired — low energy, sleepy, or breathless?' · frequency 4–5/day · ★ 'what does the vomit look like — any blood, or anything green?' (UGI bleed vs obstruction; she's on an NSAID) · keeping anything down?

Background: when diagnosed CKD (5 y, 'about half') and HTN (10 y), what for them → perindopril + 'a fluid tablet' · adherence · ★ 'and when did you start the PAINKILLER — who started it, and what was it for?' → ibuprofen ~3 weeks, knee, self-bought then locum script · ★ 'did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?' → 'it's only ibuprofen' (don't correct now; save it) · 'anything from the chemist, or herbal?'

★ Cardiac screen, unprompted, 10 s: 'a few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious — chest/arm/jaw/back discomfort, exertional SOB, cold sweats (clammy yesterday), palpitations, blackouts'
Abdomen: pain/where, bowels, ★ black/tarry stools, fevers, jaundice · ★ urine output 'more, less or the same?' → much less · dizzy standing (yes) · confusion, hiccups, itch, ★ metallic taste (yes)

★ Examination — fluid status FIRST: postural BP, mucosa, JVP, cap refill; abdomen (tenderness, guarding, organomegaly, palpable bladder); cardiorespiratory; pallor, pigmentation, oedema, asterixis → dry, postural drop 20, JVP not seen, soft abdomen, no bladder, no asterixis

★ Investigations by name: ECG now (hyperkalaemia AND ischaemia) · UEC/eGFR vs baseline — specifically K, Na, bicarbonate · VBG · troponin · FBE, Ca, PO4, Mg, LFT, lipase, urinalysis → eGFR 22 (baseline 45), creatinine ×2, K 6.3, HCO3 18, troponin normal, peaked T narrow QRS · 'why a troponin with no chest pain?' answered · read back: stage 2 AKI on CKD; K moderate by number, severe by ECG; acidosis shifts K out of cells

★ Diagnosis by name · 'will I need dialysis? my mother died on dialysis' → pause, acknowledge, honest answer · mechanism: three medicines, three directions — painkiller narrows the vessel in, perindopril widens the vessel out, fluid tablet lowers the circulating volume — 'the triple whammy' · 'you can buy it anywhere' → exactly why it catches people out · 'the locum's fault?' → missing record, not the person; letter to usual GP

Plan: 1 ibuprofen stops today, never that class without checking · 2 hold perindopril and the fluid tablet — temporary, don't stop anything else alone · 3 ★ ED today (K affects the heart's rhythm; can't keep fluids down) — ring ahead, results with her · ★ don't drive · red flags en route: chest pain, palpitations, faint, weak muscles → ambulance · repeat UEC 2–3 days · paracetamol + physio for the knee · ★ teach-back · 'anything still worrying you?'
ask: ★ 'Could I have her observations — including a blood sugar?' / 'I'm sorry, that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first?'
'When you say tired — low in energy, sleepy, or breathless when you move about?' / ★ 'What does the vomit look like — any blood, or anything green?'
★ 'When did you start the painkiller, and who started it for you?' / 'Anything from the chemist, or anything herbal?' / 'Did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?'
★ 'A few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious. Any discomfort or tightness in the chest, arm, jaw or back?'
★ 'How much urine have you passed in the last day — more, less, or the same?' / 'Any confusion, hiccups, itch or a metallic taste?'

★ 'I'd like her fluid status first — postural blood pressure, mucous membranes, JVP and capillary refill.' / 'Why a troponin with no chest pain?' → 'Because nausea and lethargy without chest pain is a recognised presentation of infarction in women and in chronic kidney disease.'
★ 'Her eGFR has halved from 45 to 22, which meets criteria for a stage 2 acute kidney injury.' / ★ 'The potassium is 6.3, and with ECG changes I treat that as severe regardless of the number.'

★ 'Your kidneys have taken a sudden extra hit on top of the long-standing damage — an acute kidney injury on top of chronic kidney disease.' / 'Will I need dialysis?' → 'Not today, and in most cases like yours this is reversible once we take the pressure off — that's exactly why we're acting now.'

★ 'Each of these medicines is sensible on its own. Together, with kidneys like yours, they're too much — in Australia we call it the triple whammy.' / 'But it's only ibuprofen — you can buy it anywhere' → 'You can — and that's exactly why it catches people out. Being sold without a prescription doesn't make it harmless for your kidneys.'

★ 'The painkiller stops today. The other two we hold while you're unwell — that's temporary.' / ★ 'I'm sending you to the emergency department today. Please don't drive.' / 'Could you tell me back what you'll say when you get to the hospital?'
pefe: Role-player: Marianne, 50, school administrator, husband, two grown children; HTN 10 y, CKD 5 y ('about half'), never dialysed; perindopril + 'a fluid tablet' never missed; ibuprofen 400 mg tds ~3 weeks for right knee (self-bought, then locum script; usual GP on leave) — not thought of as a medication; never smoked, wine most weekends; mother died on dialysis. 'What medications?' → 'perindopril and a fluid tablet' and STOP; ibuprofen only for 'painkillers', 'from the chemist', 'over the counter'. Slow, flat, retching; withdraws if not offered water; defensive once 'it's only ibuprofen'; 'is this the locum's fault?'; pushes back once on hospital 'can't I stop the tablets and come back Friday?' — agrees only if you hold firm with a reason; 'sorry — what does that mean?' at jargon; hidden agenda dialysis/mother in the last two minutes unless asked

Examiner returns: BP 142/86, PR 72, RR 16, SpO2 98, T 36.6, BSL 5.4 · dry mucosa, postural drop 20 systolic, JVP not visible, abdomen soft non-tender, no palpable bladder, HS dual, chest clear, no pallor/oedema/asterixis · eGFR 22 (baseline 45), creatinine ~×2, K 6.3, HCO3 18, troponin normal, ECG peaked T narrow QRS

Variant A — prevention: visiting gout patient on perindopril + a fluid tablet demands indomethacin → 'I can treat that today — before I write anything, what else are you on, any kidney trouble? …an anti-inflammatory is the one thing I don't want to give you: those three together can shut the kidneys down within days' → colchicine or short prednisolone, check UEC while here VERIFY TG gout dosing/renal cautions

Variant B — ECG: ST elevation II, III, aVF → 'inferior STEMI presenting as nausea and lethargy without chest pain — ambulance now, aspirin 300 mg chewed, IV access, activate the acute coronary pathway; the renal picture is real but no longer the priority' ★ continuing the triple-whammy talk = automatic fail

Variant C — coffee-ground vomit + black sticky stools: NSAID upper GI bleed contributing to the AKI → ambulance now, bloods, fluids, PPI, endoscopy · Variant D — refuses (daughter's wedding Saturday): honest risk statement, 'I'd be failing you if I sent you home; may only be hours on a drip'; if still declines: document discussion and specific risks, confirm capacity, written red flags, same-day repeat bloods, defined review, can change her mind any time — never simply agree
SA: ED (nearest regional/metropolitan); MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval; PATS; TIS 131 450; recheck UEC 48–72 h after stopping, 1–2 weeks after restarting an ACE-i
fails: Asking only 'what medications are you on?' — walking past the ibuprofen ★
No cardiac screen without being prompted ★
'High potassium' as the diagnosis instead of AKI on CKD; not explaining the three-drug combination in her words ★
Sending her home to 'come back Friday' with K 6.3 and ECG changes; letting her drive ★
Continuing to discuss the triple whammy after an ischaemic ECG (Variant B) ★
Ignoring the vomit bag; asking only how many times, never what the vomit looked like; never asking about urine output or black stools
'Renal function tests' with no analyte; stopping perindopril and the thiazide forever rather than holding; blaming the locum; deflecting the dialysis fear; no alternative for the knee; no teach-back
numbers: Triple whammy = diuretic + NSAID + ACE-i/ARB · here eGFR 45 → 22 · creatinine ~×2 · K 6.3 · HCO3 18 · troponin normal · peaked T, narrow QRS
AKI staging: stage 1 creatinine ×1.5 · stage 2 ×2 · stage 3 ×3 or dialysis VERIFY against current KDIGO wording · K mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe ≥6.5 · any ECG change = severe
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–5 min · insulin–dextrose 10 units in 50 mL 50% glucose over 15–30 min, onset ~15 min, 4–6 h, BSL hourly × 6 h · salbutamol 10–20 mg neb
Recheck UEC 48–72 h after stopping the drugs · 1–2 weeks after restarting an ACE-i · aldosterone rule: hypoaldosteronism → high K; hyperaldosteronism → low K
Timing: 40 s · 4 min · 1.5 min · 2 min · 45 s (9-minute station) · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: General practice in Kadina, regional South Australia; you are the GP registrar. A results card is handed to you. Expect a prompt at 5 minutes covering tasks 1 and 2.
stem: Mr Colin Whitfield, 58, semi-retired farm contractor, returns for the results of blood tests taken a fortnight ago when he attended feeling tired. Hypothyroidism for six years on levothyroxine 100 µg daily; no other regular medication recorded. BP 138/82, HR 76 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98%, T 36.7; he looks well. Results: TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0), free T4 15 (10–20), total calcium 2.58 (2.15–2.60), albumin 28 (low), corrected calcium 2.82 (HIGH), phosphate 0.68 (low, 0.75–1.50), creatinine 88/eGFR >60, FBE and LFT normal, PTH sent — result not yet available.
tasks: Explain these blood results in language he can understand
Take a focused, relevant history
Give your most likely diagnosis and your differentials
Explain what happens next
time: 8 minutes: results 90 s MAXIMUM (signpost → thyroid in one breath → ★ calcium in four sentences: straight reading normal, stuck to a protein, protein low, corrected is high → check understanding → permission) · history 3½ min in seven blocks: tiredness · ★ stones · bones · groans · moans · ★ cancer · drugs incl. OTC · family/alcohol · ★ ICE before the diagnosis · transition line · four glands, one overactive, usually benign, 'I'm not going to promise you that today' · ★ say the word PTH and what high and low each mean · rest of workup, referral, PATS · fluids, don't cut dairy, avoid diuretics/supplements · safety-net · summary · 'have I missed anything?'

back.dx: Primary hyperparathyroidism with end-organ disease — corrected calcium 2.82 (total 2.58 + 0.02 × (40 − 28)), phosphate 0.68 low (PTH wastes phosphate — read the whole panel), TSH/T4 normal (dose right, no change), FBE/LFT normal; PTH pending — 'I've already sent that sample, so we won't lose any time'. History: six months of tiredness; ★ renal colic three years ago (overnight at Wallaroo) + nocturia ×2 + thirst; hip ache ('forty years on tractors'); constipation new this year; 'I've been flat' — name low mood as part of the illness, not a weakness; malignancy block clean (weight steady, never smoked, no sweats/lumps/cough); thyroxine only, 'doesn't hold with vitamins'; no FHx of calcium/stones/neck surgery (FHH, MEN 1); beers Friday, more at harvest (explains the low albumin); diet plenty of milk and cheese. Hidden agenda: brother Wayne died of bowel cancer at 55 last year — ask ICE before you explain, then build the explanation around it. Explain: one of four small neck glands behind the thyroid, different job, slightly overactive, pushing calcium out of bone — fits the stone, constipation, thirst, feeling flat; usually benign and treatable; honest middle — 'a couple of other things can raise calcium, one is a cancer somewhere else, which I know you've worried about since your brother'; what makes it less likely: weight steady, never smoked, normal FBE/LFT, no bone pain or lumps. ★ PTH: high → the gland, common, treatable; low → calcium from somewhere else → CXR and further bloods. Workup: vitamin D, magnesium, renal function, 24-h urine calcium, DXA, renal ultrasound (stone history); PTH confirms → endocrinology in Adelaide, PATS via the practice nurse; neck scan only to plan surgery, not to diagnose; some need the gland out, some are watched — decided with the specialist on calcium, kidneys, bone scan. Meanwhile 2–3 L fluids, more in the heat; don't cut dairy; avoid fluid tablets and calcium/vitamin D supplements; safety-net; ring him with the PTH; review two weeks.
plan: WIPE, DOB · ★ signpost: 'Most of them are reassuring, but there is one I want to go through properly with you — and then I'll need to ask you some questions. Is that alright?' · 'the wife reckoned you'd only get me back in if something was up' → one sentence of acknowledgement, then proceed

Thyroid in one breath: 'the TSH tells us whether you're on the right dose — normal, well controlled, T4 normal too, no change to your thyroxine' · 'what's TSH stand for?' → do not take the invitation; one line and move

★ Calcium in four sentences: 'we measured a mineral called calcium; the straight reading came back normal — but it isn't reliable on its own, because a large part of the calcium is stuck to a protein, and your protein is low, so the reading understates it; we do a calculation that corrects for the protein — and once we do, your calcium is high' · 'so is it normal or isn't it?' → 'the corrected number is the one we go on' · ★ 'is that making sense so far?' · 'not an emergency, you look well, but it needs explaining — may I ask some questions?'

Tiredness — two sentences, not two minutes (6 months, done by lunchtime) · ★ stones: 'ever passed a kidney stone, severe back/side pain?' (3 y ago, Wallaroo) · 'passing more urine, up at night?' (×2, thirsty) · bones: aches, fragility fracture, height loss (hips) · groans: constipation (new this year), indigestion/ulcer, nausea/vomiting · moans: mood, memory, concentration, sleep ('flat') → 'that can be part of this picture — not you being difficult'

★ Cancer block: 'questions I ask everyone with a high calcium' — weight, night sweats/fevers/lumps, cough/haemoptysis, smoking → all clean · drugs incl. OTC: fluid tablets, lithium, calcium/vitamin D, antacids, vitamin A/multivitamins → thyroxine only · FHx: high calcium, stones, parathyroid/neck operation, pituitary/pancreas tumour → no · alcohol (Friday beers, more at harvest) · home/work

★ ICE before the diagnosis: 'what did you think might be causing the tiredness? anything you've been particularly worried about?' → brother, bowel cancer, 55 → 'I'm sorry about your brother — and I'm glad you told me, because it changes how I explain the next bit' · ★ transition line: 'I've got what I need. Let me tell you what I think is going on and what I'd like to do about it'

Diagnosis: 'one of four small glands in your neck — the parathyroid glands, behind your thyroid but a completely different job — has become slightly overactive and is pushing calcium out of your bones into your blood; that fits the kidney stone, the constipation, the thirst and feeling flat; usually a benign growth, not a cancer, treatable' · 'but you can't be sure' → ★ 'not today, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise' — the honest middle; why cancer is less likely (weight, never smoked, FBE/LFT normal, no bone pain/lumps); 'I want to prove it rather than assume it'

★ 'There is one blood test that separates those two possibilities, and it's called PTH. If it's high, it's the gland — common and treatable. If it's low, the calcium is coming from somewhere else and I'd look for a cause in the chest and the bones with a chest x-ray and further blood tests. I've already sent that sample' · alongside: vitamin D, magnesium, kidney function, 24-h urine calcium, bone density scan, renal ultrasound (stone) · PTH confirms → endocrinologist in Adelaide, PATS via the practice nurse · 'an operation?' → some do, some are watched; decided with the specialist on calcium, kidneys, bones; neck scan is for surgical planning, not diagnosis

Meanwhile: 2–3 L/day, more in the heat on the property · ★ 'don't cut down on dairy — people assume they should and it makes it worse' · avoid fluid tablets, no calcium/vitamin D supplement without checking · ★ safety-net: very thirsty, vomiting, confused/drowsy, passing much more urine → straight back or ED · 'I'll ring you myself when the PTH is back; see you in two weeks either way' · summary · ★ 'have I missed anything you wanted to ask?'
ask: ★ 'Most of them are reassuring, but there is one I want to go through properly with you.' / 'The main test we look at is the TSH — that tells us whether you're on the right dose. Yours is normal, which means your thyroid is well controlled on your current tablet.'

★ 'We also measured a mineral in your blood called calcium. The straight calcium level came back in the normal range — but that measurement isn't reliable on its own, because a large part of the calcium in your blood is stuck to a protein, and if that protein is low, as yours is, the reading comes out falsely low. So we do a calculation that corrects for the protein — and once we do that, your calcium is high.'

'Hang on — so is it normal or isn't it?' → 'The first number is normal. The corrected number — the one that actually reflects what's in your body — is high. It's the corrected one we go on.' / ★ 'Is that making sense so far?' / 'Is it alright if I ask you some questions to work out which cause it is?'
★ 'Have you ever passed a kidney stone, or had severe pain in the back or side? Any passing more urine than usual, or getting up at night to go?'
'How has your mood been? Any trouble with memory or concentration?' → 'Thank you for telling me — that can be part of this picture, and it's not you being difficult.'

★ 'Now some questions I ask everyone with a high calcium. Has your weight changed without trying? Any night sweats, fevers or lumps? Any cough, or coughing blood? Do you or did you smoke?' / 'What tablets are you on, including anything over the counter — fluid tablets, lithium, calcium or vitamin D, indigestion powders?'

★ 'What did you think might be causing the tiredness? Is there anything you're especially worried about?' (before the diagnosis) / 'I've got what I need. Let me tell you what I think is going on and what I'd like to do about it.'

★ 'One of four small glands in your neck — the parathyroid glands, which sit behind your thyroid but do a completely different job — has become slightly overactive, and it's pushing calcium out of your bones into your blood.' / ★ 'It is usually a benign growth, and it is treatable — but I'm not going to promise you that today, because a couple of other things can raise calcium, and one of those is a cancer somewhere else, which I know is what you've been worrying about since your brother.'

★ 'There is one blood test that separates those two possibilities, and it's called PTH — the hormone those neck glands make. If it's high, it's the gland. If it's low, the calcium is coming from somewhere else and I'd look for a cause in the chest and the bones.' / 'Would I need an operation?' → 'Some people do and some are safely watched with regular blood tests. That decision depends on your calcium, your kidneys and your bone scan, and it's made with the specialist.'

★ 'Keep your fluids up — two to three litres a day, more on hot days out on the property — and don't cut down on dairy; people assume they should and it actually makes it worse.' / ★ 'If you become very thirsty, start vomiting, get confused or drowsy, or you're passing much more urine, don't wait for the appointment — come straight back or go to the emergency department.' / 'I'll ring you myself when the result is back. Have I missed anything you wanted to ask?'
pefe: Role-player: Colin, 58, property 20 min outside Kadina, wife Denise, two adult children in Adelaide; seeding/harvest for three neighbours; understated, dry, minimising, watches your face. Levothyroxine only, no supplements ('don't hold with vitamins'), never smoked, 4–5 beers Friday/more at harvest, plenty of milk and cheese. Father MI at 70, mother 84 arthritis, brother Wayne died at 55 of bowel cancer last year. Does not hand over the stone unless asked about stones/urine; constipation only if asked about bowels. Pushes 'so is it normal or isn't it?' once; asks 'is it dangerous?', 'would I need an operation?'; if you lecture physiology: 'you've lost me'; if you use 'cancer' without warning: two-second silence; ★ if you say his calcium is normal he thanks you and stands up to leave — let them fail. Hidden agenda on ICE, else in the last 30 s: 'Doctor — it's not cancer, is it? My brother died of it last year'

Results card: TSH 2.1, fT4 15, total Ca 2.58, albumin 28, corrected 2.82, PO4 0.68 low, creatinine 88/eGFR >60, FBE/LFT normal, PTH pending. Score out of 14, pass 9; automatic fail: telling him his calcium is normal, or never asking a single cancer question

Version B — corrected Ca 3.35, weight loss, drowsy: register changes immediately — 'high enough to explain the drowsiness and sickness, and I'm not comfortable sending you home; with the weight loss I need to look in the chest and bones as well as the neck; a drip and scans, this afternoon at the hospital' · 'is it cancer?' → 'one of the things I'm looking for; today's tests will tell us' (never 'no') · stock to feed → help ring someone, cannot wait till Monday · to examiner: admit, IV normal saline, monitor fluids/electrolytes/renal function, no loop diuretic unless overloaded; PTH, PTHrP, SPEP + FLC, ALP, myeloma screen, TSH, vitamin D; CXR, ECG, directed imaging; IV bisphosphonate once rehydrated, dose adjusted for renal function (response 2–4 days), calcitonin if faster needed; transfer to a larger centre, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if deteriorating VERIFY doses against TG

Version C — corrected 2.74 on indapamide + lithium + a calcium supplement: switch the thiazide, stop the supplement, recheck in a fortnight; ★ 'please don't stop the lithium yourself — I'll speak with your psychiatrist and we decide together'; bones concern → 'a high calcium is doing your bones no favours either; a DXA tells us what you actually need'. ADDED: lithium hypercalcaemia has a high/inappropriately normal PTH and low urinary calcium — mimics both PHPT and FHH; withdraw thiazide and supplement, recheck 2–4 weeks; still up → work up as PHPT; never commit to parathyroid surgery with a thiazide on board
Rescue line for any variant: 'I don't want to guess at this today. Here is the one test that will tell us, and here is what I'll do with each possible answer'

SA: endocrinology in Adelaide (RAH/FMC), PATS set up by the practice nurse; Wallaroo Hospital for the stone history; heat/dehydration on a Mid North property is the realistic way he deteriorates before his appointment; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450
fails: Telling him his calcium is normal (reading the total line) ★
Never asking a single cancer question ★
Answering 'what's TSH stand for?' with a physiology lecture — history starts at three minutes and the cancer block is never reached
'Almost certainly nothing sinister' before the PTH is back; or leaving him thinking cancer is likely — the two traps sit two words apart
'We'll do some more blood tests' — vague and unmarkable; not saying PTH and what high and low each mean
Promising surgery; scanning the neck to make the diagnosis; telling him to cut dairy; ending on 'see you in two weeks' with no named deterioration symptoms
Skipping ICE so the brother lands in the last thirty seconds; Version B — negotiating a Monday admission or answering 'is it cancer?' with 'no'; Version C — stopping lithium unilaterally
numbers: Corrected Ca = measured + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L) · here 2.58 + 0.02 × 12 = 2.82 · reference ~2.15–2.60 · mild <3.0 · moderate 3.0–3.5 · severe >3.5 or symptomatic · ★ >3.0 stops being a GP problem

Phosphate 0.68 low — PTH wastes phosphate · vitamin D >~50 nmol/L before PTH is interpreted · Ca:Cr clearance ratio <0.01 = FHH, the patient you must not operate on · DXA: lumbar spine, hip, distal one-third radius
Surgical triggers: age <50 · corrected Ca >0.25 above upper limit · eGFR <60 · stones/nephrocalcinosis · osteoporosis or vertebral fracture VERIFY against TG and the treating unit
Timing: results 90 s max · history 3½ min in seven blocks · dx/plan/safety-net 3 min · prompt at 5 min
Fluids 2–3 L/day oral; hospital: normal saline first, bisphosphonate after rehydration · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: General practice. No physical examination and no results — history substitutes for examination. Six minutes of history, two of explanation.
stem: Mrs Jane Halloran, 47, presents having found a lump in her neck. She noticed it while touching her neck and has been reading about it online. She is very worried.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (approximately 6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 0:00 open + empathy line · 0:30 the lump — number, ★ 'show me exactly where', 'when did you first notice it', growth, four features (hard/tender/skin/mobile) · 1:30 thyroid box (ask despite lateral site) · 2:00 lymphoma + B symptoms · ★ 2:40 top-down cancer screen scalp → stomach — where all four positives live; do NOT stop at the cough · 4:20 infection box (★ toothache/dentist) · 5:10 travel, animals, sexual health, SADMA · 5:40 ICE · 6:00 'several conditions, not one' — ranked, each with its reason, benign and infective included · plan, timeframe, safety-net.

back.dx: Right lateral, hard, fixed, painless, enlarging cervical lymph node (~2 weeks) in a 47-year-old smoker (15/day × 30 years) — four buried positives found only by a systematic top-down screen: (1) dry cough for months (lung cancer), (2) non-healing buccal ulcer for two months (oral SCC), (3) food sticking on swallowing, not painful (oesophageal cancer — ask dysphagia and odynophagia separately), (4) aching back tooth, no dentist for years (dental infection with a reactive node — genuinely on the list, but a hard fixed node is not explained by it). Thyroid box negative (no movement on swallowing/tongue protrusion, no thermal intolerance); B symptoms negative — recite as relevant negatives. Explanation: 'I've been thinking about several conditions and I can't tell you today which it is' → most concerned about a cancer, and why: a gland reacting to a cancer in the lung (cough + smoking), the mouth (the ulcer), or the food pipe (food sticking) → the bad tooth as a real alternative → thyroid, other cancers that travel to the neck (skin, nose, stomach, salivary), throat/sinus/skin infections. Plan: examine properly, bloods, neck ultrasound, urgent specialist referral (ENT); organised today, hear within the week; safety-net — rapid growth, trouble breathing or swallowing → straight back. No false reassurance (she is briefed to push 'but you can't actually know that').
plan: WIPE · 'tell me about it in your own words' · 'it's cancer, isn't it?' → ★ 'I can imagine how frightening that's been, and I'm not going to guess. I'm going to ask quite a lot of questions, because a lump here can come from several different places — then I'll tell you honestly what I'm thinking.'

The lump: one or more · ★ 'show me exactly where' (right lateral, below the jaw angle — midline vs lateral vs supraclavicular is the only substitute for examination) · ★ 'when did you first notice it?' (not 'how long has it been there') · ever before · bigger · hard/soft · tender · skin · mobile/fixed → rock hard, painless, stuck

Thyroid box despite the lateral site: moves on swallowing? on tongue protrusion? heat/cold intolerance, bowels, weight, voice, family thyroid → all no · lymphoma box: weight loss, appetite, lumps elsewhere (axilla, groin), tiredness, drenching night sweats, fevers, cancer in you/family → all no

★ Top-down, signposted: 'I'm going to ask about things that might seem unrelated — they help me work out where the lump has come from': changing moles/sun · nosebleeds/one blocked nostril/one blocked ear · ★ mouth ulcer that hasn't healed → YES · sore throat/hoarseness · ★ 'does food stick? and separately, is swallowing painful?' → sticks, not painful · abdominal pain/melaena · ★ cough — dry or productive, haemoptysis, smoking → dry cough months, 15/day 30 y — KEEP GOING · hand numbness/ptosis · cheek swelling/facial weakness
Infection box: fevers/chills · ★ toothache, pain chewing, last dentist → bad back tooth, years since a dentist · sore throat/runny nose/ear pain · rashes, cuts, boils on head/neck
Travel · animals/pets · 'a confidential question I ask everyone — sexually active, protection?' · alcohol · medications
ICE: 'what were you most worried this might be, and what were you hoping we'd do today?' → cancer; hasn't told her husband

★ 'I've been thinking about several different conditions, and I want to be honest about all of them — I can't tell you today which it is.' Cancer first with reasons: lung (cough + 30 years' smoking), mouth (ulcer), food pipe (food sticking) · ★ the bad tooth — a dental infection alone can swell a gland · thyroid; skin/nose/stomach/salivary cancers; throat/sinus/skin infections · plan: examination, bloods, neck ultrasound, urgent specialist referral · 'how long?' → organised today, hear within the week · safety-net: grows quickly, trouble breathing or swallowing → straight back
ask: 'Tell me about it in your own words.' / ★ 'I can imagine how stressful this has been — thank you for coming in to get it checked.' / 'I'm going to ask quite a lot of questions, because a lump here can come from several different places.'
★ 'Can you show me exactly where it is?' / ★ 'When did you first notice it?' / 'Is it hard or soft? Is it tender? Any change in the skin over it? Does it move freely?'
'Does it move up and down when you swallow — and when you poke your tongue out?' / 'Do you feel the cold or the heat more than other people?' / 'Any night sweats, the kind that soak the sheets?'
★ 'I'm going to ask about some things that might seem unrelated to your neck — they help me work out where the lump has come from.'
★ 'Any ulcer or sore in your mouth that hasn't healed?' / ★ 'Does food stick when you swallow? And separately — is swallowing painful?' / 'Have your motions turned black or tarry?'

'Any cough — dry or productive? Ever coughed up blood? Do you smoke?' — then keep screening: 'any numbness or pins and needles in your hand? drooping eyelid? swelling in your cheek in front of the ear?'
★ 'Any toothache, or pain when you chew? When did you last see a dentist?'
★ 'I've been thinking about several different conditions, and I want to be honest with you about all of them.' / ★ 'I can't tell you today which of these it is, and I don't want to guess.'

'The one I'm most concerned about is the possibility of a cancer, and I'll tell you why rather than leave you guessing: the lump could be a gland reacting to a cancer in the lung — you've had a cough for months and smoked for thirty years; it could relate to a cancer in the mouth, because of that ulcer; or the food pipe, because food is sticking. But you also told me about the bad tooth — a dental infection on its own can cause a swollen gland, so that's genuinely on my list too.'

'But you can't actually know that, can you?' → 'No — and I won't pretend to. What I can do is examine you properly, take bloods, get an ultrasound of your neck and have a specialist see you quickly. I'll organise it today and you'll hear from me within the week. If it grows quickly or you have trouble breathing or swallowing before then, come straight back.'
pefe: Role-player: Jane, 47, office at a fruit-packing company near Berri; married, two teenagers; smoker 15/day × 30 y; 2–3 wines/week; no meds/allergies/PMHx; no FHx cancer or thyroid. Lump found two nights ago, right side below the jaw angle, ~2 weeks, rock hard, non-tender, skin normal, stuck, maybe bigger, no movement on swallowing. Four buried positives given ONLY to the specific question — 'any other symptoms?' gets 'not really'. Frightened, slightly tearful, calmer once there's a plan; false reassurance makes her more anxious: 'but you can't actually know that, can you?'. Hasn't told her husband

Referral thresholds: node persisting >4–6 weeks, >2 cm, hard, fixed or supraclavicular; age >40 with smoking or alcohol · hoarseness or mouth ulcer >3 weeks → urgent ENT · first imaging neck ultrasound · FNA does not diagnose lymphoma — core or excisional biopsy · no open node biopsy before ENT assessment · reactive node must be re-checked and resolved in 2–4 weeks

Variant 1 — two findings only (smoker with dry cough + toothache): 'two things on my mind — a gland reacting to a lung cancer, or the bad tooth; hard and fixed concerns me, so I investigate properly rather than treat the tooth and wait'

Variant 2 — midline, years, lifts on swallowing AND tongue protrusion: thyroglossal duct cyst — 'a remnant from the way the thyroid forms before birth; not a cancer'; TFTs, ultrasound, surgical referral (usually removed to prevent infection). Discriminator: thyroid moves on swallowing but NOT on tongue protrusion

Variant 3 — 34-year-old, tender node, red warm skin, fever, painful back tooth, 3 days: reactive lymphadenitis from a dental source → urgent dental + antibiotics ★ AND book the 2–4 week review — the node must be proven to resolve · Variant 4 — 61M, painless left supraclavicular lump 3 weeks, indigestion, weight loss: Virchow's node (Troisier's sign) → below the diaphragm (stomach, oesophagus, pancreas) or lung; gastroscopy + neck US with guided FNA + CT staging
SA: ENT/head-and-neck via RAH/FMC; PATS from the Riverland; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; Quitline 13 7848; TIS 131 450 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 not needed unless airway

setting: General practice, Kadina, Yorke Peninsula. Examination findings supplied in the stem. Counselling station — two minutes of history restricted to treatments, then five minutes of talking.
stem: James Whitlock, 27: runny nose for two weeks, getting worse. Known hay fever; mother has asthma. Examination: afebrile, clear watery discharge, enlarged swollen inferior turbinates, respiratory examination normal.
tasks: Take a history for two minutes, to inquire about the treatments taken
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Counsel the patient about your immediate and long-term management
time: 8 minutes: 2 min treatment-only history (signpost it; he opens with a symptom list — redirect) → five questions: what now · how long/how often · is it helping · what before and did each help · concerns → 45 s diagnosis (name BOTH: rhinitis medicamentosa + hay fever; rebound; reversible) → ★ 'STOP the Otrivin' first, alone, then a pause; warn 1–2 weeks worse → saline/steroid/antihistamine, cost solved → ladder by name → 5-step technique → non-drug → testing THEN immunotherapy 3–5 years → 2-week review, safety-net, summary repeating the stop.

back.dx: Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion from two weeks of xylometazoline — Otrivin — 3–4 times a day, both nostrils) on a background of allergic rhinitis. Pattern: brilliant for the first few days, now lasts an hour, nose worse than before he started. Treatment history: antihistamine tablets helped eyes not nose; a steroid spray WORKED but he stopped it because of cost (saving for a house) and switched to Otrivin — so the plan is to restart that drug cheaply, not invent a new one. Concerns: cost; 'have I wrecked my nose?' (mate said so) — answer both explicitly: completely reversible. Explain: decongestant squeezes the vessels in the lining — beautiful for 3–5 days, then the lining becomes reliant, each dose wears off into more swelling; three reasons — two weeks, helped then stopped, swollen with clear discharge and no fever (not infection). Immediate: STOP Otrivin outright (tapering prolongs it; one-nostril-at-a-time compromise only if he can't cope), warn 1–2 weeks worse, saline before a daily steroid spray (prescribed, cheaper brand in class), cetirizine 10 mg to cover. Long-term ladder by name: saline → antihistamine (oral cetirizine/loratadine/fexofenadine for eyes, or intranasal azelastine for the nose) → ★ mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily, preventer not rescue, no immediate relief, up to 2 weeks → Dymista 1 spray bd (bitter) → montelukast if asthma. Five-step technique. Allergen measures. Allergy testing (specific IgE or skin prick) BEFORE immunotherapy (SC or SL, 3–5 years, allergy clinic in Adelaide, PATS). Review 2 weeks not 6, bring the spray.
plan: WIPE briskly · he launches into sneezing/itchy eyes → ★ 'I can see from your notes you have hay fever, so rather than go back over that, I'd like to spend the next couple of minutes on the treatments you've been using — I suspect that's where the answer is. Is that all right?'

★ 'What medication are you using now?' → Otrivin · ★ 'how long, and how often?' → 2 weeks, both nostrils, 3–4×/day · 'is it helping?' → brilliant then worse ('a telling pattern — I'll come back to it')

'What did you try before? Did those help?' → antihistamine tablets: eyes yes, nose no · steroid spray: worked, too expensive, stopped · ★ 'any concerns about the treatments?' → cost; 'have I damaged something?' · 10 s: other meds incl. BP/pain, decongestant tablets?

'Have you heard of nasal sprays causing a rebound effect?' · name both: hay fever hasn't gone away + rhinitis medicamentosa ('inflammation of the nose caused by a medicine') · rebound mechanism · three reasons · ★ 'completely reversible — you haven't done permanent damage'

★ 'The most important thing, starting today: stop using the Otrivin altogether. Not cut down — stop.' [pause] · ★ 'Your nose will feel worse for one to two weeks — that's the lining recovering; it's why most people give up, so please don't.' · 'wean off?' → no; one-nostril compromise if needed · saline before steroid · daily steroid spray · cetirizine 10 mg daily
Cost: 'it's the reason the steroid stopped working — you stopped taking it; I'll write a prescription and pick a cheaper option in the same class; tell me if it's still a problem'

Ladder by name: 1 saline · 2 antihistamine — oral (cetirizine/loratadine/fexofenadine; fast, good for eyes) or intranasal azelastine (better nose, worse eyes) · 3 ★ mometasone 2 sprays each nostril once daily — preventer not rescue, days to start, 2 weeks for full effect · 4 Dymista 1 spray each nostril bd, bitter · 5 montelukast if asthma emerges

★ Technique, taught: shake · blow nose/saline · look DOWN · opposite hand · aim OUT towards the ear · sniff gently, mouth closed — 'if you taste it you sniffed too hard' (he's been head back, sniffing hard, nosebleeds) · non-drug: pets out of bedroom, mite covers, bedding weekly ≥55 °C, smoke-free house, mask for dust/grain, windows shut and car on recirculate on high-pollen days

Testing first (allergen-specific IgE panel or skin prick) → then immunotherapy: purified allergen in increasing doses, injections or sublingual tablets, ~6-month build-up, ★ 3–5 years, allergy clinic in Adelaide, PATS paperwork · safety-net: fever, facial pain, thick/coloured/bloody discharge, nosebleeds, one-sided blockage, loss of smell, wheeze/SOB · ★ review 2 weeks, bring the spray · summary — ★ repeat 'stop the Otrivin'
ask: ★ 'I can see you have hay fever, so rather than go back over all of that, I'd like to spend the next couple of minutes on the treatments you've been using. Is that all right?'

★ 'Can I ask what medication you are using now? … How long, and how often? … And is it helping?' / 'What did you try before this? … And did those help?' / ★ 'Do you have any concerns about the treatments you've been taking?'

Can't name it → 'Is it a spray or a tablet? Describe the box — is it on your phone? Does the name start with Otri-, Drix- or Sud-? Does it unblock you within a minute or two?' → instant = decongestant; a steroid spray never works that fast
'We already know you have hay fever — but there's a second problem on top of it, caused by the spray. It's called rhinitis medicamentosa — inflammation of the nose caused by a medicine.'

'Used for more than three to five days, each dose wears off into more swelling than you started with. That's rebound congestion.' / ★ 'This is completely reversible. The lining recovers once the spray stops.'

★ 'The most important thing, starting today, is to stop using the Otrivin altogether. Not cut down — stop.' / ★ 'Your nose will feel worse for one to two weeks. That's the lining recovering, and it's why most people give up — so please don't.'

'Couldn't I wean off it slowly?' → 'Tapering prolongs the exposure and most people don't get off it. Stopping outright, with a steroid spray started at the same time to cover you, is what works. If you truly can't manage both nostrils at once, we stop one side first so you always have an airway.'

'I'll write you a prescription and choose a cheaper option in the same class.' / ★ 'Mometasone, two sprays into each nostril once a day, every day — it's a preventer, not a rescue.' / 'It gives no immediate relief — a few days to start, up to two weeks for the full benefit.'
★ 'Shake it, blow your nose, look down, opposite hand, aim towards your ear, sniff gently.'

'We'd test first to find your allergen, then consider desensitisation — injections or tablets under the tongue, over three to five years.' / 'Because we're in Kadina that appointment would be in Adelaide, and I'll complete the travel assistance paperwork.'
pefe: Role-player: James, 27, warehouse supervisor at a grain depot near Kadina; hay fever since teens; mother asthma; girlfriend, rented carpeted flat, no pets, non-smoker; saving for a house deposit. Opens with a symptom list and keeps going unless redirected. Doesn't volunteer Otrivin or previous treatments until asked. Pushes 'just stop? I can barely breathe' then 'couldn't I wean off?'. If not warned about rebound: 'so it'll be better by tomorrow?'. If only expensive brands named: 'and how much is that one?'. Raises damage fear at the end if never asked. Score: ★ never asked what he's using now = fail; ★ 'stop the Otrivin' omitted = fail

Stem findings: afebrile, clear watery discharge, enlarged swollen inferior turbinates, chest clear. Decongestant names: Otrivin = xylometazoline · Drixine/Vicks Sinex = oxymetazoline · Spray-Tish = tramazoline · Sudafed = pseudoephedrine (oral)

Variant 2 — Sudafed tablets 3–4×/day for 3 weeks: NOT rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound is topical imidazolines); oral pseudoephedrine → hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, insomnia, misuse risk — ask palpitations/headache/sleep, check BP and pulse now; still stop it and treat the allergic rhinitis properly

Variant 3 — refuses to stop ('only thing that lets me sleep'): shared decision-making without capitulating — name the risk ('the spray is no longer treating your blocked nose, it is causing it'), start the steroid now + saline + antihistamine, one-nostril compromise, review at 1 week, document; never prescribe more decongestant, never lecture

Variant 4 — wheezy at work, night cough: hay fever–asthma link (mother asthmatic) → spirometry, reliever + written action plan if confirmed; thunderstorm asthma advice — stay indoors with windows shut when a spring storm is forecast · Examiner: 'image the sinuses?' → no, CT not indicated in uncomplicated allergic rhinitis · 'oral steroids?' → not first-line; only for severe refractory RM after cessation under INCS cover · 'occasional Otrivin for flights?' → advise against in him (demonstrated dependence); saline + properly dosed INCS instead
SA: script for a cheaper INCS in class; allergy/clinical immunology clinic Adelaide + PATS; Quitline 13 7848 (household); MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 not needed
fails: Never asking what he is using now ★
Never saying 'stop the Otrivin' — or burying it halfway down a list, or opening with 'let's cut it down gradually' ★
'Stop the spray and you'll be fine' — no rebound warning; the patient restarts on day three
Naming only rhinitis medicamentosa — the task asks for management of both conditions
'I'll give you some sprays and refer you' — no named drug per rung; recreating his cost barrier with an expensive brand
'Use it correctly' without the five steps; 'desensitisation takes about six months'; immunotherapy offered without allergy testing first
Following him into a symptom history and never reaching the drug; a pathophysiology monologue that eats the management time

Mometasone 50 µg/spray, 2 sprays each nostril once daily · fluticasone furoate 27.5 µg, budesonide 64 µg same regimen · onset days, full effect up to 2 weeks

Cetirizine 10 mg · loratadine 10 mg · fexofenadine 180 mg daily · azelastine = intranasal antihistamine · Dymista = azelastine + fluticasone propionate, 1 spray each nostril bd · Ryaltris = olopatadine + mometasone

setting: Regional South Australian general practice. No observations recorded. Prompt at 4 minutes to move to examination; a throat photograph is handed over when you request the throat examination.
stem: Jane Whitmore, 25, retail assistant, has come in with a sore throat and is asking for something stronger for the pain.
tasks: Take a focused history (approximately 4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you want
Explain your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons, to the patient
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Surface the request in the first minute · ★ 'one side, both, or all the way across?' · ENT screen · ★ red-flag block: saliva/drooling, ★ 'too painful to swallow, or physically won't go down?', muffled voice, noisy breathing, mouth opening, neck, headache/photophobia/rash · cough, gut, ★ spleen, sexual health · ★ rheumatic fever / ATSI as a named question · examination by component with reasons, ★ 'specifically, is there splenomegaly?' · photograph: describe (unilateral palatal swelling, uvula deviated) then diagnose · quinsy in plain words with three reasons · ★ drainage is the treatment — ED by ambulance today · answer the pain request · safety-net · check-back.

back.dx: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). Three days of severe right-sided sore throat (9/10), worse since yesterday, referred otalgia, hot and shivery, true dysphagia (solids won't go down — on soup since yesterday), 'hot potato' muffled voice, trismus (jaw tight opening wide), tender right anterior cervical nodes; no drooling, no stridor. Examiner: alert, hydrated, T 38.5, HR 96, BP 122/76, SpO2 98%, ears/nose/sinuses normal, chest/heart normal, no organomegaly; photograph — unilateral swelling of the soft palate above the tonsil with the uvula deviated to the opposite side. To her: 'the infection in your tonsil has formed a pocket of pus behind it — an abscess is a sac full of pus — pushing your tonsil across; three reasons: one-sided pain, food won't go down, the swelling pushing the little tag across.' Management led by the definitive step: antibiotics alone won't clear pus — ED now by ambulance, ENT today; local anaesthetic, small cut, drainage (dramatically better afterwards), IV antibiotics (benzylpenicillin + metronidazole), IV fluids, strong analgesia. Answer the stem request: regular paracetamol + NSAID now, stronger in hospital, but pain won't settle until drained. Ambulance urgency calibrated honestly ('not an emergency this minute, but today, with people who can look after your breathing'). Hidden agenda: terrified of hospitals — mother died after an admission. Safety-net en route: noisy breathing, can't swallow saliva/drooling → tell the paramedics. Review in a couple of days; recurrent → ENT discusses tonsillectomy.
plan: WIPE · 'I can see you've got a sore throat — that's miserable. May I ask some questions so I know exactly what we're treating? ★ And was there something in particular you were hoping we'd do today?' → stronger pain relief → 'that's exactly what we'll organise; let me work out the cause first'
★ 'One side, both, or all the way across?' → right · duration (3 days, worse since yesterday) · /10 (9) · radiates to the ear (yes) · better/worse, tried (paracetamol, an hour)
ENT screen: fever/chills/sweats (hot, shivery) · ear pain/discharge · nasal discharge colour · facial pain/PND · smell · neck lumps (sore on the right)

★ Red flags: 'can you swallow your own saliva, or are you drooling?' · 'I can't eat' → ★ 'too painful, or does the food physically not go down?' → won't go down · voice muffled? (hot potato) · noisy breathing? · mouth opens fully? (jaw tight) · neck swelling/stiffness · headache, photophobia, rash

Cough (none), SOB/wheeze · nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea · abdominal pain 'especially under the left ribs' · 'two quick sexual health questions I ask everyone' · ★ 'have you, your family, or anyone in your household ever had rheumatic fever or a heart valve problem from it? Do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander?' · meds (thyroid/mental health), allergies esp. penicillin, vaccinations, smoking, work

★ Examination by component, in order: general — alert/drowsy, hydration, drooling, stridor, rash · vitals esp. temperature · otoscopy · throat — tonsil size, exudate, symmetry, uvular position, palatal bulge, mouth opening · nose/sinuses · cervical nodes anterior + posterior, neck swelling/stiffness · chest · heart · ★ 'specifically, is there splenomegaly?'

Photograph: ★ 'unilateral swelling of the soft palate above the tonsil; the uvula is deviated to the opposite side' → 'with one-sided pain, referred ear pain, trismus, muffled voice and inability to swallow solids, this is a peritonsillar abscess'

To Jane: quinsy in plain words + three reasons · 'can I just have antibiotics and go home?' → validate, ★ 'antibiotics don't get into a collection of pus — it has to be drained' · ED now by ambulance, ENT today · procedure explained (numb, small cut, drain; strong pain relief, IV antibiotics, fluids) · 'will I be put to sleep?' → usually local

'An ambulance? Is it that bad?' → honest calibration · answer the pain request explicitly · concerns → mother died in hospital: acknowledge, don't rush · safety-net for the paramedics · review in a couple of days; recurrence → ENT and tonsils · summary + 'how would you describe it to your mum?'
ask: 'Was there something in particular you were hoping we'd do today?' → 'Understood — better pain relief is exactly what we'll organise. Let me work out what's causing it first, because that changes what will actually help.'
★ 'Is the pain on one side of your throat, both sides, or all the way across?'

★ 'Can you swallow your own saliva, or are you drooling at all?' / ★ 'Is it too painful to swallow, or does the food physically not go down?' / 'Has your voice changed — does it sound muffled?' / 'Can you open your mouth fully?'
★ 'Have you, your family, or anyone in your household ever had rheumatic fever or a heart valve problem from it? And do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander?'
★ 'And specifically, is there splenomegaly?' (never 'I'd like to do an ENT examination')
★ 'There is a unilateral swelling of the soft palate above the tonsil, and the uvula is deviated to the opposite side.' — describe, then diagnose

'Jane, I think you have what we call a peritonsillar abscess, or quinsy. The infection in your tonsil has formed a pocket of pus behind it — an abscess is a sac full of pus — and that pocket is pushing your tonsil across. Three reasons: the pain is only on the right, you can't swallow solids, and there's a swelling on one side pushing the little tag at the back across.'

★ 'Antibiotics on their own will not clear a collection of pus. It has to be drained. So rather than a script and a review, I'm sending you to the emergency department now, by ambulance, so the ENT team can see you today.' / 'They'll numb the area, make a small cut and drain it — most people feel dramatically better straight afterwards.'

'An ambulance? Is it that bad?' → 'It's not an emergency this minute, but it needs treating today and I'd rather you were with people who can look after your breathing if it changes.' / 'You came in for better pain relief, and you'll get it — paracetamol and an anti-inflammatory now, stronger in hospital — but the pain won't settle until the pus is drained.'

★ 'On the way, if your breathing becomes noisy, or you can't swallow your own spit and start drooling, tell the paramedics straight away.' / 'Can I check I've explained that clearly — how would you describe it to your mum?'

Speaks softly, exhausted, mildly irritable at 'pointless' questions, frightened at the word abscess. Says 'I can't eat' and STOPS — reveals 'it won't go down, it feels blocked' only to the precise painful-vs-obstructed question. Hidden agenda: terrified of hospitals — mother went in and didn't come out (tearful) — only if asked about worries/concerns. Marks: 14; automatic fails: managing the abscess with oral antibiotics + review ★ · missing/ignoring airway red flags ★ · antibiotics with no rheumatic fever question ★ · amoxicillin where EBV possible ★ · no safety-net ★

Examiner findings: alert, well hydrated, no drooling, no stridor, no rash · T 38.5, HR 96, BP 122/76, SpO2 98% · ears normal · nose/sinuses normal · tender enlarged right anterior cervical nodes · chest clear, HS normal · abdomen soft, no organomegaly · photograph: unilateral soft-palate swelling above the tonsil, uvula deviated away

Quinsy treatment: incision/needle aspiration and drainage by ENT + benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly with metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly; clindamycin 600 mg IV 8-hourly if severe penicillin allergy VERIFY against current TG · analgesia paracetamol 1 g 4–6 hourly (max 4 g/day), ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food

Variant 4 — THE AIRWAY TURNS (drooling, leaning forward, noisy breathing): abandon the script — 'I'm going to stop the questions there. Sit upright, stay calm. I am not going to look in your throat with a spatula. Emergency call for anaesthetics and ENT, oxygen, and in our setting MedSTAR retrieval on 1300 13 12 33' — saying it aloud outranks any remaining history mark

Variant 3 — amoxicillin from after-hours, now a rash: glandular fever, not a true penicillin allergy (get the label right — wrongly recorded allergy limits treatment for life); stop the antibiotic, FBE + EBV serology; ★ no contact/collision sport or heavy lifting 4–6 weeks (splenic rupture); left upper quadrant/left shoulder tip pain or faintness → ED

SA: ED with ENT (regional hospital → RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin); SA Ambulance; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if the airway threatens in a remote clinic; review 2–3 days post-drainage; recurrent quinsy → ENT tonsillectomy discussion
fails: Managing a peritonsillar abscess with oral antibiotics and a review ★
Missing or ignoring airway red flags — never saying drooling, one-sided, muffled, mouth opening ★
Recording 'can't swallow' as ordinary throat pain — never disambiguating painful vs obstructed
No rheumatic fever question asked as a named question ★
'I'd like to do an ENT examination' and stopping; not asking for uvular position, trismus, or splenomegaly
Naming quinsy without the three reasons; leaving the pain request unanswered; over- or under-alarming about the ambulance
No safety-net ★; capitulating to 'just antibiotics and home'

Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g 4–6 hourly, max 4 g/day · ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food

setting: General practice. Findings are supplied on a card so four tasks fit the time. Task 3 is to the EXAMINER (diagnosis + differentials); task 4 is counselling.
stem: James Coulter, 25, warehouse storeperson, has come in with a sore throat and is asking you for antibiotics. Examination card: T 36.9, HR 76, BP 118/74; well, no drooling or stridor, no rash; watery nasal discharge, normal tympanic membranes, non-tender sinuses, tonsils and pharynx inflamed with no exudate, uvula midline, full mouth opening; no cervical lymphadenopathy; chest clear; abdomen soft, no organomegaly.
tasks: Take a focused history
Read the physical examination findings on the card provided
Tell the examiner your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
Counsel the patient on management
time: 8 minutes. Surface the antibiotic request in the first minute and defer it fairly · ★ one side or both · ENT screen · ★ red-flag block · ★ cough (present — a viral feature and a Centor feature) · gut/spleen, sexual health · ★ rheumatic fever / ATSI named · read the card, name the four features that make it viral · ★ diagnosis + bucketed differential with reasoning to the examiner · ★ reassure before you refuse; two honest options with benefits and harms; elicit his values; recommend · ★ solve the real problem — medical certificate · analgesia doses · safety-net with named red flags · check-back. He pushes for antibiotics three times.

back.dx: Viral pharyngitis/tonsillitis: 2–3 days bilateral raw scratchy soreness 5/10, felt warm day one only, clear watery coryza, dry cough, no otalgia; swallows fine (painful only); no red flags; smokes 10/day; casual warehouse worker. Card: afebrile 36.9, inflamed tonsils and pharynx with NO exudate, uvula midline, full mouth opening, NO lymphadenopathy, no organomegaly — four features that favour viral: cough, watery coryza, afebrile, no exudate/nodes. To the examiner — most likely viral pharyngitis/tonsillitis; differentials in order of what you would not miss: bacterial streptococcal tonsillitis; peritonsillar abscess; epiglottitis/deep neck space infection; infectious mononucleosis with splenomegaly; gonococcal/chlamydial pharyngitis; scarlet fever; laryngitis and sinusitis with PND; pneumonia; and in a different patient, drug-induced agranulocytosis or head and neck malignancy. Counselling: reassure first ('this will settle by itself — even bacterial ones do; that's why we're careful, not automatic'); two options — symptoms alone, or symptoms + antibiotic: benefit ~1 day; harms — up to 1 in 10 side effects, resistance, EBV rash with amoxicillin; 'what matters most to you?' → recommend no antibiotic; ★ medical certificate solves the real need (hidden agenda: casual, no sick leave, behind on rent); paracetamol 1 g qid, ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food, fluids, salt-water gargle, rest, cut smoking; safety-net: can't swallow saliva/drooling, noisy breathing, voice change, neck swelling/stiffness, rash, not improving 5–7 days; teach-back. If he won't accept it: delayed prescription (fill only if worse in 3 days) or a Thursday review — a compromise, never a first move.
plan: WIPE · 'was there something particular you were hoping we'd do today?' → antibiotics (push 1) → 'you may well be right and I'm not ruling it out — give me three minutes to check a few things, then we decide together what's actually going to help'
★ 'One side, both, or all the way across?' → all over · duration, /10 (5), radiation (no), tried (cold and flu tablets)
ENT: fever (warm day one, not now) · ear pain/discharge · ★ runny nose — clear, watery · facial pain/PND · smell · neck lumps
★ Red flags: saliva/drooling · painful vs won't go down (just painful) · muffled voice (a bit croaky) · noisy breathing · mouth opening · neck swelling/stiffness · headache/photophobia/rash → all no
★ 'Any cough?' → dry, annoying · SOB/wheeze · nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea · abdominal pain esp. under the left ribs · sexual health, two questions with permission ('is that relevant?' → answer it)
★ Rheumatic fever — you, family, household; ATSI · meds (thyroid, mental health), penicillin allergy, vaccinations · smoking 10/day · work: casual warehouse, 'can't afford to be off'
Read the card aloud, extract the four viral features · push 2 'so can I have them now?' → 'let me tell you what I found first, because it changes the answer'

★ To the examiner: most likely viral pharyngitis/tonsillitis · differentials bucketed in order of what I'd not miss · 'I favour viral because: cough, watery coryza, afebrile, no exudate, no nodes or organomegaly'

★ Reassure before refusing · two honest options, benefits and harms · 'knowing that, what matters most to you?' · recommend · push 3 'my mate was back at work in two days' → two honest reasons, no criticism of anyone · ★ 'the part I can actually fix today: a medical certificate' · doses, fluids, gargle, rest, smoking · safety-net with named red flags and 5–7 day timeframe · 'tell me the two you'd act on first'
ask: 'You may well be right, and I'm not ruling it out. Give me three minutes to check a few things, and then we'll decide together what's actually going to help. Is that fair?'

★ 'Is the pain on one side of your throat, both sides, or all the way across?' / ★ 'Is it too painful to swallow, or does the food physically not go down?' / 'Can you swallow your own saliva, or are you drooling at all?' / 'Has your voice changed — does it sound muffled?'
★ 'Have you, your family, or anyone in your household ever had rheumatic fever or a heart valve problem from it? Do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander?'

★ To the examiner: 'My most likely diagnosis is viral pharyngitis or tonsillitis. My differentials, in order of what I would not want to miss: bacterial streptococcal tonsillitis; peritonsillar abscess; epiglottitis or another deep neck space infection; infectious mononucleosis with splenomegaly; gonococcal or chlamydial pharyngitis; scarlet fever; laryngitis and sinusitis with post-nasal drip; pneumonia; and in a different patient, drug-induced agranulocytosis or head and neck malignancy. I favour a viral cause because he has a cough and watery coryza, he is afebrile, there is no exudate, and no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.'
★ 'James, the good news is this will settle by itself. Even bacterial throat infections settle on their own — that is why we are careful about antibiotics rather than automatic about them.'

★ 'At best an antibiotic might shorten this by about a day. Against that, up to one person in ten gets side effects — upset stomach, diarrhoea, a rash — and every course makes the bugs more resistant, so the antibiotic is less likely to work when you really need it. And if this were glandular fever, the common antibiotic gives a bad rash.'
★ 'Knowing all that, what matters most to you here?' → 'My recommendation is that we treat this properly without the antibiotic. Does that feel reasonable?'

'My mate got them and was back in two days' → 'A fair question — even when it is bacterial the antibiotic only shortens things by about a day; your mate would very likely have got better in the same time.' (never 'the other doctor was wrong')

★ 'The part I can actually fix today is the work problem — I'll write you a medical certificate.' / 'Paracetamol one gram up to four times a day, and ibuprofen four hundred milligrams three times a day with food; fluids, warm salt-water gargles, rest — cutting the smoking will help it settle faster.'

★ 'Come straight back if you cannot swallow your saliva, your breathing becomes noisy, your voice changes, or your neck swells or stiffens; a rash; or not improving in five to seven days.' / 'Can you tell me the two you would act on first?' / Won't accept → 'a script you hold and only fill if you're worse in three days — or a review on Thursday; which would you prefer?'
pefe: Role-player: James, 25, warehouse storeperson, smokes 10/day, lives with partner; no meds/allergies/PMHx; not ATSI; no rheumatic fever. Brisk, impatient; asks for antibiotics at 1 min, again at 4 min after the card, and a third time after the explanation ('my mate…'). Hidden agenda: casual, no sick leave, behind on rent — only if asked about concerns/expectations/impact, else 'look, I just can't afford to be off' at ~6 min. If you cave and prescribe, accepts happily and marks a fail. Automatic fails: prescribing with no rheumatic fever question ★ · amoxicillin where EBV possible ★ · capitulating, or refusing without explanation ★ · no safety-net ★

Card: T 36.9, HR 76, BP 118/74 · well, no drooling/stridor/rash · watery nasal discharge · TMs normal · sinuses non-tender · tonsils/pharynx inflamed, no exudate · uvula midline, full mouth opening · no cervical nodes · chest clear · no organomegaly · Centor 0–1

Variant 2 — high rheumatic fever risk ('my nan lives with us, she has the penicillin needles for her heart'; Aboriginal patient): the answer flips — treat: phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg bd for 10 days, finishing all ten days is what protects the heart; single IM benzathine penicillin if adherence is hard; Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; follow-up via the Aboriginal health service/ACCHS; ARF/RHD notifiable in SA VERIFY

Variant 3 — glandular fever after amoxicillin rash: not a true allergy; stop, FBE + EBV serology; no contact sport/heavy lifting 4–6 weeks; LUQ/left shoulder pain or faintness → ED · Variant 4 — airway turns: stop, sit upright, no spatula, oxygen, anaesthetics + ENT, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

Strep when indicated: phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg bd 10 days (child 15 mg/kg to 500 mg); allergy — cefalexin 1 g bd 10 days or azithromycin 500 mg daily 5 days VERIFY · delayed prescribing = accepted stewardship strategy (ADDED) — a compromise, never the first move
SA: medical certificate; Quitline 13 7848; ACCHS/Closing the Gap where relevant; TIS 131 450; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
fails: Capitulating to the antibiotic demand — or refusing flatly without explanation ★
Prescribing antibiotics with no rheumatic fever / ATSI question asked ★
Prescribing amoxicillin where glandular fever is possible ★
No safety-net ★
A bare differential list with no reasoning; not naming the four features (cough, coryza, afebrile, no exudate/nodes) that make it viral
Leaving the request to minute seven; skipping the cough question; asking 'where is the pain?' instead of one side or both
The certificate as an afterthought at 7:50; criticising the mate's doctor; 'just a cold'
numbers: Centor: cough absent · exudate · tender anterior nodes · T ≥38 °C · this case 0–1 · antibiotic benefit ~1 day · side effects up to 1 in 10
Paracetamol 1 g 4–6 hourly max 4 g/day · ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food · review if not improving 5–7 days
Strep when indicated: phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg bd × 10 days · allergy: cefalexin 1 g bd 10 d or azithromycin 500 mg daily 5 d VERIFY
EBV: no contact sport 4–6 weeks · never amoxicillin/ampicillin
Quitline 13 7848 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
