setting: General practice, regional South Australia. No observations supplied. Prompt at 4 minutes to move to examination; a photograph is handed over when you ask for Horner's syndrome. Indirect laryngoscopy is unavailable.
stem: Margaret Ellis, 45, primary school teacher, presents with a change in her voice — hoarseness.
tasks: Take a focused history (approximately 4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you want
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the further investigations you would arrange
time: 8 minutes, four tasks — lost on time far more than knowledge. 0:00 short open + agenda · 0:25 ★ timing and pattern: constant, 'does voice rest help?', 'same all day or worse by evening?' — two months is a red flag on its own · 1:15 infection, airway red flags, overuse tested and DISCARDED out loud ('I'm a teacher' is the red herring) · 2:00 cancer screen throat → oesophagus → thyroid → ★ lung: cough, haemoptysis, SOB, shoulder pain, ★ pack-years aloud · ★ the two Pancoast questions (hand numbness ulnar side; droopy eyelid) · 3:20 reflux, myasthenia, hypothyroid, neck surgery, ★ 'steroid inhalers or puffers' by class, alcohol, FHx, ICE · 4:00 examination by component with targets — Horner's, C8–T1 · ★ basal signs = effusion secondary to the apex · 5:20 warning shot, pause, plain words, two reasons · differentials in three buckets · 6:50 ★ three numbered investigations · ownership of the result, safety-net, Quitline.

back.dx: Pancoast (apical lung) tumour with left recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, left Horner's syndrome, C8–T1 lower brachial plexus involvement and a secondary left pleural effusion. Two months of constant, slowly worsening hoarseness, no better with two weeks' voice rest at Easter, same morning and night (kills overuse); dry cough three months, puffed on stairs, left shoulder ache 'blamed on marking', couple of kilos lost; 20/day since 20 = 25 pack-years; ★ left hand numb along the ulnar edge, husband said her eye 'looked lazy in a photo'. Examination: not cachectic, no neck mass, T 36.8, throat/nose/nodes/thyroid normal; left lower zone — reduced expansion, dullness, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance (effusion); photograph — partial ptosis, miosis (ask about anhidrosis) = left Horner's → sympathetic chain → lung apex; C8–T1 weakness and sensory loss. Resolve the apparent contradiction before the examiner asks: an apical mass produces no chest signs itself; the basal signs are an effusion caused by it. To her: 'a growth in the upper part of your left lung — a lung cancer; can't be certain today' + two reasons (hoarseness/cough/smoking; fluid around the lung with eye and hand changes fitting a growth at the top pressing on nerves). Never 'Pancoast', 'Horner's', 'pleural effusion' to the patient. Differentials in three buckets with a why: infections (no fever, too long), strain (rest didn't help), growths — cords, thyroid, oesophagus, lung; rarer — reflux, hypothyroid, myasthenia, inhaled steroids. Investigations: 1 CXR today · 2 urgent ENT laryngoscopy · 3 CT chest + biopsy (then PET-CT, MRI thoracic inlet, TFTs, bloods). Own the result: call her personally, see her this week, bring her husband; safety-net; Quitline once, no lecture; Cancer Council 13 11 20. Hidden agenda: mother died of lung cancer at 58 — why she waited.
plan: WIPE · 'that must be difficult when you teach' · ★ 'what's been worrying you about it?' → 'probably nothing, my sister nagged me' (hidden: mother's lung cancer)

★ 'When did you first notice it? Constant or comes and goes? Getting worse? Does it improve if you rest your voice — a weekend, the holidays? Worse by the end of the day, or the same?' → 2 months, constant, worse, holidays no help, same all day — react to two months as a red flag

Fever/chills, sore throat, nose, facial pain · ★ 'three important ones: drooling, difficulty swallowing, noisy breathing?' · overuse: work (teacher, volunteers it warmly), singing, shouting/concert/carnival → ★ 'your work means you use your voice heavily, so that was my first thought — but rest made no difference and it's the same all day, which doesn't fit simple strain, so I want to keep looking'

Cancer screen: dysphagia/food sticking, vomiting, one-sided ear pain, weight loss (couple of kilos), neck lumps, heat/cold intolerance · ★ lung: cough (dry, 3 months), haemoptysis (no), SOB (stairs), wheeze, chest pain, ★ shoulder/interscapular pain (left shoulder, 'marking') · ★ 'how many a day, for how many years? — so that's around 25 pack-years'

★ Two Pancoast questions: 'any numbness, tingling or weakness in your hand, particularly on the little-finger side?' → left hand numb · 'has anyone said one of your eyelids looks droopy, or one side of your face doesn't sweat?' → husband, photo → 'it may be connected — let me finish and examine you'

Reflux/water brash · diplopia by evening, tiring while chewing (myasthenia) · cold, tired, constipated (hypothyroid) · neck surgery/injury · 'do you mean any particular medication?' → ★ 'steroid inhalers or puffers, the sort used for asthma' · alcohol (wine nightly) · FHx cancer → mother, lung, 58

★ Examination by component with targets: general — cachexia, visible neck mass · temperature · throat — masses, swelling/redness/exudate · nose — septum, mucosa · cervical nodes · thyroid — enlargement, nodule · respiratory — expansion, percussion, breath sounds, vocal resonance · ★ 'does she have Horner's syndrome — partial ptosis, small pupil, reduced sweating?' · ★ 'upper limb neurological examination looking specifically for C8–T1 weakness, small-muscle wasting, ulnar sensory loss'

Photograph: 'partial ptosis of the left upper lid, constricted left pupil — I'd ask about sweating — a left Horner's syndrome, localising to the sympathetic chain, in this context the left lung apex' · ★ 'the four signs at the left base are a pleural effusion; with the hoarseness, Horner's and C8–T1 signs the primary lesion is at the apex and the effusion is secondary — a small apical mass would not itself produce chest signs'

★ Warning shot: 'Margaret, I'm afraid the examination has shown something I wasn't expecting, and I need to be honest with you about it.' STOP · 'go on' · ★ 'I'm concerned there may be a growth in the upper part of your left lung — a lung cancer. I can't be certain today.' Two reasons only · she goes quiet, one frightened question → acknowledge, no false reassurance, no outlook number, 'this moves quickly from here'

Differentials in three buckets, each with a why: infections (no fever, too long) · strain (rest didn't help) · growths — cords, thyroid, food pipe, lung; rarer — reflux, underactive thyroid, myasthenia, asthma inhalers — none fit · 'given the smoking, the cough and what I found in your chest, it's the lung I'm most concerned about'

★ 'Three things, in this order: one, a chest X-ray today; two, an urgent ENT referral for a laryngoscopy — a camera to look directly at your vocal cords; three, depending on the X-ray, a CT scan of your chest and a biopsy. Plus bloods including your thyroid.' · ★ 'I will call you personally with the X-ray result and see you this week whatever it shows — bring your husband' · safety-net: noisy/harder breathing, haemoptysis, severe pain → ED · Quitline 13 7848 once, Cancer Council 13 11 20 · summary
ask: ★ 'Does it improve if you rest your voice — over a weekend or the holidays?' / ★ 'Is it worse at the end of the day, or the same all day?' / 'Any drooling, any difficulty swallowing, any noisy breathing?'
★ 'Your work does mean you use your voice heavily — but the pattern doesn't fit simple strain, so I want to keep looking.'
★ 'How many a day, and for how many years? … So that's around 25 pack-years.'

★ 'Any numbness, tingling or weakness in your hand, particularly on the little-finger side?' / ★ 'Has anyone said one of your eyelids looks droopy, or that one side of your face doesn't sweat like it used to?'
'Do you mean any particular medication?' → ★ 'Specifically, any steroid inhalers or puffers — the sort used for asthma. They can cause a hoarse voice.'
★ 'Does she have Horner's syndrome — partial ptosis, a constricted pupil, reduced sweating on that side?' / ★ 'An upper limb neurological examination, looking specifically for C8 and T1 involvement.'
★ 'Those findings at the left base are a pleural effusion. I think the primary lesion is at the apex and the effusion is secondary to it.'

★ 'I'm afraid the examination has shown something I wasn't expecting, and I need to be honest with you about it.' (then stop) / ★ 'I'm concerned there may be a growth in the upper part of your left lung — a lung cancer. I can't be certain today, which is why I want to organise tests urgently.'

'Am I going to be alright?' → 'I'm sorry to be giving you this today. I honestly can't tell you the outlook until we know exactly what it is — that's what the tests are for, and they'll happen quickly.'

★ 'Three things, in this order: a chest X-ray today, an urgent ENT referral for a laryngoscopy, and then a CT scan and a biopsy.' / ★ 'I will call you personally with the X-ray result, and I'll see you again this week whatever it shows.' / 'When you're ready, Quitline on 13 7848 — and Cancer Council on 13 11 20 if you'd like someone to talk to.'
pefe: Role-player: Margaret, 45, primary teacher, regional SA; husband Peter, two teenagers; 20/day since 20, tried twice; wine nightly; no meds/allergies/PMHx/surgery. Brisk, minimising ('probably nothing'); volunteers 'I'm a teacher' early and warmly — the trap; withholds the hand and eyelid unless asked directly; pushes back once on medications 'do you mean any particular medication?'; calls the clock at 4 and 6; goes QUIET (not tearful) at the warning shot, one frightened question; 'what does that mean?' at Pancoast/Horner's/pleural effusion. Hidden agenda: mother died of lung cancer at 58 — reveal if asked what worried her/why she waited, else at ~6 min. If you finish early: 'so what do you actually think it is?'

Examiner: not cachectic, no visible neck mass, T 36.8 · throat no masses/swelling/redness/exudate · nose normal · no cervical nodes · thyroid normal · chest: reduced expansion, dullness, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance LEFT LOWER ZONE · left Horner's (photograph) · C8–T1 weakness and sensory loss · indirect laryngoscopy unavailable

To the examiner if asked for the differential (technical register, what-not-to-miss order): Pancoast tumour with malignant effusion · laryngeal/vocal cord carcinoma · thyroid carcinoma invading the recurrent laryngeal nerve · oesophageal carcinoma · deep neck space infection/epiglottitis · acute laryngitis/URTI · vocal overuse, nodules, polyps · laryngopharyngeal reflux · myasthenia gravis · hypothyroidism · surgical/traumatic RLN injury · inhaled corticosteroids

Variant 1 — benign (2 weeks since school camp, better mornings, worse by home time): overuse/nodules — voice rest, don't whisper, hydrate, avoid caffeine/alcohol, stop smoking, no antibiotics, speech pathology; ★ 'if still hoarse at three weeks come back — ENT laryngoscopy regardless' — the mark is the built-in review · Variant 2 — 6 weeks post-thyroidectomy: RLN injury; ★ ask stridor/exertional breathlessness first (bilateral palsy = airway emergency); ENT laryngoscopy to document the side, speech pathology, check calcium and TFTs · Variant 3 — voice fades through the day, diplopia and heavy lids by dinner, fine on waking: fatigability → myasthenia gravis; ask chewing fatigue, dysphagia, breathlessness; AChR antibodies, neurology; breathing/swallowing difficulty → ED same day

Variant 4 — examination-station version (45M smoker, neck lump; task 1 upper limb neuro → C8–T1 loss; task 2 'further relevant examination' → ★ 'a C8–T1 lesion with a neck lump in a smoker makes me think of a lesion at the lung apex involving the lower trunk of the brachial plexus — I'd examine the respiratory system and look for Horner's and cervical nodes' → left basal effusion; task 3 → Pancoast tumour with lower brachial plexus involvement, secondary effusion, metastatic node; CXR, CT chest, tissue diagnosis, lung cancer MDT)
SA: urgent ENT (RAH/FMC), respiratory/lung cancer MDT, PATS; Quitline 13 7848; Cancer Council 13 11 20; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if the airway is threatened; TIS 131 450
fails: Running out of time before the investigations task ★
Accepting vocal strain as the diagnosis and sending her away ★
Abandoning the cancer diagnosis when the basal (not apical) chest signs appear ★
No laryngoscopy anywhere in the plan ★
Saying 'cancer' with no warning shot ★; no follow-up or ownership of the result ★
Recording 'two months' and 'smoker' without reacting — no pack-years; not asking the two Pancoast questions because you don't expect a yes
'I'd like to do an ENT examination'; 'Pancoast', 'Horner's', 'pleural effusion' to the patient; a smoking lecture in the same breath as the diagnosis; explaining each investigation at length
numbers: Hoarseness >3 weeks in an adult = laryngoscopy whatever else you find · here 2 months, cough 3 months, ~2 kg lost
Pack-years = cigarettes/day ÷ 20 × years · 20/day × 25 y = 25 pack-years

Pancoast: apex + Horner's (partial ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) + C8–T1 + shoulder pain + hoarseness · Horner's vs III nerve: partial ptosis + small pupil vs complete ptosis + dilated pupil, eye down and out
Effusion, four signs in order: reduced expansion · stony dullness · absent breath sounds · reduced vocal resonance · massive effusion pushes the trachea away; collapse pulls it towards
Investigations 1–3: CXR today → direct laryngoscopy → CT chest/abdomen/pelvis + biopsy; then PET-CT, MRI thoracic inlet, TFTs · Quitline 13 7848 · Cancer Council 13 11 20 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Initial observations supplied. Findings from the examiner on request. History closes at 3:00 — this station is scored in the second half.
stem: Mr Jason Whitfield, 28, warehouse team leader, presents with a three-day sore throat. He told the receptionist he needs something to fix it fast because he cannot afford to miss work. T 37.4, HR 78, RR 14, BP 124/76, SpO2 99% on air.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Ask the examiner for your examination findings
Explain the likely diagnosis and your management to the patient
Address the patient's concerns
time: 8 minutes: 0:00 greet, ★ agenda question up front, signpost · 0:45 history — course, cough/coryza/hoarseness, fever/nodes, ★ signposted red-flag sweep (saliva, drinking, muffled voice, mouth opening, one-sided, breathing, neck stiffness/rigors), ★ rheumatic fever + ATSI + medications (thyroid/mental health/arthritis), ICE and impact · 3:00 named findings from the examiner · 3:30 diagnosis in plain English — viral and why; never 'just a virus' · 4:30 ★ solve the work problem FIRST — certificate, employer letter, modified duties · 5:15 analgesia doses, fluids, rest · ★ three pillars (no benefit · harm · resistance) · 'how does that sit with you?' · 7:00 six named safety-net symptoms, destination, review 3–4 days, teach-back. He pushes three times; the 'just in case' script is a fail.

back.dx: Viral pharyngitis: three days, 6/10, bilateral, dry cough and runny/blocked nose from the start, voice normal, swallows and drinks fine, felt warm the first night only, no red flags, no rheumatic fever/ATSI risk, no meds (paracetamol irregularly), no allergies. Examiner: T 37.4, pharynx and tonsils erythematous without exudate, uvula midline, no lymphadenopathy, no trismus, normal voice, no rash, spleen not palpable — Centor 0–1. Explain: 'everything points to a virus — the same family that causes a cold: red inflamed throat but no pus, no swollen glands, normal temperature; the cough and blocked nose actually tell me it's viral; settles over 3–5 days, throat last to go' — and ★ 'viral doesn't mean mild; these can knock you flat.' Hidden agenda: short-staffed, supervisor questioning his reliability, frightened of losing the team-leader role — solve it BEFORE antibiotics: medical certificate, a short letter to the employer (unwell, infectious, rest gets him back faster), or duties away from the team; the register softens and the antibiotic request loses its force. Symptomatic: paracetamol 1 g qid max 4 g, ibuprofen 200–400 mg tds with food, fluids, rest, gargles/lozenges. Three pillars: wouldn't work (kills bacteria, not a virus — not a day shorter); can harm (~1 in 10 diarrhoea/rash; amoxicillin-clavulanate hepatitis/jaundice); costs later (resistance when he genuinely needs one). 'Last time I was better in two days' → validate natural history, never criticise the prior GP ('every throat is different'). No 'just in case' script — offer review in 3 days and name what would change your mind. Safety-net six symptoms + destination + review 3–4 days + teach-back.
plan: WIPE · ★ 'before we get into it — is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd sort out today? I'd rather know now' → 'antibiotics' (push 1) → 'fair enough — I might well be able to help with that; can I ask a few questions first so I know what we're dealing with?'
Course: onset, better/worse, /10 · cough, blocked nose, hoarseness (cough + coryza = viral evidence) · fever/shakes, neck lumps

★ Signposted: 'a few quick questions to make sure this isn't something more serious' — swallow saliva? managing to drink? voice muffled? mouth opens fully? much worse on one side? trouble/noisy breathing? neck stiffness, shakes and shivers? → all no

★ 'A couple of routine background questions I ask everyone with a sore throat' — rheumatic fever or heart-valve problem? Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander? regular medications — thyroid, mental health, arthritis? allergies? · ICE + impact: 'how's it affecting you day to day, and what were you worried it might be?' → work, short-staffed, team falls apart

★ 'Examiner, may I have my findings: temperature and observations; the tonsils and whether there is exudate; asymmetry or deviation of the uvula; anterior cervical nodes; trismus or a muffled voice; any rash; and whether the spleen is palpable' → viral picture

'Everything points to a virus…' with the four features · 'it should settle over three to five days, the throat can be the last thing to go' · 'so it's just a cold?' → ★ 'it's a viral infection, and viral doesn't mean mild — it can floor you for a few days' · 'does that make sense so far?'

★ 'Now, you mentioned work, and I want to deal with that first because I suspect that's the bit really weighing on you' — certificate for the days he needs; a short letter to the employer; or duties away from the team while infectious — 'which would be most useful?' → register softens

Analgesia with doses, fluids, rest, gargles/lozenges · ★ three pillars, signposted: 'you asked about antibiotics and I want to give you a proper answer rather than just saying no' — 1 wouldn't work · 2 can harm · 3 costs later · push 2 'better in two days last time' → natural history, no criticism · push 3 'some to have on hand?' → ★ no script; review in three days and what would change my mind

★ 'I'm going to ask a few quick questions to make sure this isn't something more serious.' / ★ 'Can you swallow your own saliva? Has your voice changed? Can you open your mouth fully? Is it much worse on one side?'

★ 'A couple of routine background questions I ask everyone — have you ever been told you had rheumatic fever? Do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander? Any regular medications — anything for thyroid, mental health or arthritis?'

'Everything points to a virus — the same family of bugs that causes a cold. Your throat is red and inflamed, but there's no pus on the tonsils, no swollen glands, and your temperature is normal. The cough and the blocked nose actually help me here.' / ★ 'Viral doesn't mean mild. These can knock you flat for a few days.'

★ 'Let me deal with work first, because I think that's the real worry.' / 'I can write you a medical certificate, and a letter to your employer if that would help — or we could ask about duties away from the team while you're infectious. Which would be most useful?'

★ 'I want to give you a proper answer rather than just saying no. First, they wouldn't work — antibiotics kill bacteria; they do nothing to a virus. Second, they can do harm — around one in ten get diarrhoea or a rash, and occasionally they inflame the liver. Third, they cost you later — every unnecessary course makes the bacteria more resistant, so next time you genuinely need one it's less likely to work.'

'Last time I was better in two days' → 'That's a really common experience and it makes sense — most sore throats settle in about that time either way, so it's hard to tell what did the work. If I thought an antibiotic would get you back to work faster, I'd write it right now.' (never criticise the previous prescriber)

'Some to have on hand, just in case?' → 'I'd rather see you again in three days than give you a script to hold. What would change my mind is pus on the tonsils, swollen glands, a real fever, or the cough disappearing — if any of that happens, I'll treat it.'

★ 'How does that sit with you — is there anything about it you're not comfortable with?' / 'Come straight back, or go to the emergency department, if you can't swallow your saliva or start drooling; your voice goes muffled or you can't open your mouth; the pain gets much worse on one side; a high fever with shakes; dizzy or can't keep fluids down; or short of breath. back.dx: Allergic rhinitis (hay fever) — perennial (cat on the bed, dust mite in an older fully carpeted house, grain dust at the depot, partner smoking indoors) with a spring pollen flare; persistent and moderate–severe by ARIA (sleep, work, taste, embarrassment). Six months, intermittent weeks, ★ bilateral, clear watery copious discharge, no smell, no blood; worse in spring, worse at home in the mornings and in bed; chemist antihistamines help for hours. Atopic package: itchy nose, sneezing fits, red streaming eyes, itchy throat, no chest symptoms (harder version: night cough, puffed at netball → asthma), childhood eczema, sister asthma, mother hay fever. Occasional decongestant spray ('not really a medication') — a week here and there: counsel the 5-day limit, stop it. Two exclusions signposted and clean: chronic rhinosinusitis (no facial pain/pressure, fever, PND, upper toothache, smell loss) and sinonasal/nasopharyngeal malignancy (no epistaxis, weight loss, neck lumps, unilateral ear blockage, diplopia, facial numbness). Hidden agenda: aunt had 'a growth in her nose' — surfaces at the red-flag questions; reassure with the specific negatives, after the screen. PEFE normal → 'a normal examination doesn't change my diagnosis — it reassures me there's no infection, polyp or growth; hay fever is diagnosed on the story'. Three reasons: clear watery bilateral discharge; the travelling symptoms (sneeze, itch, eyes); trigger exposure + family atopy. 'Why all year?' → perennial (mite, cat) plus seasonal (pollen). Mechanism: allergen → mast cell → histamine → inflammation and leaky dilated vessels → blockage and watery discharge (two waves: early histamine = itch/sneeze/run, antihistamines work; late inflammatory cells = blockage, needs the steroid, 1–2 weeks). Plan: cat out of the bedroom, mite covers, hot-wash bedding, lift/vacuum the carpet, recirculate on pollen days; mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily (technique, 2 weeks); cetirizine 10 mg; eye drops; stop the decongestant; smoke-free home, Quitline; review 4–6 weeks with the spray; escalate to combination spray or testing/immunotherapy if uncontrolled.

I'll ask some questions to find the cause, then we'll make the best plan. Is that all right?' · ★ 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' (she deflects — note it, move on)

Is that all right with you?' / 'Before I start — was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'

My aunt had a growth in her nose' → 'Thank you for telling me — I'm glad you have, because it explains why you've been so worried, and it's exactly what those questions were for. Let me examine you and then I'll tell you what I think.'
★ 'A normal examination doesn't change my diagnosis — it reassures me there's no infection, no polyp and no growth. Hay fever is diagnosed on the story.'

★ 'Most likely you have allergic rhinitis, which most people know as hay fever. Three reasons: the discharge is clear, watery and from both sides; you have the symptoms that travel with it — sneezing, itchy nose, red watery eyes; and you're around the common triggers — a cat on your bed, an older carpeted house full of dust mite, grain dust at work, smoke in the house — with hay fever and asthma in the family.' / 'Yours is year-round from the cat and the dust mite, with a spring flare from pollen.'

Mechanism: ★ 'An allergen activates a mast cell, which releases histamine, which causes inflammation and widens the small blood vessels in the lining of your nose — that swelling and leaking is the blockage and the watery discharge, and it's why antihistamines help.' / 'Why don't antihistamines fix the blockage?' → 'Two waves — the first is histamine, itch and sneeze; the second, hours later, is inflammatory cells arriving, which causes the blockage; that's what the steroid spray is for, and why it takes a week or two.'

★ 'Use it every day, not just on bad days — aim it outwards towards your ear, don't sniff hard, and give it up to two weeks.' / 'Can I ask you to stop the decongestant spray? Used more than about five days it makes the blockage worse.' / ★ 'Come back sooner if it becomes one-sided, nosebleeds, coloured or bloody discharge, facial pain or fever, loss of smell, one ear blocking, or a lump in your neck.'

Assess and treat the asthma NOW: RR, SpO2, peak flow; salbutamol via spacer; ± oral prednisolone; his own reliever + spacer, written action plan, spirometry with reversibility once settled — not his sister's inhaler. HIV seroconversion; complications (orbital cellulitis, meningitis, sepsis — screened, negative).

If asked what you'd assess before disposition: RR, SpO2, HR, peak flow, work of breathing, speech; salbutamol 4–12 puffs via spacer, repeat as needed; oral prednisolone if moderate–severe; reassess; spirometry with reversibility once settled; own reliever + spacer + written action plan · rhinosinusitis: saline, INCS (mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily), cetirizine 10 mg, analgesia, topical decongestant max 3–5 days

Variant 1 — puffy left eye, painful lateral gaze, diplopia: EMERGENCY — orbital (post-septal) cellulitis until imaging proves otherwise: ABC, obs incl. temperature; visual acuity, pupils/RAPD, eye movements, proptosis; IV access, blood cultures, FBE, CRP; empirical IV antibiotics without waiting for imaging; urgent CT sinuses/orbits, same-day ENT + ophthalmology; from Kadina ★ MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — start treatment locally while retrieval is arranged. 'Could it just be periorbital?' → painful eye movement, diplopia and proptosis = post-septal; changes oral → IV, mandates imaging and specialist review

Variant 2 — purple spots on the legs + shocking headache: non-blanching purpura in an unwell adult = meningococcal disease — immediate IV/IM benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone before transfer; cultures only if no delay; IV fluids; MedSTAR; notify public health, contact prophylaxis · Variant 3 — muffled, leaning forward, drooling: epiglottitis/quinsy — no throat examination or instrumentation, upright, calm, oxygen, ENT + anaesthetics for airway in a controlled setting, IV antibiotics + steroids, retrieval called early

Variant 4 — day 12, improved around day 6 then worse: thick green discharge, severe right cheek pain, fever two nights → double worsening + fever + severe unilateral pain + >10 days = bacterial rhinosinusitis → amoxicillin, saline, analgesia, review 3 days · Examiner: 'allergic with no fever? plenty of colds are afebrile' → can't exclude viral (leading alternative); favour allergic on atopy, itch/sneeze, clear discharge, triggers — and a virus commonly triggers both flares · 'image the sinuses?' → no; clinical diagnosis; image urgently only for orbital/intracranial suspicion · 'asthma secure on a borrowed inhaler?' → supportive not diagnostic — spirometry once settled; treat the exacerbation now on clinical grounds · 'why sexual history for a blocked nose?' → the complaint was undifferentiated malaise; HIV seroconversion, chlamydial/gonococcal pharyngitis and conjunctivitis

setting: General practice. Vitals in the stem. Examination findings on a card when you ask — Version A card (hepatitis) or Version B card (gastroenteritis). Six minutes of history.
stem: Jane Whitmore, 30, has come in feeling unwell. She reports there has been an incident at work. No further detail is given. T 38.1, HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
You will be given the examination findings on screen or card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 0:00 open + concern · 0:30 'unwell' in four questions · ★ 1:15 'you mentioned an incident at work — tell me more' · say the exposure back ('urine and faeces') · ★ four exposure questions: PPE · fluid in eyes/mouth · incident report · head injury · 2:15 three infection groups: hepatitis (jaundice, RUQ pain, nausea, dark urine/pale stools) · gastroenteritis (diarrhoea loose vs watery, blood, fever/chills) · leptospirosis (rash, nodes, calf pain, red eyes) · ★ 4:15 PTSD screen — coping, mood, sleep, nightmares, avoidance · 5:00 the rest fast incl. hepatitis vaccination · examination by name incl. urine dipstick and calves · diagnosis with reasons · differential with named organisms + leptospirosis + psychological · safety-net, notification, teach-back.

back.dx: Version A — acute viral hepatitis (A or E) after falling chest-deep into sewage five days ago while sampling for the water utility (full PPE; doesn't know if fluid entered mouth/eyes; incident report filed; no head injury): five days of fever, aches, night sweats, anorexia, RUQ pain, mild nausea, no diarrhoea; card — no jaundice yet, T 38.1, tender hepatomegaly, RUQ tenderness, no splenomegaly, no rash, no calf tenderness, ★ urine dipstick bilirubin positive (bilirubinuria precedes visible jaundice — the point of the card). Explain: 'acute hepatitis — inflammation of the liver — most probably hepatitis A or a close relative, hepatitis E; both picked up by swallowing something contaminated with sewage; not yellow yet but the pigment is already building up in the urine'; settles over weeks, doesn't become chronic; infectious via the bowel — handwashing, household vaccination. Version B card (no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, mild lower abdominal tenderness, dipstick normal; history of loose stools 4–5/day, lower abdominal pain) → gastroenteritis, said cleanly: 'not hepatitis' — no hedging with 'might be early hepatitis'. Differentials aloud: sewage-borne — gastroenteritis viral (rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus), bacterial (Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Campylobacter), protozoal (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba); leptospirosis (rat urine; no calf pain/red eyes but treatable — test); liver abscess (needs ultrasound); PTSD/adjustment reaction (replaying it, two dreams, hasn't been back down); further down EBV, CMV, HIV, syphilis, travel infections, lymphoma/leukaemia, thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, coeliac, autoimmune ('cancer?' → 'not worried about that here — it's on the list I work through'). Plan: LFTs, clotting, hepatitis and leptospirosis serology, liver ultrasound; rest, fluids, no alcohol; notify hepatitis A; vaccinate household (3-year-old son); employer letter — off work while infectious; ReturnToWorkSA; safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, can't keep fluids down, turning yellow; review 2 days, talk about the dreams properly then.
plan: WIPE · 'I understand you've been unwell and something happened at work — I'll ask questions, examine you, then explain' · ★ 'is there anything you're particularly worried this might be?'
'Unwell' — feverish/tired/pain? duration (5 days), constant, worse, better/worse, impact (2 days off) — four questions, then move

★ 'You mentioned an incident at work — can you tell me more?' → slipped climbing into a sewer, fell into sewage → react: 'that sounds horrible, thank you for telling me — so you were exposed to urine and faeces'

★ Four exposure questions: PPE? (full kit) · ★ fluid in eyes or mouth? (doesn't know) · incident report? (yes — 'that matters, it protects you if you need time off') · ★ head injury or other injury? (landed on side)

Hepatitis: jaundice, abdominal pain + site (A: RUQ; B: lower), nausea/vomiting, dark urine/pale stools · gastroenteritis: diarrhoea — loose or watery, blood/mucus (A: none; B: loose ×4–5, no blood), fever/chills · leptospirosis screen: rash, nodes, ★ severe calf aches, ★ red/sore eyes → no (the mark is for asking)

★ 'Falling into a sewer would shake anyone — how have you been coping? Mood? Sleep — nightmares or flashbacks? Avoiding going back? Other stress?' → replaying it, two dreams, hasn't been back — 'thank you, that's important and we'll come back to it'

Fast: weight/appetite/lumps · travel · new partners ('I ask everyone') · chest pain/SOB · PMHx, meds, allergies · alcohol, smoking · ★ 'have you had hepatitis vaccinations for work?' (thinks so, not sure)

★ Examination by name: appearance/hydration · jaundice sclerae and under the tongue · vitals · nodes · abdominal tenderness and site · liver size/tenderness · spleen · ★ calf tenderness, conjunctival suffusion · rash · ★ urine dipstick → Version A card

Diagnosis + reasons (fever, liver pain, tender enlarged liver, bile pigment in urine) · 'serious? damage?' → settles over weeks, not chronic · 'infectious — my little boy?' → bowel route, handwashing, vaccinate family · differentials with named organisms · plan, notification, employer, safety-net · review 2 days + the dreams · teach-back: 'what will you tell your partner tonight?'
ask: 'Is there anything in particular you are worried this might be?' / ★ 'You mentioned an incident at work — can you tell me more about that?' / 'That sounds horrible. Thank you for telling me.' / 'So you were exposed to urine and faeces.'
★ 'Were you wearing protective equipment?' / ★ 'Did any fluid get into your eyes or your mouth?' / 'Did you file an incident report?' / ★ 'Did you hit your head?'
'Is the diarrhoea loose, or completely watery? Any blood?' / 'Any severe muscle aches, particularly in your calves? Any red or sore eyes?'
★ 'Falling into a sewer would shake anyone. How have you been coping?' / ★ 'Any nightmares? Have you been avoiding going back to work?'
★ 'Could I have the examination findings, including a urine dipstick' — and the calves and conjunctivae by name

★ 'Acute hepatitis means inflammation of the liver, picked up by swallowing something contaminated. You're not yellow yet, but the urine test shows the pigment is already building up, and that comes first.'

Version B: 'The examination changes what I think, so let me be clear: you're not yellow, your liver is not enlarged or tender, your urine test is normal — this is not hepatitis. What you have is gastroenteritis — an infection of the bowel, viral, bacterial or protozoal — most likely from a bug you swallowed when you fell in.'

'Leptospirosis comes from rat urine in sewers — you don't have the severe calf pain or red eyes that usually go with it, but it's treatable, so I want to test for it.' / 'Cancer?' → 'No — I'm not worried about that at all here. I mention it because it's on the list I work through, and nothing points that way.'

'Will my little boy catch it?' → 'It's infectious through the bowel, so handwashing, not preparing food for others, and I'll arrange vaccination for the people you live with.' / 'If this goes to public health I'll lose my job' → ★ 'Hepatitis A is notifiable and I have to report it — but the notification is what protects you: it confirms this came from work, it supports your ReturnToWorkSA claim, and it gets your workmates checked. It is not a complaint about you.'

★ 'Come back straight away — or go to hospital — if you become confused or drowsy, if you bruise or bleed, if you cannot keep fluids down, or if you go yellow.' / 'Just to check I explained it clearly — what will you tell your partner tonight?'
pefe: Role-player: Jane, 30, sampling technician, regional water utility; partner, 3-year-old son; non-smoker, 4–6 drinks/week; no meds/allergies/PMHx; one partner six years; no travel; thinks she had work hepatitis shots. Fell chest-deep five days ago, full PPE, doesn't know about mouth/eyes, report filed. Embarrassed, disgusted, matter-of-fact; softens and volunteers the dreams if you're warm; keeps them if you're brisk. Hidden agenda: hasn't been back down, two dreams, worried she can't do the job — only if asked about coping/sleep/mood/work, else 'doctor, can I ask you something else?' at the end. Tearful at avoidance

Cards — Version A: no jaundice, T 38.1, tender hepatomegaly, RUQ tenderness, no splenomegaly, no rash, no calf tenderness, dipstick bilirubin POSITIVE · Version B: no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, mild lower abdominal tenderness, dipstick normal

Variant 1 — jaundice + calf tenderness + creatinine 210: leptospirosis (Weil's) — 'carried in rat urine, a recognised hazard of sewer work; treatable with antibiotics, start today rather than wait; admit' — doxycycline or benzylpenicillin VERIFY TG · Variant 4 — bloody diarrhoea with high fever: bacterial colitis — stool sample today, UEC; ★ no antibiotics or antidiarrhoeals yet (STEC → HUS risk); wait for the result

Variant 3 — flat answers, never mentions the dreams: 'That was a frightening thing. Some people find afterwards they replay it, dream about it, or feel uneasy going back — has any of that happened?' → normal in the first weeks, review at a month if persisting (PTSD needs >1 month; before that acute stress reaction); book the review

Automatic fails: ★ never asks about the incident · ★ never asks fluid in eyes/mouth · ★ never asks head injury · ★ never screens mood/sleep/coping · ★ Version B still diagnoses hepatitis after a normal card · agreeing not to notify (Variant 2)

SA: notify hepatitis A/E, leptospirosis, salmonellosis, shigellosis, campylobacteriosis, STEC; ReturnToWorkSA for the claim; SafeWork SA for the confined space; healthdirect 1800 022 222; TIS 131 450; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
fails: Never asking about the incident — the lead point of the stem ★
Never asking whether fluid entered the eyes or mouth; never asking about a head injury ★
No mood, sleep, nightmare or avoidance screen — or 'how is your mood?' alone ★
Version B: still calling it hepatitis, or hedging 'it might be early hepatitis', after a normal card ★
Agreeing not to notify ★
'An abdominal examination' and stopping — no dipstick, no calves, no conjunctivae; two minutes spent on 'unwell'
A differential without named organisms, without leptospirosis, without a psychological differential; no reaction when she says what happened
numbers: Hepatitis A incubation 15–50 days (mean ~28) · hepatitis E 15–60 days · neither chronic in the immunocompetent VERIFY · jaundice visible at bilirubin ~40–50 µmol/L — bilirubinuria comes first
PTSD >1 month; before that acute stress reaction; review at 4 weeks · gastro work exclusion until 48 h after symptoms settle, longer for food handlers VERIFY SA Health
Organisms: rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus · Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Campylobacter · Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba · leptospirosis: calves, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, AKI
Notifiable SA: hep A/E, leptospirosis, salmonellosis, shigellosis, campylobacteriosis, STEC

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Vitals on request. Examination findings on card/screen: febrile, generalised lymphadenopathy, all other systems normal — ask for palms and soles, spleen and mouth. Six minutes of history.
stem: Ben, 27, hospitality, attends alone: feeling unwell for eight days; for the last two days he has noticed a rash. BP 110/71, HR 88, RR 12, SpO2 98%, T 38.5.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6 minutes)
Physical examination findings will be provided
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. ★ 'Is my patient haemodynamically stable?' · define unwell · rash: redness/blisters/bruising, where it started, spread (not 'worse'), itch/pain, ★ blanches? · fever, travel · ★ 'do you use condoms?' → the hinge — 90 s of sexual history, no apologising: stable partner, multiple, ★ male/female/both, ★ oral/vaginal/anal ('tells me which sites to swab'), previous STI, alcohol/drugs · four rapid screens incl. ★ genital sores/ulcers now OR in the past months (the chancre) · meningism ×4 · immunisations, antibiotics · closing sweep — night sweats, lumps, new medications · findings aloud + ★ palms/soles, spleen, mouth · name HIV and syphilis with reasons · pause after the news · grouped differentials · ★ name the HIV test and seek consent · three-site swabs · contact tracing anonymised · safety-net.

back.dx: HIV seroconversion illness ± secondary syphilis. Eight days of fever, chills, aches, headaches, exhaustion (sick twice), mild early sore throat; two days of a flat red blotchy non-itchy non-painful ★ blanching rash chest → back and upper arms; lumps in neck and axillae, night sweats, appetite down, weight steady. Sexual history: MSM, several casual partners in six months, no stable partner, never condoms, oral and anal insertive and receptive, never diagnosed, alcohol involved, never injected, no travel. ★ Hidden detail: a small painless penile sore ~two months ago that healed alone — the primary chancre, given only to a specific sores/ulcers question. Findings: febrile, generalised lymphadenopathy, ★ lesions on the palms (ask), no splenomegaly, mouth clear. To Ben: 'I'm concerned about a sexually transmitted infection — specifically HIV, or syphilis, or possibly both'; reasons from history (MSM, no condoms, casual partners; eight days of fever/aches/headache/exhaustion, spreading rash) and examination (fever, glands everywhere, rash on the palms — characteristic of syphilis; the painless sore fits); 'they look identical at this stage, which is exactly why we test for both'. Long silence → 'Am I going to die?' → pause, 'what's going through your mind?' (uncle died of AIDS in the 90s) → HIV today is not that illness: treatment, normal lifespan, undetectable = untransmissible; syphilis cured with an injection; don't promise a result you don't have. Differentials grouped: meningococcal (unlikely — blanching, no meningism) · other STIs (herpes, mpox, disseminated gonococcal) · rash viruses (EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, measles) · travel (dengue, Ross River — no travel) · infective endocarditis · leukaemia/lymphoma · drug reaction (nothing new). Plan: bloods today — ★ 'one of them is for HIV and I need your permission for that specifically' — syphilis (treponemal EIA + RPR), hepatitis, FBE; swabs throat, anorectal, first-pass urine; sexual health clinic referral; phone with results; partner notification anonymised via the clinic; safety-net non-blanching rash, headache with stiff neck/photophobia, much worse → 000/ED.
plan: ★ 'Examiner, is my patient haemodynamically stable? BP, pulse, RR, sats, temperature?' → stable, T 38.5 · WIPE · 'over a week is a long time, and a new rash is unsettling — questions, findings, then what I think'

'Unwell — low energy, sleepy, or feverish?' · duration 8 days, constant, worse, sick twice · rash: 'redness, blisters, or bruising?' · where it started, has it spread (never 'worse') · itchy/painful (neither) · ★ 'does it fade when you press it?' → yes → aloud: 'a blanching rash makes a serious blood infection much less likely — I'll still check the neck symptoms'
Temperature measured? chills? paracetamol? · travel (none) · sexually active? · ★ 'do you use condoms?' → pause → 'no, not really' → everything now pivots

'Thanks for being straight with me. A few questions about your sex life — routine when someone's unwell with a rash, and it stays between us. Okay?' → stable partner? · multiple? · ★ 'male, female or both?' → men · ★ 'oral, anal, or both — I ask because it tells me which sites to swab' → both, both ways · previous STI? · alcohol/drugs?

Four screens: ★ 'any sores or ulcers on your genitals — now, or in the past few months?' → painless sore two months ago, healed · groin lumps · jaundice/abdominal pain/nausea · discharge/dysuria · scrotal pain · ★ meningism: dizziness, headache (yes), stiff neck, photophobia (no) · childhood immunisations, sore throat/coryza/cough, recent antibiotics, diarrhoea · bites/bushwalking, animals, chest pain/palpitations/dental work, ★ injected drugs (never)

Closing sweep: weight loss (no), appetite (down), lumps (neck, axillae), night sweats (yes), FHx cancer, medications/anything new, allergies, joints, smoking/alcohol — keep leukaemia/lymphoma on the spoken list

'May I have the examination findings?' → say them aloud: febrile, generalised lymphadenopathy, other systems normal → ★ 'can I confirm — rash on the palms or soles? splenomegaly? oral ulceration?' → lesions on the palms; no spleen; mouth clear

★ Name HIV and syphilis with reasons from history and examination · 'I can't tell which by looking — they look identical at this stage, which is why we test for both' · silence → ★ 'that's a lot to hear — what's going through your mind?' · uncle → honest hope, no promised result

Grouped differentials · plan: bloods — ★ HIV test named, consent sought · syphilis, hepatitis, FBE · ★ swabs throat, back passage, urine · sexual health clinic · phone with results · 'do I have to tell anyone?' → partners need testing; clinic does it anonymously · safety-net → summary · 'anything I haven't covered?'
ask: ★ 'Examiner, is my patient haemodynamically stable?' / 'When you say unwell — low in energy, sleepy, or feverish?' / 'Is it redness, blisters, or bruising?' / ★ 'Does it fade when you press on it?'

'Do you use condoms?' → 'Thank you for being straight with me.' / ★ 'I'm going to ask a few questions about your sex life — they're routine when someone's unwell with a rash, and this stays between us. Is that okay?' (not 'sorry, I have to ask this')

★ 'Are your partners male, female, or both?' / ★ 'What kind of sex do you have — oral, vaginal, anal? I ask because it tells me which sites to swab.' / 'Have you ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection? Has any of it happened when you'd been drinking or using drugs?'
★ 'Any sores or ulcers on your genitals — now, or in the past few months?' / 'Any dizziness, headache, stiff neck, or eyes sensitive to light?' / 'Have you injected any drugs?'

'So he is febrile with generalised lymphadenopathy and every other system normal. ★ Can I confirm whether there is rash on the palms or soles, whether there is splenomegaly, and whether there is any oral ulceration?'

'Ben, I'm concerned about the possibility of a sexually transmitted infection — specifically HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus, or syphilis, or possibly both. From your history: you have sex with men, you don't use condoms, several casual partners; eight days of fever, aches, headaches and exhaustion, and a rash that spread from your chest. On examination: a fever, enlarged glands all over, and the rash involves your palms, which is quite characteristic of syphilis. That painless sore two months ago fits too.' / ★ 'I can't tell which of these it is by looking at you, which is exactly why we test for both.'

'Am I going to die?' → (two-second pause) 'That's a lot to hear. What's going through your mind?' → 'HIV today is not the illness it was in the nineties. With treatment, people live a normal life span and cannot pass it on. And syphilis is cured with an injection. But I don't want to promise you a result I don't have — let's test and find out.'

'The most serious one I considered is meningococcal disease — but your rash fades when pressed and you've no neck stiffness or light sensitivity, so I think that's unlikely. Then other STIs — herpes, mpox, a spread-out form of gonorrhoea; the rash viruses — glandular fever, CMV, toxoplasmosis, measles; travel infections like dengue and Ross River, much less likely with no travel; infective endocarditis; blood cancers such as leukaemia and lymphoma; and a medication reaction, but you haven't started anything new.'

★ 'Some blood tests today — one of them is for HIV, and I need your permission for that specifically — plus syphilis, hepatitis and a blood count. And swabs from your throat, your back passage and a urine sample, because we swab every site.' / ★ 'The clinic can notify your partners anonymously — your name does not have to go anywhere. You won't have to make those calls yourself.'

'If that rash stops fading when you press it, or you get a bad headache with a stiff neck or light hurting your eyes, or you feel much worse — call 000 or go straight to emergency.' / Non-blanching variant: 'I'm going to stop and act on something — that rash doesn't fade, and with your fever and headache that could be meningococcal disease. I'm giving you an antibiotic injection now and calling an ambulance. I'm not waiting for tests, because waiting is the risk.'
pefe: Role-player: Ben Whitaker, 27, bar supervisor, share house, regional SA; fit, no meds/allergies; social smoker, weekend drinker. Says 'partners' until asked gender directly. Pauses before 'no, I don't use condoms'. Goes guarded (one-word answers) if you apologise or look uncomfortable. setting: General practice. Examination card at six minutes — three versions: (1) hepatitis card, (2) HIV seroconversion card (scripted here), (3) endocarditis card. Six minutes of history.
stem: Gary, 26, attends alone feeling unwell. He has recently returned from an overseas trip in South-East Asia, and used heroin while he was away.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6 minutes)
You will be given a physical examination card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the fear in one sentence · ★ signpost three blocks: the unwellness, the trip, the heroin · define, time, impact · ★ full travel history A B C D E F G S (don't accept 'just fun with mates'); write down 'no sex overseas' · ★ heroin in three steps IN ORDER: open question → route → shared needles · ★ three BBV boxes every time: hepatitis · HIV · injection/endocarditis · ★ go BACK for the sexual history ('ever been sexually active?') · ★ guilt ×3 → mood, anhedonia, self-harm, use since · card — interrogate for jaundice, organomegaly, murmur, injection sites, dipstick · name the version's diagnosis with reasons · grouped differentials · ★ HIV test named, consent · malaria films · harm reduction · confidentiality with the notification caveat · safety-net.

back.dx: Version 2 — HIV seroconversion illness: a week of no energy and fever, constant, worsening, bed-bound two days; three weeks in Indonesia, back two weeks; one night injected heroin — first ever use — one needle shared between the group, none since; street food nightly; pre-travel GP gave a hepatitis shot; no bites, sick contacts, animals, tattoos, transfusion; 'no sex overseas' — but ever sexually active: yes, never condoms, multiple partners at times, women. HIV box positive: sore throat, chest rash, fever/chills, drenching night sweats, some weight loss, neck lumps; hepatitis box negative; injection box negative. Card: T 38.2, morbilliform rash, generalised lymphadenopathy, exudative tonsillitis; on request — no jaundice, no hepatosplenomegaly, no murmur, injection sites unremarkable, dipstick negative. EBV is the trap answer — say it is the closest mimic. Explain: 'I'm concerned you contracted HIV when you shared that needle — the first stage, seroconversion illness, causes exactly this: fever, sore throat, rash, glands, night sweats, exhaustion — it looks like flu and is very commonly missed'; reasons — the route, the symptoms, the findings. 'I've ruined my life over one stupid night' → pause, 'what's going through your mind?' → concern not result; treatment today — normal lifespan, undetectable = untransmissible. Differentials: EBV/CMV/toxoplasma · hepatitis B and C ('your shot covers A and B; no vaccine for C — curable with tablets 8–12 weeks') · infective endocarditis (no murmur, reassuring) · malaria, dengue, typhoid (films) · syphilis · leukaemia/lymphoma · depression/anxiety. Plan: ★ HIV test with specific permission (4th-gen Ag/Ab ± RNA, repeat 6 weeks), HBV/HCV, syphilis, EBV, LFT, FBE, thick/thin films ×3; sexual health referral; confidentiality honest — notifiable, contacts traced sensitively, name not given; NSP and take-home naloxone 'not because I assume you'll use again'; mood review next week; safety-net confusion/drowsiness, jaundice, chest pain/SOB → ED/000.
plan: WIPE · 'a week of that, and not getting out of bed, is frightening — let's work through it' · ★ 'three things I want to cover: what the unwellness feels like, your trip, and the heroin'
'Low in energy, sleepy, or feverish?' · duration, constant, worse, better with anything, impact (off work, bed-bound)

★ Travel A B C D E F G S: where/how long (Indonesia, 3 weeks) · 'what did you actually DO?' (push past 'fun with mates') · bites/bushwalking · contacts — sick people, animals, farms · drugs (coming) · exposures — tattoos, piercings, dental, surgery, transfusion · food/water (street food nightly) · GP before — vaccines, malaria tablets (hepatitis shot) · sex overseas → 'no' → WRITE IT DOWN

★ Heroin, three steps: 'the notes mention you used heroin — can you tell me more about that?' (let him talk: one night, first time ever, 'I feel so guilty') → 'how did you use it — how did it go in?' (injected) → 'did you share needles?' (one needle between us) · 'thank you for being honest'

★ Three BBV boxes: hepatitis — jaundice, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, dark urine/pale stools (no) · HIV — sore throat, rash, fever/chills/night sweats, weight loss, lumps, diarrhoea (yes, yes, soaking, some, neck) · injection/endocarditis — injection-site redness/swelling, chest pain, palpitations, hand/palm marks (no)

★ Go back: 'you told me you didn't have sex while away, and I accept that — but these same infections are also passed on sexually, so if you have picked one up I need to know who else needs testing. Have you EVER been sexually active?' → yes · condoms (never) · multiple (at times) · ★ male/female/both (women)

★ Guilt ×3 picked up: 'how are you coping? mood? still enjoying things? — I ask everyone — any thoughts of harming yourself? any use since you got back?' · meds, allergies, conditions, alcohol/smoking, FHx · 'what were you particularly worried this might be?' → 'something I can't get rid of'
Card read aloud → ★ 'can I also confirm: jaundice? hepatosplenomegaly? murmur? injection sites? dipstick?' → all negative; T 38.2 → excludes versions 1 and 3 out loud

Name HIV seroconversion with reasons · silence → pause → 'what's going through your mind?' → concern not result; treatment today · differentials grouped (EBV closest) · plan: ★ HIV test named + permission · HBV/HCV, syphilis, EBV, LFT, FBE, ★ malaria films · sexual health referral · confidentiality with the notification caveat · NSP + naloxone · mood review next week · safety-net · summary
ask: 'When you say unwell — low in energy, sleepy, or feverish?' / ★ 'There are three things I want to cover: the unwellness, your trip, and the heroin.'

★ 'What did you actually do while you were over there?' / 'Any tattoos, piercings, surgery or a blood transfusion while you were away? And did you see a doctor before you went, for vaccinations or malaria tablets?' / 'Any sexual contact while you were away?'
★ 'Can you tell me more about that?' (first heroin question, then let him talk) / 'Can you tell me how you used it — how it went in?' / 'Did you share needles?' — in that order
'Thank you for being honest, that helps me a lot. Sharing a needle can pass on infections carried in blood, so I need to check for those.' → hepatitis box, HIV box, injection box
★ 'These infections are also passed on sexually, so I need to come back to this. Have you ever been sexually active? Do you use condoms? Ever had multiple partners? Male, female, or both?'

'You've said a few times that you feel guilty. How are you coping with it? How's your mood been? Still enjoying the things you normally enjoy? — I ask everyone this — any thoughts of harming yourself? Any use since you got back?'
'May I have the examination findings? ★ And can I confirm: any jaundice? Any hepatosplenomegaly? Any murmur? Anything at the injection sites? And the urine dipstick?'

'Gary, I'm concerned about the possibility that you contracted HIV when you shared that needle. The very first stage is called seroconversion illness, and it causes exactly this picture: fever, sore throat, a rash, swollen glands, night sweats and exhaustion. It looks so like the flu that it's very commonly missed.' → 'I've ruined my life' → (pause) 'That's a hard thing to hear. What's going through your mind?' → 'First, we don't know yet — this is a concern, not a result. Second, if it is HIV, treatment today is extremely effective: a normal life span and, on treatment, cannot pass it on.'

★ 'The hepatitis shot covers A and B. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C' — 'but it is now curable with tablets, usually over two to three months.' / ★ 'One of these is an HIV test — I need your permission for that specifically.' / 'Also hepatitis B and C, syphilis, glandular fever, liver tests, a blood count and malaria films.'

'What you tell me is confidential, though some infections have to be reported to public health so contacts can be traced — that's done sensitively and your name isn't given to your contacts.' (never 'everything is completely confidential') / 'I'll give you information about free needle and syringe services and take-home naloxone — not because I assume you'll use again, but because it costs nothing to have.'
pefe: Role-player: Gary Whelan, 26, warehouse worker, two housemates; weekend drinker, few cigarettes; no meds/allergies/hospital. Slow, flat, genuinely unwell. Vague on open travel questions — detail only to specific ones. 'No' to sex overseas, then waits; fully forthcoming if you come back. Says 'I feel so guilty' at least three times (a fourth, heavier, if ignored). If 'did you share needles?' is your FIRST heroin question: 'yes' flatly, no guilt, no first-time detail. At the diagnosis: long pause, 'I've ruined my life over one stupid night'; if rushed: 'you're just saying that'. If total confidentiality promised: 'so nobody else will ever know?'. Hidden agenda: 'scared I've given myself something I can't get rid of'

Card Version 2: T 38.2, morbilliform rash, generalised lymphadenopathy, exudative tonsillitis; no jaundice, no organomegaly, no murmur, injection sites clean, dipstick negative · Version 1: tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, urine bilirubin positive → acute viral hepatitis, most likely B or C via the needle ('if B we vaccinate those around you; if C no vaccine but curable') · Version 3: murmur + raised JVP, bibasal crepitations, ankle oedema → ★ infective endocarditis complicated by heart failure — 'you have heart failure' is the fail; 'endocarditis stays primary because acute valvular regurgitation explains the failure; heart failure alone misses the treatable cause and delays cultures and antibiotics' — hospital today, 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics, modified Duke

Tests: 4th-gen HIV Ag/Ab ± HIV RNA, repeat 6 weeks; PEP window 72 h (passed) · HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HBs; HCV Ab + RNA · syphilis · EBV/CMV · LFT, FBE, CRP · thick and thin films ×3 · dipstick: urobilinogen normal, bilirubin never normal
Harm reduction: NSP, take-home naloxone, ADIS 1300 13 1340 VERIFY · mood review next week; Lifeline 13 11 14 · HCV DAA cure typically 8–12 weeks VERIFY
SA: sexual health (SHINE SA/Clinic 275); notifiable — HIV, hepatitis B/C, malaria; DASSA; TIS 131 450; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33
fails: 'Did you share needles?' as the first heroin question — a memorised recall that loses the guilt and the detail ★
Not coming back for the sexual history after 'no sex overseas' — the most designed trap in the station ★
Asking only the hepatitis box (the version you revised) — all three boxes, every time
Hearing 'guilty' four times and never asking about mood or self-harm
'Everything you tell me is completely confidential' — not for a notifiable disease; 'you have heart failure' in Version 3
Accepting 'just having fun with mates' as a travel history; reading the card silently without asking for jaundice, organomegaly, murmur, injection sites
Plan without naming the HIV test and seeking consent; no malaria films; harm reduction omitted or delivered with judgement; rushing past his silence

Hepatitis: HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HBs; HCV Ab + RNA · HCV cure with DAAs 8–12 weeks VERIFY · hepatitis shot = A and B; no vaccine for C

Dipstick: urobilinogen normal; bilirubin never normal

setting: General practice, Kadina. Nine-minute station. He coughs harshly and repeatedly throughout — the acting is data. Observations from the examiner include the fifth vital sign. Two headings: infection, and malignancy.
stem: Jack Mullins, 30, has come in feeling unwell and feverish. He is a known case of HIV and stopped his antiretroviral medication six months ago.
tasks: Take a history from the patient (about 6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings, or read them from the card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 9 minutes: 0:00 ★ all five observations incl. SpO2 · one empathic sentence · ★ 'I can hear that cough' · unwell and fever explored separately · 1:30 HIV history — diagnosed when, ★ why stopped (no moralising), follow-up, complications · 2:15 ★ signposted whole-body infection screen (breadth not depth; characterise the cough in three questions) incl. sexual history despite HIV, injecting, chest pain · 4:45 ★ open the malignancy heading — weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, mouth ulcers/patches, purple marks, haemoptysis, smoking, asbestos, moles · mood · 5:45 examination in one run incl. vocal resonance and a full node survey · ★ the white patch — painful? scrapes off? colour? where? · ★ 'normal chest but febrile, tachypnoeic, hypoxic — in advanced HIV a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia' · 7:00 pneumonia named and reasoned · opportunistic infection as a concern not a diagnosis · ★ the cancers named honestly, reaction contained · other infections individually · restart ART · safety-net.

back.dx: Pneumonia in a man with untreated HIV (ART stopped six months ago — felt well, tablets nauseated him, long trip to Adelaide; no specialist review for a year; no prior complications), with opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis, TB) and malignancy on the list. Three to four days feverish with rigors, worsening, paracetamol useless; dry cough; new exertional breathlessness on stairs; everything else negative; smokes 10/day; mood flat. Examiner: alert, no rash/jaundice, mildly dehydrated; T 38.0, HR 104, BP 118/74, RR 24, ★ SpO2 92% RA; ★ a white patch in the mouth — scrapes off, on tongue and buccal mucosa (candidiasis — but describe before naming: Kaposi = violaceous, raised, hard palate, doesn't scrape; OHL = white, corrugated, lateral tongue, doesn't scrape); no lymphadenopathy; ★ respiratory examination entirely normal; HS dual; abdomen and dipstick normal. To the examiner: 'although the chest is normal he is febrile, tachypnoeic and hypoxic — in advanced HIV there isn't enough immune function to produce consolidation, crackles or an effusion, so a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia — the same principle as febrile neutropenia'. To Jack: 'the most likely thing is a pneumonia — fever, cough, unwell, Panadol not helping; on examination your oxygen is low and you're breathing fast — your lungs aren't picking up oxygen properly, even though listening sounded normal'; 'but my chest sounded fine?' → 'the low oxygen tells me more than my stethoscope does'. Opportunistic concern named (Pneumocystis, TB) alongside common causes (COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcus, Legionella, Mycoplasma) — don't call it Pneumocystis with no CD4, viral load, white cells or film. ★ 'HIV also raises the risk of certain cancers, and I have to be honest with you': lung cancer (cough, smoker), Kaposi sarcoma (the patch — exclude), lymphoma, leukaemia → he is shaken → contain: 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer; I'm telling you what I have to rule out; the most likely explanation today is still an infection'. Other infections named individually (tonsillitis, pharyngitis, sinusitis; gastroenteritis; hepatitis; syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea; meningitis; cellulitis); then low mood/adjustment, anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, OSA. Plan: send in today — CXR, bloods incl. CD4/viral load, start treatment; reconnect with the HIV team; ★ restarting ART is one of the most important things we do — and look at what made it hard last time. 'Is this because I stopped my tablets?' — hidden agenda at ~7 min.
plan: ★ 'Before I begin, could I have his observations — BP, pulse, RR, temperature AND oxygen saturation?' → 118/74, 104, 24, 38.0, 92% · 'Hello Jack, I'm sorry to hear you've not been well — let's work out what's going on together' · ★ 'I can hear that cough — we'll come to it'
Unwell: sleepy/low energy/feverish? duration (3–4 days), constant, worse, better/worse · fever block: measured? chills? (yes) taken anything, helped? (Panadol, nothing)

HIV: 'when were you diagnosed? (5 y) I know you've stopped your medication — can you tell me what led to that? (felt fine, nausea, long trip to Adelaide) — no judgement here · regular follow-up? (not for a year) · any complications before? (never)'

★ 'I'm going to run through the whole body fairly quickly, area by area — most of these will be a simple no, and that's what I'm hoping for': sore throat/coryza/facial/ear pain · ★ cough — dry or chesty? SOB? noisy breathing? (dry; puffed on the stairs — three questions, keep going) · nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain/diarrhoea · dysuria/frequency · headache/stiff neck/photophobia · ★ sexual health (active in 3 months? condoms? discharge/rash/ulcers/scrotal pain) — despite HIV · jaundice/dark urine/pale stools · rash, hot painful skin · travel · ★ recreational drugs, ever injected? chest pain/palpitations (endocarditis) · animals

★ Malignancy heading: 'a few more — weight loss without trying? appetite? lumps or bumps? night sweats? ulcers or patches in your mouth? new purple or red marks on your skin? ever coughed up blood? do you smoke? (10/day) what work — asbestos? new or changing moles?' · if time: 'how has your mood been?' (flat)

★ Examination in one run: general — alert/drowsy, rash, jaundice, dehydration · all five vitals · throat — swelling/redness, ★ any lesion in the mouth · full lymph node survey, thyroid · respiratory — expansion, percussion both sides, added sounds, ★ vocal resonance ('I'm looking for consolidation') · CVS — S1 S2, murmurs · abdomen — tenderness, splenomegaly · dipstick → 'there is a white patch in his mouth'; respiratory entirely normal

★ The patch, two questions: 'is it painful to touch with a tongue depressor? can it be scraped off? colour? where?' → white, scrapes off, tongue and buccal mucosa → describe first, name second · ★ the normal-chest sentence to the examiner

To Jack: pneumonia named + reasons (fever, cough, unwell, Panadol failed; low oxygen, fast breathing) · 'but my chest sounded fine?' answered · opportunistic concern — Pneumocystis, TB — alongside common viruses/bacteria · ★ 'HIV also raises the risk of certain cancers, and I have to be honest with you about that' — lung, Kaposi (the patch), lymphoma/leukaemia → shaken → ★ 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer; I'm telling you what I have to rule out' · other infections named individually · then low mood, anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, OSA

'Is this because I stopped my tablets?' → honest, not blaming · plan: send in today — CXR, bloods incl. a check of the immune system, treatment started · ★ 'restarting your HIV treatment is one of the most important things we can do — and we can look at what made it hard last time' · safety-net: more short of breath, confused/drowsy, severe headache/stiff neck, haemoptysis → ambulance · confidentiality/Adelaide follow-up if he prefers · questions
ask: ★ 'All five observations, including oxygen saturation.' / ★ 'I can hear that cough — tell me about it.' / 'I'm sorry you're feeling like this, Jack. Let me ask you a few questions, and we'll work out what's going on together.'
'When were you diagnosed? Can you tell me what led to stopping?' / 'Are you still having regular follow-up with your specialist?' / 'Thank you for telling me that, and there's no judgement here.'

★ 'I'm going to run through the whole body quickly — most of these will be a simple no.' / 'Is the cough dry or chesty? Short of breath? Coughed up blood?' / 'Can I ask about sexual health? Sexually active now or in the last three months? Condoms? Any discharge, rash or ulcers?' / 'Any recreational drugs — have you ever injected? Any chest pain or racing of the heart?'
★ 'Any weight loss, appetite change, lumps, night sweats, mouth ulcers or patches, new purple or red marks on your skin, coughed-up blood? Do you smoke? Any asbestos at work?'

'Is vocal resonance increased anywhere — I'm looking for consolidation.' / ★ 'Is the patch painful to touch with a tongue depressor, and can it be scraped off? What colour is it, and where in the mouth?'

★ 'Examiner, although the respiratory examination is normal, he is febrile, tachypnoeic and hypoxic. In advanced HIV there isn't enough immune function to produce consolidation, crackles or an effusion, so a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia here — the same principle as febrile neutropenia in a child on chemotherapy.'

★ 'Jack, the most likely thing is a pneumonia — an infection in your lung. Fever, cough, feeling unwell, Panadol not helping — and on examination the oxygen level in your blood is low and you're breathing faster than normal.' / 'But you said my chest sounded fine?' → 'When the immune system is weakened the body can't mount the response I'd normally hear. The low oxygen is telling me more than my stethoscope is.'

'Because you have HIV there's a higher chance of unusual infections — we call them opportunistic — things like Pneumocystis and tuberculosis. But it could still be a common virus such as COVID-19 or influenza, or a common bacterial pneumonia — pneumococcus, Legionella or Mycoplasma.' / Examiner: 'why not just say Pneumocystis?' → 'Because I have no CD4 count, viral load, white cell count or chest film. I'm calling it a pneumonia, and Pneumocystis is at the top of the list of causes.'

★ 'I also have to be honest that HIV raises the risk of certain cancers. Because you have a cough I'm thinking about lung cancer. Because of the white patch in your mouth I want to exclude a cancer that occurs specifically in HIV called Kaposi sarcoma. Lymphoma and leukaemia are also more common.' → (shaken) ★ 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer. I'm telling you what I have to rule out, because ruling it out properly is how we make sure nothing is missed. The most likely explanation today is still an infection.'

★ 'Restarting your HIV treatment is one of the most important things we can do — and we can look at what made it difficult last time.' / 'Am I dying?' → 'I can't answer that today and I'm not going to guess. What I think is happening — an infection in your lung — is treatable, and getting you back on treatment changes your outlook a great deal.' / 'If you become more short of breath, confused or drowsy, develop a severe headache or stiff neck, or cough up blood — that's an ambulance, not a waiting room.'
pefe: Role-player: Jack, 30, grain terminal Wallaroo, lives alone in Kadina; 10 cigarettes/day; social drinker; never injected; no meds/allergies. HIV 5 years, did well on ART; stopped 6 months ago (felt well, nausea, long trip to Adelaide); no specialist for a year; never a complication. Coughs harshly mid-sentence throughout. Crisp negatives. If 'cancer' is said: visibly shaken, quiet for a beat — see if you notice and contain. If judged about stopping: defensive, shorter answers for the rest. Hidden agenda: half-suspects it's his fault — 'is this because I stopped my tablets?' at ~7 min if you're warm

Examiner: alert, no rash, no jaundice, mildly dehydrated · T 38.0, HR 104, BP 118/74, RR 24, SpO2 92% RA · 'there is a white patch in his mouth' → white, scrapes off, tongue and buccal mucosa · no lymphadenopathy, thyroid normal · respiratory examination entirely normal · HS dual, no murmur · abdomen normal · dipstick normal

Three answers for the patch: candidiasis (white, creamy, scrapes off) · Kaposi sarcoma (violaceous, raised, hard palate, doesn't scrape, painless — AIDS-defining, biopsy; can involve the lung) · oral hairy leukoplakia (white, corrugated, lateral tongue, doesn't scrape). Variant — 'raised violaceous plaque on the hard palate, doesn't scrape': ★ Kaposi, not thrush. CD4 landmarks: <200 Pneumocystis, toxoplasmosis; <50 MAC, CMV retinitis; Kaposi at any count ADDED

Investigations in hospital: CXR, ABG/VBG, FBE, UEC, LFT, CRP, LDH, CD4 count, HIV viral load, blood cultures, sputum MCS + AFB ×3 (induced sputum/BAL for PJP), COVID/influenza PCR, urinary Legionella/pneumococcal antigen, syphilis serology; PJP empirical treatment if suspected VERIFY TG · TB is notifiable — 'done discreetly; Kadina is a small town — follow-up in Adelaide if you prefer'

Variant — three weeks of diarrhoea, same stem: structure unchanged — infection screen then malignancy screen; infective: Cryptosporidium, Isospora, microsporidia, CMV colitis, MAC + Campylobacter, Salmonella, Giardia, C. difficile; malignancy: lymphoma, Kaposi of the gut
SA: admit via regional hospital → RAH ID/HIV service; PATS; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if hypoxic and deteriorating; TIS 131 450
fails: Telling him his chest was fine and therefore this was probably not serious ★
Never mentioning cancer at all — never opening the malignancy heading ★
'That's thrush' without checking anything — sticking with thrush after being handed 'violaceous' ★
Lecturing him about stopping his medication ★
Forgetting the fifth vital sign; ignoring the cough as stage direction
Turning the cough into a four-minute respiratory history; skipping the sexual history because he already has HIV; omitting the injecting/chest pain questions
'ENT infections' / 'GI infections' as differentials to the patient — categories are not diagnoses; false reassurance or blunt confirmation to 'am I dying?'

CD4 <200: Pneumocystis, toxoplasmosis · <50: MAC, CMV retinitis · Kaposi sarcoma at any count ADDED
Patch: candidiasis white/creamy/scrapes · Kaposi violaceous/raised/hard palate/no scrape · OHL white/corrugated/lateral tongue/no scrape
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS · TIS 131 450
