setting: General practice, Moonta. EXAMINATION-FIRST station — no history taking. Findings from the examiner for four minutes; the results card is handed over at exactly four minutes; then you explain results, diagnosis and differentials to Jane.
stem: Jane Whitmore, 40, has come in feeling unwell — tired and nauseated, no fever. She has recently returned from a trip to the Philippines. No sexual activity overseas, no mosquito bites, no needle exposures. Appendicectomy ten years ago.
tasks: Begin with a physical examination, asking the examiner for the findings — there is no history taking
At four minutes you are given the investigation results; explain them to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: ★ 0:00 GREET JANE FIRST — name, role, what will happen, when I'll be back, is that all right (15 s) · 0:20 examination as one run across the differentials, not at the liver: general (jaundice) · four vitals · throat, ears · thyroid, full node survey · chest · heart · abdomen → 'hepatomegaly' → ★ don't accept it: span, tender?, border, shifting dullness, scratch marks, bruising, bowel sounds · DRE · ★ 'with the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone' pelvic · ★ two office tests: dipstick (bilirubin) and ★ pregnancy test · 4:00 turn back to Jane, acknowledge the wait · results in three sentences (test → plain English → meaning), under a minute, no numbers, no abbreviations · 5:30 'most likely' hepatitis A + reasons incl. bilirubin in the urine · 6:30 differentials — ★ TRAVEL FIRST, then liver/abdominal incl. cancer, then pregnancy, then the generic tiredness list · plan, notification, hygiene, alcohol, safety-net.

back.dx: Acute hepatitis A (most likely — confirmatory anti-HAV IgM pending): three weeks in the Philippines with relatives, home cooking and street food, back a fortnight; a week tired, nauseated, off food, afebrile; husband noticed yellow eyes two days ago. Examination: alert, ★ jaundiced, no rash/pallor, mildly dehydrated; BP 120/80, HR 88, RR 12, T 36.9; throat/ears/thyroid/nodes normal; chest clear; HS dual; abdomen not distended, ★ hepatomegaly 3 cm, non-tender, smooth regular border, no splenomegaly, no ascites, no scratch marks/bruising, bowel sounds normal; DRE and pelvic normal; ★ dipstick bilirubin positive, urobilinogen raised; ★ pregnancy test negative. Results card: WCC 13.2, bilirubin 68, ALT 780, AST 640, ALP 130, GGT 110, INR 1.1, albumin 38, HBV and HCV negative — hepatocellular pattern (to the examiner). Explain in three beats each: FBC — white cells, immune cells, raised = fighting infection/inflammation · liver test — enzymes raised = inflammation in the liver · hepatitis B and C negative. 'Damaged?' → 'inflamed rather than damaged; the two numbers that measure how well it's doing its job are normal today'. Diagnosis 'most likely', never certain: enlarged liver, jaundice, bilirubin in the urine ('made by the liver, normally never reaches the urine — finding it there tells me the problem is in your liver'), raised enzymes, B and C negative, recent travel, nausea; spreads via contaminated food/water. Settles over 2–8 weeks, no specific treatment, never chronic, lifelong immunity. Differentials in the order the case demands: (1) travel — malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis, hepatitis E, EBV, HIV, TB; (2) liver/abdominal — hepatitis B/C (negative), autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, gallstones/cholangitis, ★ cancer of the liver or pancreas ('particularly because your liver was not tender'); (3) pregnancy (tested, negative); (4) anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, haemochromatosis, lymphoma/leukaemia, autoimmune, depression, heart failure, OSA. Plan: anti-HAV IgM, liver ultrasound, review this week; no alcohol, check before any medication (paracetamol at reduced dose VERIFY); handwashing, don't prepare food for others, don't share towels; notify — household vaccinated (within 14 days VERIFY); safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, worsening jaundice, can't keep fluids down. Hidden agenda: sister died of pancreatic cancer — tearful at the word cancer; name it, proportion it, say what resolves it.
plan: ★ 'No questions, thank you. — Hello Jane, I'm Dr [name], one of the doctors here, and I'll be looking after you today. I'm going to speak with my colleague for a few minutes and go through an examination, then I'll come straight back to you and explain everything I've found. Is that all right?'

One continuous run: general — alert/drowsy, ★ jaundice, rash, pallor, dehydration · all four vitals · throat (swelling, redness, exudate), ears (red bulging TM) · thyroid, ★ full lymph node examination every chain · respiratory — air entry, added sounds · CVS — S1 S2, murmurs · abdomen — inspection (distension, redness, bruising), palpation (tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly)

'Hepatomegaly' → ★ 'what is the span? is it tender? border regular or irregular? shifting dullness? scratch marks? bruising? bowel sounds?' → 3 cm, non-tender, smooth, no ascites, no scratch marks/bruises, BS normal

'I would like a digital rectal examination. ★ And with the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone, a pelvic examination — inspection for discharge or rash, speculum for cervical discharge, bimanual for cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, and the adnexae' → all normal (there IS time here — judge by the clock you're given)
★ 'Two office tests: a urine dipstick — I'm looking particularly for bilirubin — and a urine pregnancy test' → bilirubin positive, urobilinogen raised; pregnancy negative → results card handed over

★ Turn back: 'thank you for waiting, Jane — I've examined you and I have your results; let me talk you through them, then tell you what I think' · three sentences, test → plain English → meaning: white cells raised · liver enzymes raised · hepatitis B and C negative · 'is my liver damaged?' → inflamed, not damaged; the job-numbers (INR, albumin) are normal

'Most likely hepatitis — your liver is inflamed — most likely caused by a virus called hepatitis A' + reasons (enlarged liver, jaundice, bilirubin in the urine, raised enzymes, B and C negative, recent travel, nausea) · 'from the food?' → most likely · 'will I get better?' → 2–8 weeks, no specific medicine, never long-term, immune for life · 'can I pass it on?' → hands, food, towels; notification → household vaccine

★ Differentials, travel FIRST: malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis, hepatitis E, EBV, HIV, TB · liver/abdomen: B/C negative, autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced (antibiotics), gallstones/cholangitis, ★ cancer of the liver or pancreas — 'particularly because your liver was not tender' → tearful, sister → name it, proportion it (travel, pattern, bilirubinuria point to a virus), what resolves it · pregnancy — tested · the generic list

Plan: confirmatory blood test, liver ultrasound, review this week · no alcohol, check before any medication ('Panadol for headaches?' → reduced dose, ask me) · handwashing, no food preparation for others, no shared towels · notification, household vaccination · work certificate · safety-net: confused/unusually sleepy, bruising/bleeding, yellowing much worse, can't keep fluids down → hospital · questions
ask: ★ 'Hello Jane, I am Doctor [name] — give me a few minutes with my colleague and I will come straight back to you.'
'Examiner, on general appearance: is she alert or drowsy? Any jaundice? Any rash? Any pallor? Any dehydration?' — findings, not regions
★ 'What is the span? Is the liver tender? Is the border regular or irregular?' / ★ 'Is there shifting dullness? Any scratch marks? Any bruising?'
★ 'With the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone…' / ★ 'Two office tests: a urine dipstick, looking particularly for bilirubin, and a urine pregnancy test.'

'The first test is a full blood count. The white blood cells are the cells of your immune system, and they're higher than normal — your body is fighting an infection or inflammation.' / 'Your liver enzymes are raised — that means there is inflammation in your liver.' / 'We tested for two viruses that commonly cause liver inflammation, and both are negative.'
'Is my liver damaged?' → ★ 'Inflamed rather than damaged. The liver is a remarkably good healer. There are two numbers that tell me how well it's doing its job, and both are normal today.'
★ 'Bilirubin is made by the liver and normally does not reach the urine at all — finding it there tells me the problem is in your liver.' / To the examiner: 'This is a hepatocellular pattern.'

'I think you most likely have hepatitis — your liver is inflamed — most likely caused by a virus called hepatitis A.' / 'It settles over two to eight weeks, there's no specific medicine, it does not become long-term, and afterwards you are immune for life.'

★ 'Because you have been overseas, the first group I thought about was travel-related infections: malaria, dengue fever, typhoid, leptospirosis, and hepatitis E.' / 'Is it cancer?' → 'That's a fair thing to ask, and I'd rather answer it honestly. Cancer of the liver or pancreas is on my list, and one reason it stays there is that your liver wasn't tender. But the whole picture — you've just come back from overseas, the pattern of your blood tests, the bilirubin in your urine — points much more strongly to a viral infection. The blood test I'm arranging should settle it, and the ultrasound looks directly at the liver.'

'We notify this routinely, which means your household can be offered a vaccine.' / 'Avoid alcohol completely, and check with me before any medication.' / 'Come back straight away, or go to hospital, if you become confused or unusually sleepy, if you start bruising or bleeding easily, if the yellowing gets much worse, or if you cannot keep fluids down.'
pefe: Role-player: Jane, 40, council administration, Moonta; husband, two teenagers; a wine most weekends; non-smoker; no meds/allergies; appendicectomy 10 y. Three weeks in the Philippines with relatives, home cooking and street food, no malaria tablets, back a fortnight; a week tired, nauseated, off food, afebrile; yellow eyes noticed two days ago. Composed, tired, quietly frightened; warm if greeted at the door and returned to as promised; if ignored for four minutes: cool, short answers, 'I did not know what was happening, nobody said anything to me'. Asks at least two questions; 'I'm sorry, I don't know what that means' at jargon (hepatocellular, transaminases). Hidden agenda: sister died of pancreatic cancer three years ago — tearful at the word cancer: 'my sister had pancreatic cancer — is that what this is?'

Findings: alert, jaundiced, no rash/pallor, mildly dehydrated · 120/80, 88, 12, 36.9 · throat/ears/thyroid/nodes normal · chest clear, HS dual · no distension · hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin, non-tender, smooth regular border · no splenomegaly, no shifting dullness, no scratch marks/bruises, BS normal · DRE/pelvic normal · dipstick bilirubin +, urobilinogen raised · pregnancy negative · card: WCC 13.2, bilirubin 68, ALT 780, AST 640, ALP 130, GGT 110, INR 1.1, albumin 38, HBV/HCV negative

Examiner: 'the raised white cell count?' → CORRECTION: 'a neutrophilia isn't typical of hepatitis A — the count is more often normal or low with a relative lymphocytosis; I'd want the differential and a CRP; afebrile with a non-tender liver and no rigors makes ascending cholangitis unlikely, but that's why I'd check'

Variant — INR 2.4, drowsy and vague: ★ acute liver failure — check BSL immediately, asterixis, formal conscious state; urgent admission and discussion with a liver unit; do not send her home; 'one of your tests shows your liver isn't doing one of its jobs, and I'm not happy to manage that from here — hospital today; is there someone who can come with you?' — the station stops being a counselling station

Variant — childcare worker: exclusion until ~1 week after the onset of jaundice VERIFY; public health works with the centre so children and staff can be vaccinated; certificate today · household contacts vaccinated within 14 days VERIFY (HAV vaccine ± immunoglobulin) · work exclusion 7 days after jaundice onset VERIFY
SA: notify SA Health (hepatitis A); public health contact management; Moonta → Wallaroo Hospital/RAH liver unit if failure; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; TIS 131 450
fails: Never speaking to Jane until four minutes have passed — walking in and addressing the examiner ★
A generic tiredness list with travel infections never mentioned — or not said first ★
'You definitely have hepatitis A' with no confirmatory test ★
Dismissing the cancer question ('oh no, nothing like that') — or agreeing too heavily ★
Examining 'at the liver' instead of across the differentials; accepting 'hepatomegaly' without span, tenderness, border, ascites, stigmata; omitting the pregnancy test; omitting consent and chaperone
Explaining AST/ALT/GGT abbreviations, the three cell lines, reading numbers out — burning the differential minute
Explaining a diagnosis at length when the INR demands escalation; no hygiene/notification/alcohol advice; no safety-net
numbers: 8 min: examination 4 · results 1.5 · diagnosis 1 · differentials 1.5 · results card at exactly 4:00 · greeting 15 s
Hepatomegaly 3 cm, non-tender, regular · WCC 13.2 · bilirubin 68 · ALT 780, AST 640 · ALP 130, GGT 110 · INR 1.1, albumin 38 · HBV/HCV negative — hepatocellular pattern
Recovery 2–8 weeks · never chronic · lifelong immunity · contacts vaccinated within 14 days VERIFY · work exclusion until 7 days after jaundice onset VERIFY
Three-beat explanation: test → plain English → significance · differential order: travel → liver/abdomen (incl. cancer) → pregnancy → generic
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450 · notify SA Health

setting: General practice. Vitals in the stem. Examination findings on screen/card when asked. Five minutes of history. No management task — but a plan and a safety-net still earn marks.
stem: Ben Alderton, 25, has come in feeling unwell. He attends a sauna regularly with friends, and his friends have similar symptoms. He is currently taking PrEP. T 38.4, HR 96, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
tasks: Take a focused history (5 minutes)
You will be given the examination findings on screen or card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the worry · 'unwell' in four questions · ★ open the sauna: how often, ★ 'what do your friends have?', what do you do there (sex) · ★ three water infections: Legionella (cough, SOB, fever, diarrhoea, confusion) · hepatitis A (abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice, dark urine/pale stools) · Pseudomonas (itchy spots under swimwear) · ★ PrEP block, three separate marks: adherence · 3-monthly screening · hepatitis A/B vaccination · ★ normalise once, then the full sexual history (partners, number, gender, condoms, practices, previous STI, alcohol/drugs) — don't stop to counsel · STI symptoms incl. ulcers, discharge, scrotum, back passage · the rest · examination by name incl. throat, nodes, palms/soles, genitals, dipstick · acute viral hepatitis WITHOUT guessing the subtype · differentials by exposure: sauna ×3 + crypto, STIs with ★ HIV high on the list despite PrEP · ★ three-site swabs · confidentiality accurately · vaccinate · 3-monthly reviews · safety-net.

back.dx: Acute viral hepatitis (subtype deliberately not guessed — A via faecal-oral including sexual transmission between men, or B/C via sex) in an MSM on PrEP: a week of fever, anorexia, upper abdominal pain, vomiting, partner says he looks yellow, urine darker; no cough/SOB/diarrhoea/confusion (Legionella less likely), no rash (Pseudomonas less likely). Sauna 2–3×/week, same group, a couple of friends off work with unknown symptoms; 'we have sex there as well' (say it back: both a water exposure and a sexual exposure). PrEP: misses the odd dose when he stays out; last review two months ago but ★ never screened for STIs; doesn't know if he's had hepatitis A/B vaccines. Sexual history: no stable partner, several partners, all men, no condoms, oral and anal, never diagnosed, sometimes after drinks. No STI symptoms. Card: jaundiced, T 38.4, tender hepatomegaly span >13 cm, no splenomegaly, chest clear, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no genital/perianal lesions or discharge, dipstick bilirubin positive. Differentials grouped by exposure: sauna — Legionella (warm-water spray; no cough/SOB), Pseudomonas folliculitis (no rash), cryptosporidium (chlorine-resistant; no diarrhoea); STIs — ★ HIV high on the list ('PrEP is very effective but not absolute, and it depends on taking it consistently — you miss doses; one blood test'), syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea and chlamydia (throat and rectum often asymptomatic — urine alone misses them); then EBV/CMV, travel, lymphoma/leukaemia, depression, thyroid/diabetes/anaemia/coeliac. Plan: LFT + clotting, full hepatitis panel, HIV (4th-gen ± RNA), syphilis; ★ swabs throat, anorectal, first-pass urine; rest, fluids, no alcohol, no shared food preparation, no sex until results; hepatitis A/B vaccination if not covered; PrEP reviews back to 3-monthly with a full screen; confidentiality accurate (notifiable as a case, not a name; partner notification anonymised; cousin in town → flag the file, results to a chosen number); safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, can't keep fluids, worsening jaundice; review 2 days; teach-back.
plan: WIPE · 'I can hear that you're worried, and I want to get to the bottom of it — questions, examination, then a plan together' · 'unwell' — describe, duration (a week), constant, worse, better/worse, impact (off since Monday)

★ 'Tell me more about the sauna and your friends — how often? do you know what symptoms they have? what do you do there?' → 2–3×/week, same group, couple off work, 'we have sex there as well' → say it back

★ Three water infections: Legionella — cough? SOB? fever/chills? diarrhoea? confused/muddled? · hepatitis A — abdominal pain? nausea/vomiting? yellowing? dark urine/pale stools? → pain across the top, vomited, partner says yellow, darker urine · Pseudomonas — rash, ★ itchy spots where swimwear sits?

★ PrEP, three separate marks: 'taking it every day without missing doses?' (most days) · 'three-monthly sexual health screening and regular review?' (2 months ago; never actually checked for STIs → 'we'll fix that today') · 'hepatitis A and B vaccinations?' (not sure)

★ 'I'm going to ask some personal and quite detailed questions about your sex life. I ask everyone these, they're relevant to working out what's making you unwell, and what you tell me is confidential. Is that all right?' → active · stable partner · multiple · ★ male/female/both · condoms always? · oral/vaginal/anal · previous STI · under alcohol/drugs → note the condoms, keep going

STI symptoms: sore throat, body rash, nodes neck/axilla/groin, night sweats, genital rash/sore/ulcer, penile discharge, scrotal pain/swelling, ★ pain or discharge from the back passage → none · quickly: weight/appetite/lumps/sweats, travel, mood, PMHx, meds (PrEP only), allergies, alcohol, smoking, other drugs

★ Examination by name: appearance/hydration · jaundice sclerae/under tongue · vitals · throat and mouth ulcers · nodes neck/axillae/groins · rash incl. trunk, ★ palms and soles · chest · abdomen — tenderness, liver size/tenderness, spleen · ★ genitals and perianal area — ulcers/discharge · urine dipstick → card

'Most likely acute viral hepatitis — your liver is inflamed, almost certainly from a virus: enlarged, tender liver, yellow skin, bile pigment in the urine' · 'which one — the bad one?' → ★ 'I'm deliberately not going to guess — A through contaminated water/food and also sex between men, or B or C through sex; the blood tests will tell us'

Differentials by exposure: sauna ×3 + crypto, each with why less likely · STIs: ★ 'HIV is high on my list' → 'but I'm on PrEP' answered · syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea, chlamydia (throat/rectum silent) · then EBV/CMV, travel, blood cancers, depression, generic · 'who else finds out?' → accurate confidentiality · plan: bloods, ★ three-site swabs, rest/fluids/no alcohol/no sex until results, vaccinate A and B, 3-monthly PrEP reviews · safety-net · review 2 days · teach-back: 'what are you going to avoid?'
ask: 'I can hear that you are worried, and I want to get to the bottom of it.' / ★ 'Tell me more about the sauna and your friends.' / ★ 'Do you know what symptoms your friends are having?'
'Any cough, breathlessness — and any diarrhoea? Have you felt confused or muddled?' / ★ 'Any itchy spots where your swimwear sits?'
★ 'Are you taking your PrEP every day without missing doses?' / ★ 'Are you having your three-monthly screening?' / ★ 'Have you had your hepatitis A and B vaccinations?'
★ 'I'm going to ask some personal questions about your sex life. I ask everyone these, and they are confidential.' / 'What kind of sex do you have — oral, vaginal or anal?'
'Any sore or ulcer on your private parts, any discharge, any pain or swelling in the scrotum, any pain or discharge from the back passage?'

'Could I have the examination findings — appearance and hydration, jaundice in the sclerae and under the tongue, vital signs, throat and mouth ulcers, lymph nodes, any rash including palms and soles, chest, abdominal tenderness with liver size and spleen, genitals and perianal area, and a urine dipstick.'
★ 'Acute viral hepatitis means your liver is inflamed, almost certainly from a virus.' / ★ 'I am deliberately not going to guess which type — the blood tests will tell us.'

★ 'HIV is high on my list.' → 'But I'm on PrEP, I can't get HIV' → 'PrEP is very effective and taking it was a good decision. But it's not absolute, and how well it works depends on taking it consistently — you've told me you miss doses. Testing costs one blood test. If it's negative we both stop wondering; if it's positive, finding it early makes an enormous difference.'

★ 'I want swabs from three places — your throat, your back passage and a urine sample — because gonorrhoea and chlamydia in the throat and back passage very often cause no symptoms at all, and a urine test alone misses them.'

'Who else finds out? My cousin works in this town' → 'What you tell me stays between us. Some infections I have to report to public health, but that goes as a case, not as a name in the community. If something is positive your partners need to know they may have been exposed — there are services that contact them anonymously. I can flag your file so only clinicians see it, and send results to a number you choose.' / 'Rest, fluids, and no alcohol at all until your liver recovers — and hold off sex until we have results.'
pefe: Role-player: Ben Alderton, 25, hospitality, share house, MSM; non-smoker, weekend drinker, occasional recreational drugs; PrEP only; no PMHx/allergies. Sauna 2–3×/week; adds 'we have sex there as well' to a second open question or 'what do you do there?'. Never screened for STIs — only if asked directly. Open, sheepish; guarded and marks you down if you hesitate, apologise repeatedly or look uncomfortable — or if your tone changes at 'no condoms'. Hidden agenda: frightened it's HIV and who will find out (cousin in town) — 'can I ask you something?' at the end if never asked about concerns. When HIV is mentioned: 'But I am on PrEP. I cannot get HIV.'
Card: jaundiced · T 38.4 · tender hepatomegaly, span >12–13 cm · no splenomegaly · chest clear · no rash · no lymphadenopathy · no genital/perianal lesions, no discharge · dipstick bilirubin positive

Variant 1 — HIV seroconversion card (sore throat, trunk rash, oral ulcers, lymphadenopathy, no hepatomegaly, dipstick normal): 'not hepatitis — a seroconversion illness, the body's first reaction to HIV, a few weeks after unprotected sex'; 4th-gen Ag/Ab + HIV RNA today (antibodies take weeks); same-day sexual health referral if reactive; do NOT simply continue PrEP · Variant 4 — healed painless penile ulcer + palm/sole rash: secondary syphilis; benzathine penicillin after serology VERIFY TG; partners tested

Variant 2 — Legionella card (cough, SOB, diarrhoea, confusion, Na 126): pneumonia — CXR, urinary Legionella antigen, antibiotics today; hypoxic → admit; ★ notify — the sauna's water system gets investigated, 'that's how we protect your friends' · Variant 3 — 'my brother works on reception' before the history: records confidential, access only for their own work, curiosity = serious breach; flag the file; results to a chosen number — accurate, not 'nobody will ever see anything'

Automatic fails: ★ no sexual history, or 'are you sexually active?' only · ★ never opening the sauna · ★ HIV 'excluded' because he's on PrEP, or declining to test · ★ urine-only gonorrhoea/chlamydia testing · ★ judgemental about partners or the sauna
SA: Clinic 275; SHINE SA; notifiable — HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, hepatitis A/B/C, legionellosis; PATS; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; TIS 131 450; healthdirect 1800 022 222
fails: Taking no sexual history — or only 'are you sexually active?' ★
Never opening the sauna — not asking what the friends have ★
Saying HIV is excluded because he's on PrEP, or declining to test ★
Ordering a urine test only for gonorrhoea and chlamydia ★
Judgemental about his partners or the sauna — a tone change at 'no condoms' fails the communication domain ★
Naming a hepatitis subtype you cannot prove; recording PrEP as a medication and moving on (adherence, screening interval and vaccination are three marks)
Stopping the history to counsel about condoms; 'an abdominal examination' without throat, nodes, palms/soles, genitals, dipstick; promising nobody will ever see anything
numbers: 8 min, history 5 · PrEP review THREE-monthly — script, full STI screen and renal function each time · PrEP protects against HIV only (not syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, hepatitis, mpox) · monitored adverse effect: renal
Three-site screen: throat · anorectal · first-pass urine + serology HIV, syphilis, HBV, HCV · HIV 4th-gen Ag/Ab (p24) + RNA if seroconversion suspected; retest 6 weeks and 3 months VERIFY

Seroconversion 2–4 weeks: fever, sore throat, non-itchy maculopapular rash, nodes, myalgia, mouth/genital ulcers · secondary syphilis palms/soles 6 weeks–6 months after the chancre · liver span >12–13 cm = hepatomegaly

Water infections: Legionella (pneumonia + diarrhoea, confusion, hyponatraemia) · Pseudomonas folliculitis (itchy pustules under swimwear, self-limiting 7–10 days) · hepatitis A · cryptosporidium (chlorine-resistant)

setting: General practice, Wallaroo. Four tasks in eight minutes — examination begins at 4:00, management at 7:00. Observations from the examiner at the door (online: 'I'm taking you through to the treatment room to check your observations').
stem: Mary Ellis, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has come in because she has been feeling unwell for the past few days. First pregnancy; antenatal care so far uncomplicated.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings (2 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: 8 minutes: observations first, one sentence · empathic sentence · ★ offer the word FEVERISH — she won't volunteer it · fever block: measured, chills, medication · urinary upper and lower: dysuria, frequency, haematuria, nausea/vomiting, ★ flank pain — site and radiation only · sexual health with a permission sentence · other infection: throat, cough, headache/neck, travel · ★ pregnancy-specific: vision, swelling, headache (pre-eclampsia) · thirst and polyuria separately (GDM) · jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch (cholestasis/AFLP) · palpitations/SOB (anaemia) · obstetric close — tightenings, fluid/bleeding, movements · ★ allergies BEFORE naming an antibiotic · 4:00 examination as one run: findings not regions, four vitals again, ★ fundal height, uterine tenderness, fetal heart · ★ 'is there any renal angle tenderness?' · dipstick — leucocytes and nitrites · 6:00 pyelonephritis with reasons; the baby question in one sentence; differentials LISTED not explained · 7:00 ★ ED today, admission, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, culture first.

back.dx: Acute pyelonephritis at 20 weeks: 3–4 days hot and shivery with rigors last night, worsening, paracetamol useless; dysuria and frequency, no visible haematuria; vomited 3–4 times; right flank/back pain radiating to the groin (Version B: low central suprapubic pain — the diagnosis is unchanged when renal angle tenderness is positive). Pregnancy-specific screen negative: no visual blurring, swelling, headache (pre-eclampsia); no thirst/polyuria (GDM); no jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch (cholestasis/AFLP); no palpitations/SOB (anaemia); no tightenings, fluid, bleeding; baby moving; pregnancy vitamins only; no allergies. Examiner: alert, flushed, mildly dehydrated; BP 110/70, HR 108, RR 18, ★ T 38.7; throat/chest/heart normal; mild suprapubic tenderness, no RUQ tenderness, no organomegaly; ★ fundal height 20 cm consistent with dates, uterus non-tender, FHR 145; ★ right renal angle tenderness POSITIVE; dipstick leucocytes +++, nitrites +, blood ++, protein trace. To Mary: 'pyelonephritis — an infection in your kidney: burning, going more often, fever, vomiting, tender over your kidney, urine test showing infection'; 'dangerous for the baby?' → 'it can be, which is exactly why we treat it properly and quickly — today is the best thing for both of you'. Differentials LISTED in 25 s: pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, other infections (STIs incl. herpes and HIV, throat, chest, meningitis), the liver conditions of pregnancy (cholestasis, acute fatty liver), appendicitis, renal stone, anaemia. Management, the four things first: ★ ED today, expect admission, IV antibiotics + IV fluids ('too serious to treat with tablets at home'), MSU for culture before antibiotics; then oral switch once afebrile 24–48 h, 10–14 days total, test-of-cure culture 1–2 weeks after, obstetric team checks the baby; 'do I have to go?' → sepsis and preterm labour risks; 'safe for the baby?' → yes, well-studied antibiotics. Safety-net: worse, shaking chills, can't keep fluids down, tightenings, bleeding, fluid, reduced movements → straight back.
plan: ★ 'Before I begin, could I have her observations — BP, pulse, RR and temperature?' → 110/70, 108, 18, 38.7 · 'Hello Mary, I'm sorry to hear you've not been well — questions, examination, then a plan together. Tell me what's been happening' → 'I'm worried about the baby' → acknowledge

★ 'Can you describe it — are you tired and low in energy, sleepy, or feeling feverish?' → hot then shivery · onset (3–4 days), constant, worse, better/worse · fever block: measured? chills? (badly, last night) taken anything, helped? (Panadol, no)

Urinary: burning/pain passing urine (yes) · frequency (constantly) · blood (no) · nausea/vomiting (3–4×) · abdominal pain · ★ 'any pain in your side or back, around your kidneys — where exactly, and does it travel?' → right flank to groin (site + radiation, then MOVE)

'Can I ask a few confidential questions about sexual health? active? condoms? genital rash/ulcers? discharge? lumps or night sweats?' → husband, no condoms, nothing · other infection: sore throat/coryza/cough, headache/stiff neck, travel

★ Pregnancy-specific: 'blurring of vision? swelling of legs, hands or face? bad headache?' · 'more thirsty? passing large amounts of urine?' (separately) · 'yellowing, darker urine, pale stools, itching?' · 'racing heart or breathlessness on exertion?'

Obstetric and medication close: 'how has the pregnancy been? tightenings, fluid or bleeding from below? baby moving normally? regular medicines? ★ any allergies to antibiotics?' (ask NOW, not after naming a drug)

★ One continuous run: general — alert/drowsy, jaundice, rash, dehydration · all four vitals again · throat — swelling/redness · respiratory — air entry, added sounds · CVS — S1 S2, murmurs · abdomen — inspection; palpation: suprapubic tenderness? RUQ tenderness? hepatomegaly? · ★ 'fundal height? is the uterus tender? fetal heart rate?' → 20 cm, non-tender, 145 · ★ 'is there any renal angle tenderness?' → right positive · ★ 'urine dipstick — leucocytes and nitrites' → leucocytes +++, nitrites +, blood ++, protein trace · no full pelvic — the clock killer

Pyelonephritis named + reasons · 'is the baby all right?' → one sentence, then move · differentials LISTED, 25 s, not explained: pre-eclampsia, GDM, other infections (STIs incl. herpes/HIV, throat, chest, meningitis), cholestasis and acute fatty liver, appendicitis, renal stone, anaemia — 'your picture fits the kidney infection best'

★ 'I'm going to send you to the emergency department today, and I expect you'll be admitted — antibiotics through a drip and fluids through a drip; a kidney infection in pregnancy is too serious to treat with tablets at home. We'll send a urine sample for culture before the antibiotics start.' · 'do I really have to? work tomorrow' → 'untreated, this can spread to the bloodstream and bring on early labour' · 'safe for the baby?' → well-studied antibiotics · if the clock allows: oral switch when afebrile, 10–14 days, test-of-cure, obstetric review · safety-net · summary
ask: 'Could I have her observations — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature?' / ★ 'Are you tired and low in energy, or are you feeling feverish?' / 'Have you measured it? Any chills? Did anything help?'
'Any burning or pain when you pass urine? Are you going more often? Any blood?' / ★ 'Any pain in your side or back, around your kidneys? Where exactly, and does it travel?'
'Any blurring of vision? Any swelling of the legs, hands or face?' / 'More thirsty than usual? Passing large amounts of urine?' / 'Any yellowing of your skin, dark urine, pale stools or itching?'
'How has the pregnancy been? Any tightenings, any fluid or bleeding from below? Is the baby moving normally? Any regular medicines? Any allergies to antibiotics?'

★ 'Examiner, what is the fundal height, is the uterus tender, and what is the fetal heart rate?' / ★ 'Is there any renal angle tenderness?' / 'Urine dipstick — I am looking for leucocytes and nitrites.'

★ 'Mary, I think you most likely have pyelonephritis — that is an infection in your kidney. I say that because you have burning when you pass urine, you're going more often, you have a fever, you've vomited, and on examination you're tender over your kidney with a urine test showing infection.'

'Is that dangerous for the baby?' → 'It can be, which is exactly why we treat it properly and quickly. Treating it today is the best thing we can do for both of you. Let me finish telling you what else I considered, and then what I want to do.'

stem: Jane Miller, 17, Year 12 student, presenting with tiredness over two to three months. Your completed assessment: recent examinations with considerable stress; bed after 1 am, up at 6:30; easy-going personality; mood normal, no anxiety disorder; three to four cups of coffee every night while studying. No weight loss, fever, night sweats, lumps or travel; no snoring or witnessed apnoeas; no medications, alcohol or drugs; periods regular and not heavy. Examination and vital signs normal.
tasks: Explain your assessment to the patient — diagnosis and cause of the tiredness (about 3 minutes)
Counsel her regarding your management plan
Answer the patient's questions
time: 8 minutes. 30 s: open question, empathy, ★ 'anything you were hoping we'd sort out today?' (the temazepam line — park it explicitly), ★ 'is it all right if I explain what I think, then we make a plan together?' · Task 1, four blocks, three minutes: NAME it (sleep restriction) · DEFINE it (8–10 h needed; she gets ~5) · REASON it (exam trigger, pattern persisting, caffeine) · SAY WHAT YOU EXCLUDED · teach-back · Task 2, eight headings one sentence each: hygiene · diary · ★ CBT-I first line · caffeine · relaxation · lifestyle · named organisation · review 4 weeks + conditional bloods/sleep study · Task 3, ★ VALIDATE → DECLINE with ≥2 reasons → SUBSTITUTE (not second best) → CONTRACT (four weeks, a date) · safety-net incl. mood/self-harm · driving.

back.dx: Chronic insufficient sleep — behaviourally induced sleep restriction — in a 17-year-old: ~5 hours on school nights (bed 1–2 am, up 6:30), studies and scrolls in bed, 3–4 instant coffees each evening (last ~11 pm, ~380 mg, half still circulating at bedtime), set off by exam stress and persisting after it; catches up to midday at weekends and feels much better (the pattern that says 'not enough sleep', not blood or thyroid); mood normal, no self-harm, no snoring/apnoeas/sleep attacks. 'Nothing wrong with me?' → 'there is something wrong — it just isn't a disease'. Management aim: improve quantity and quality of sleep — (1) sleep hygiene: fixed bed and wake time seven days, bed for sleep only (no phone/laptop/study/TV), dark quiet cool, out of bed if not asleep in 20–30 min, warm shower/milk; (2) sleep diary two weeks (bedtime, sleep onset, hours, quality/10); (3) ★ CBT-I — first line in Australia, more effective than hypnotics and durable — psychologist referral or Australian online programmes; cognitive half (the 'if I don't sleep I'll fail' worry) + behavioural half (stimulus control, relaxation, time-in-bed matching); (4) caffeine: half-life ~5 h, nothing after early afternoon, cut the total, expect a headache; (5) relaxation — mindfulness, breathing, PMR, yoga; (6) lifestyle — daytime exercise, regular meals, no alcohol/smoking/vaping, screens off; (7) named: Sleep Health Foundation fact sheets, headspace (12–25); (8) review 4 weeks with the diary → if no better TSH, FBE, ferritin → sleep study if another disorder is suggested. Temazepam: validate (exhausted, worked for a friend) → decline with reasons (dependence/tolerance/withdrawal, next-day drowsiness for driving and study, not recommended under 18, doesn't fix the cause) → substitute (CBT-I works better and lasts) → contract (four weeks, then we look together). 'Just a few for exams?' → exam time is when grogginess costs most; two weeks is enough to start dependence. 'So you're not going to help me?' → 'I'm not doing the thing that helps for two weeks and causes a problem for two years — everything else starts today.' Safety-net: mood drops, hopelessness, self-harm thoughts, sudden daytime sleep attacks, snoring/apnoeas → sooner. Driving: don't drive sleepy, pull over (P-plater).
plan: 'Hello Jane, how have you been feeling since we last spoke?' · 'I'm sorry — that sounds miserable, especially in Year 12' · ★ 'before I start explaining — anything you were hoping we'd sort out today, or anything you've been worried about?' → temazepam → 'a really good question and I'll answer it properly — can I first tell you what I think is going on?' · ★ 'is it all right if I explain, and then we make a plan together?'

1A NAME: 'the most likely cause is a sleep problem — there are breathing types like sleep apnoea, body-clock types, nightmare disorders; yours is sleep restriction, or sleep deprivation — your sleep itself is fine, there just isn't enough of it'
1B DEFINE: 'enough good-quality sleep is a basic requirement — concentration, memory, mood, appetite, immune system; at your age eight to ten hours; bed after one, up at half six, is about five'

1C REASON: 'it started when your exams started — stressed, up late; sleep problems are often triggered by a stressful stretch and keep going after it, because the pattern is set; and three or four coffees in the evening is still working at bedtime' · 'I'm fine on weekends' → 'that's exactly what we see when the problem is not enough sleep rather than something in the blood or thyroid'

1D EXCLUDED: 'no weight loss, fevers, sweats, lumps, travel; normal periods; no snoring or breathing pauses; mood fine; normal examination — that's what lets me be confident' · 'nothing wrong with me?' → 'there is something wrong — it just isn't a disease' · 'anaemic? mum said bloods' → not needed now; bloods at review if no better · teach-back: 'if a friend asked tonight what the doctor said?'

2D caffeine: 'the big one for you — hangs around five hours; nothing caffeinated after early afternoon; cut the total; expect a headache' (defensive 'I need it' → no lecture) · 2E relaxation · 2F lifestyle · 2G ★ Sleep Health Foundation, headspace — named · 2H review 4 weeks with the diary → bloods (thyroid, FBE, iron) → sleep study if indicated

★ 'In your case I think it's sleep restriction — your sleep is fine, there just isn't enough of it.' / 'Someone your age needs eight to ten hours.' / 'These problems are often triggered by stress and then keep going after the stress has passed.'

★ 'I've looked for the other causes and not found them — that's what lets me be confident.' / 'So there's nothing wrong with me?' → 'There is something wrong — it just isn't a disease. Not getting enough sleep is a real problem with real effects and a real treatment. I'm not dismissing it.'
'Bed for sleep only. If you're not asleep in twenty to thirty minutes, get up, do something boring in dim light, and come back when you feel sleepy.'

★ 'CBT for insomnia is first line — more effective than sleeping tablets, and it keeps working after you stop.' / 'What will the psychologist actually do?' → 'Two halves. The cognitive half works on the thoughts that keep it going — the "if I don't sleep I'll fail" worry that itself keeps you awake. The behavioural half teaches stimulus control, relaxation, and matching your time in bed to the sleep you're actually getting.'
'Caffeine hangs around about five hours, so four cups in the evening is half still circulating at bedtime. Nothing with caffeine after early afternoon.'

★ 'I can see why you're asking — you're exhausted and you've heard it worked for someone else. But I don't think a sleeping tablet is the right answer for you. It helps for a short time, but it comes with real problems. The main one is dependence — your body gets used to it, it stops working at the same dose, we end up increasing it, and if you try to stop you get withdrawal: worse sleep than before, anxiety, shakiness. There's next-day drowsiness, which matters for driving and study, and these tablets aren't recommended at your age. And most importantly — it doesn't fix the cause.'

★ 'What I'm offering instead isn't second best. The psychological treatment works better than the tablets do, and it keeps working after you finish.' / ★ 'Give me four weeks with the diary and the plan. Come back and we'll look at it together — and if it hasn't worked we think again, properly, not by reaching for a tablet.'

'Just a few, to get through exams?' → 'Exam time is exactly when the next-day grogginess would cost you most, and two weeks is long enough to start the dependence problem. What I can do this week is get the diary going, fix the coffee, and get you a psychology appointment quickly.' / 'So you're not going to help me?' → 'I am helping you — I'm just not doing the thing that would help for two weeks and cause a problem for two years. Everything else on that list I will start today.'

'Come back sooner if your mood drops, if you feel hopeless or have thoughts of harming yourself, if you start falling asleep suddenly during the day, or if anyone tells you that you snore or stop breathing at night.' / ★ 'And please — don't drive when you feel sleepy. Pull over.'

setting: Emergency Department. Vitals on request. The stem is deliberately silent on loss of consciousness — establishing it is your first job. Version A (aortic stenosis) scripted; Variants B–F on the card. Cluster master card for the whole syncope spine.
stem: Bill Hartley, 62, has come in because he had a fall yesterday afternoon.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Ask the examiner for relevant physical examination findings
Explain your provisional diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 4–5 history · findings · ~1 explanation. Syncope spine: vitals · WIPE · ★ 'complete LOC or aware of your surroundings?' · witnessed · ★ seizure screen ×3 (jerking, tongue bite, incontinence) · duration, first time, ★ describe EACH episode · context ×5 (doing, hot/humid, position change, prolonged standing, emotion) · BEFORE ×4 (★ any warning, meals/fluids, head injury, fever/rash) · AFTER ×3 (★ confusion vs tiredness, pallor, injuries) · signpost 'before, after, or not at all' → CNS → CVS (palpitations follow-up) → RS → GI → travel/jaundice/thermal → drugs incl. ★ recently stopped → psychogenic last → PMHx → ★ FHx sudden death · PEFE: postural BP + pulse rhythm (only what's missing), neuro, CVS (★ murmur — react to it), RS, abdomen, glucose, dipstick, ECG · diagnosis + mechanism · differentials across systems · admit · ★ driving + occupational advice · 000.

back.dx: Cardiac (exertional) syncope from aortic stenosis. 'Out cold', <1 min, witnessed by his wife, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, not confused after (shaken only), grazed elbow, no head strike. ★ Walking up the driveway with the shopping (exertion), ★ no warning at all, prior light-headedness twice on the golf course walking uphill, months of chest tightness and breathlessness on hills 'put down to age' — the AS triad. No meds, none stopped; no FHx sudden death. PEFE: no postural drop, pulse regular slow-rising (ask: low volume? heave? thrill?), ESM RUSE radiating to the carotids, soft S2, neuro normal, glucose 5.6, ECG SR with LVH. To Bill: 'not a trip — a blackout from the heart rather than a simple faint: no warning (faints almost always give a few seconds of dizziness or sweating), and it happened on exertion; a murmur — a narrowed, stiff valve, the door blood leaves the heart through; on exertion the body asks for more blood, the valve can't let enough through, the brain briefly goes short'. Differentials: arrhythmia (still needs excluding), cardiomyopathy, PE, stroke/seizure. Plan: admit to a monitored bed, bloods, echo, cardiology; if severe → valve replacement, works very well. ★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you' (Austroads; SA Registrar of Motor Vehicles; notification duty) · no heights, machinery, swimming alone · 000 if recurrent, chest pain, palpitations, severe SOB. Hidden agenda: brother-in-law's stroke; 'can I drive home and come back tomorrow?' — always asked.

★ 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?' / 'Did anyone see it happen?' / ★ 'Did you have any jerky movements of your arms or legs? Did you bite your tongue? Did you wet or soil yourself?'

'How long were you unconscious? Is this the first time? Can you describe each episode for me?' / ★ 'What were you doing when it happened?' / ★ 'Did you have any warning at all — did you know you were about to go down?'

'Had you missed any meals, and were you drinking normally that day?' / ★ 'When you came round, were you confused, or just tired?' / 'Did you injure your head, or any other part of you, when you fell?'

'For the next few questions, tell me whether you had it before this happened, after it, or not at all — I won't ask you everything twice.' / ★ 'Do you take any medications regularly, or have you recently stopped any?' / ★ 'Has anyone in your family died suddenly and unexpectedly, especially at a young age?'

★ 'Examiner, I have the blood pressure and pulse rate — may I have the postural blood pressure and the pulse rhythm?' / 'That murmur is very significant. Is the pulse volume low as well as slow-rising, and is there a heave or thrill?'

'What you had wasn't a trip — you blacked out, and I think the blackout came from your heart rather than being a simple faint. Two things point me there: you had no warning at all — simple faints almost always give a few seconds of dizziness or sweating first — and it happened while you were exerting yourself.'

'There's a murmur — an extra sound — which suggests one of the valves has become narrowed and stiff. That valve is the door blood leaves your heart through. When you exert yourself your body asks for more blood, the narrowed valve can't let enough through, your brain briefly goes short, and you black out. It also explains the chest tightness and breathlessness on hills.'

'Is it serious?' → 'I want to be straight with you: blacking out with this kind of valve problem is serious, and it's treatable. I'd like to admit you today to a bed with heart monitoring, do bloods, and arrange an echo to see exactly how narrow that valve is. If it's significantly narrowed the treatment is to repair or replace it, which works very well.'

★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you — and don't work at heights, use machinery, or swim alone.' / Examiner on driving: 'Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive — the non-driving period depends on cause, treatment and licence type; commercial stricter; I'd check the current standard rather than quote from memory; in SA the Registrar of Motor Vehicles, and doctors carry a duty to notify where a patient is unfit and continues to drive.'

back.dx: Vasovagal (reflex) syncope — third episode, each with a textbook trigger and a prodrome: (1) jumped out of bed to answer the phone, (2) the sight of blood, (3) today after 1–2 hours standing still in a hot, packed, exciting parade — blurry vision and light-headedness first, 30 s LOC, went floppy (no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence), tired but oriented after, 'white as a sheet', hip bruise. Chronic headaches on Nurofen (distractor): no morning vomiting, weight loss, nocturnal/positional worsening; fundoscopy normal → refer to GP, medication-overuse flagged. No palpitations, chest pain, SOB; periods regular; no alcohol/drugs; no FHx sudden death. PEFE: BP 120/80 sitting → 94/62 standing (drop 26/18 — name it), pulse 82 reg, neuro/fundi/CVS/RS/abdo normal. Explain: nerves overactive → vessels in the legs widen → blood pools → brain short for seconds → lying flat fixes it. Three reasons: setting (hot, prolonged standing, crowd, excitement); earlier episodes fit classic triggers; clear prodrome. Postural drop = supporting evidence, not the diagnosis (postural hypotension causes dizziness/near-fainting more than true LOC; reflex syncope produces a transient drop). Differentials by system: cardiac (arrhythmia — no palpitations; HOCM — no chest pain/SOB/FHx, had a warning; valve/ischaemia), brain (seizure — friends' account; SOL, bleed, meningitis), chemistry (glucose, sodium), blood (anaemia — periods), drugs/alcohol/medications, panic. Management: lie down legs up or head between knees at the warning; counter-pressure; fluids in heat; don't skip meals; keep calves moving; FBC + pregnancy test today; caution heights/swimming alone; GP 1–2 weeks (headaches, ibuprofen frequency); driving — a triggered, prodromal, standing faint generally doesn't restrict; tell the GP if the pattern changes; return if no warning, supine, exertional, or chest pain/palpitations first. Hidden agenda: brain tumour fear from googling the headaches; the licence.

Lying flat fixes it straight away — which is why you came round so quickly.'

I'll write to your GP.' / 'Will this stop me getting my licence?' → 'A faint like yours — clear trigger, clear warning, while standing — generally doesn't restrict you. back.dx: Provoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Standing at the fridge after getting up late; no warning, no aura (smell/taste/déjà vu), no chest pain/palpitations; complete LOC 1–2 min, bilateral jerking, eyes rolled up, went blue, sore tongue, incontinent, bruised elbow; confused and drowsy ~15 min, whole body aches, no focal weakness. Two febrile convulsions as a toddler ('is that why?' — modestly raises later risk, doesn't explain today). No fever/headache/neck stiffness/rash, no head injury, no morning headache/vomiting/weight loss. Version A: party last night, champagne, ~2 h unaccounted for, woke at home; doesn't use drugs but 'can't tell you what happened after I blacked out' — spiking/safety asked without pressing, service offered; missed breakfast, little water yesterday. Version B: no alcohol; temazepam nightly for a year, ran out two days ago — benzodiazepine withdrawal seizure; restart the usual dose today, GP taper over weeks, never abruptly. PEFE: normal, no postural drop, GCS 15, no meningism, fundi normal, ECG normal QTc, β-hCG negative. To Chloe: 'a seizure — a brief burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain, like a short electrical storm; stopped by itself; full recovery; examination, sugar and tracing normal'; 'a single seizure with a clear trigger is not the same as epilepsy'. Trigger (A): most likely alcohol — any amount lowers the threshold ('not about how much you drank'); can't exclude something taken or spiked; missed breakfast → low sugar may have contributed. Differential named so 'nothing is brushed aside': meningitis/encephalitis, bleed (esp. after a head knock), SOL, electrolytes/glucose, cardiac arrhythmia (no prodrome keeps it live), faint, functional episode. Plan: FBC, EUC + Ca/Mg, LFT, alcohol level, urine drug screen; observe to baseline; first-seizure clinic — EEG ± MRI. ★ No driving — legal duty to notify the licensing authority; in SA the doctor is also required to notify; letter for work; no swimming/baths alone, shower, no heights, someone with her tonight; return for another seizure, >5 min, severe headache, fever, neck stiffness, weakness. Hidden agenda: 'is this epilepsy? my aunt lost her licence'.

time: 8 minutes: 0:00 vitals, WIPE, ★ confidentiality statement, open question, empathy, ★ declare neutrality on the allegation · 0:40 ★ 'complete LOC or aware?' → aware; witnessed; seizure screen → ★ jerking + awareness — RECONFIRM THE CONTRADICTION OUT LOUD · timing (20–30 s), first, context (mid-argument) — don't announce the diagnosis at two minutes · 2:30 BEFORE ×4 incl. ★ 'did you hit your head, or did anything happen physically?' · AFTER ×3 (★ confusion vs embarrassment) · 3:30 organic exclusion signposted — CNS, CVS, GI, drugs/meds/cessations, travel/jaundice/thermal — negatives are your reasoning · 4:45 hyperventilation, ★ 'did you feel frightened you were about to die?', mood/sleep/appetite/anhedonia, home and work, ★ RISK — self-harm and harm to others, PMHx/epilepsy/FHx · explanation: functional seizure named, ★ 'what happened to you was real', three reasons, honest differentials with EEG/ECG/glucose, no antiepileptics, driving, safety-net, crisis numbers.

back.dx: Psychogenic (functional) non-epileptic seizure — provisional, diagnosis of exclusion. Collapse mid-argument after being accused of shoplifting; 20–30 s; bilateral arm and leg shaking WITH retained awareness (heard people talking, the ambulance being called, remembers all of it) — incompatible with a generalised epileptic seizure; no tongue bite, no incontinence, no warning, clear-headed immediately (mortified, not confused), no injury, first episode; nobody touched her — shouting only; organic sweep entirely negative; no alcohol/drugs/meds/cessations; not breathing fast; ★ did not feel she was about to die (panic screened); mood stressed, sleep poor, appetite fine, still enjoys things, home fine with partner, work hard — manager 'on at me for months'; ★ no thoughts of self-harm or harming others (if positive — stop, explore ideation/plan/intent/means/previous/protective, same-day mental health); no PMHx/epilepsy/FHx. Explain: 'a psychogenic seizure — also called a functional seizure; looks very like an epileptic seizure and your arms and legs really were shaking, but it doesn't come from abnormal electrical activity in the brain'; ★ 'what happened to you was real — you weren't putting it on, and you couldn't have stopped it; under intense emotional stress the body can respond physically, outside your control'. 'So you think I faked it — that's what he said too' (scripted) → ★ 'No — I'm saying the opposite. I believe what happened, and I don't think you had any control over it. A recognised condition with a name and a treatment — the treatment isn't epilepsy tablets, it's working with someone on the stress.' Three reasons: aware throughout; clear-headed after; the exact moment of confrontation. Differentials, honestly: true epileptic seizure — frontal lobe type can mimic → EEG (video-EEG telemetry definitive); brain bleed/infection/growth (no headache, focal signs, fever); arrhythmia → ECG; glucose/electrolytes → bloods; alcohol/drugs/cessation (none); panic (didn't feel she was dying). Plan: ECG, finger-prick glucose, bloods; neurology + psychology (talking therapy is the most effective treatment); no antiepileptics; ★ no driving until assessed — after any blackout, whatever the cause; no heights/machinery/swimming alone; return if recurrent, injured, prolonged; crisis numbers. Words to avoid: 'not a real seizure', 'nothing wrong', 'all in your head', 'pseudoseizure', 'faking'. Medical certificate offered; nothing written about the allegation; anything written is hers to share.
plan: Vitals → normal · WIPE · ★ 'everything we talk about today stays between you and me, unless there's a risk of harm to you or someone else — is that alright?' · 'tell me more about what happened' → accused, argued, went down, 'I didn't take anything' · empathy · ★ 'my job here isn't to work out what happened at the shop — it's to work out why you collapsed'

★ 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?' → aware, heard everything · witnessed (manager + colleagues) · 'jerky movements? tongue? wet or soil?' → shaking all over; no; no · ★ 'Can I just check something, because it's important — your arms and legs were shaking, but you were aware the whole time and you remember it. Is that right?' → yes
Duration 20–30 s · ever before (never) · doing (mid-argument) · hot/stuffy, standing long, position change → no — keep excluding for another three minutes

BEFORE: warning (not really) · meals/fluids (normal) · ★ 'did you hit your head at all, or did anything happen physically during the argument?' → nobody touched me, just shouting · fever/rash · AFTER: ★ 'confused, or clear-headed straight away?' → clear-headed, just embarrassed · pale (no) · injured (no)

Signpost 'before, after, or not at all': CNS (headache, vision, speech, weakness, numbness) · CVS (chest pain, palpitations, SOB, cough, leg swelling) · GI · alcohol, drugs, ★ medications or recently stopped · travel, jaundice, thermal intolerance → all negative = organic excluded on history

'Breathing fast just before?' · ★ 'during the episode — did you feel frightened that you were about to die?' → no · mood, sleep, appetite, enjoyment · 'who do you live with, stresses at home?' · 'tell me about work generally — difficulties with anyone?' → months of it

★ 'Jane, I ask everyone this and I'd like to check with you too — with everything that's happened today, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else?' → no (positive → stop and explore) · PMHx, epilepsy/fits, FHx similar episodes or sudden death

★ Name it — psychogenic/functional seizure, looks like epilepsy, not electrical · ★ 'what happened to you was real; you weren't putting it on; you couldn't have stopped it' · scripted challenge 'so you think I faked it' → pause, ★ deny explicitly, restate belief · three reasons

Differentials honestly: epileptic seizure (a type that mimics — EEG), bleed/infection/growth, rhythm (ECG), sugar/salts (bloods), alcohol/drugs/cessation (none), panic (no fear of dying) · plan: ECG, glucose, bloods today; neurology (EEG) + psychology; no epilepsy medication · ★ 'please don't drive until you've been assessed — that applies after any blackout, whatever the cause' · no heights/machinery/swimming alone · return if recurrent, injured, prolonged · crisis numbers written down · 'is it going to happen again?' → may, especially under stress; very treatable · summary · questions ('nobody believes me' → answered)

★ 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?' / 'Did you have any jerky movements? Did you bite your tongue? Did you wet or soil yourself?' / ★ 'Can I just check — your arms and legs were shaking, but you were aware the whole time and you remember it?'
★ 'Did you hit your head at all, or did anything happen physically during the argument?' / 'When it stopped, were you confused, or clear-headed straight away?'
★ 'During the episode itself — did you feel frightened that you were about to die?' / 'Tell me about work — how have things been there generally?'

★ 'I ask everyone this — have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else?' → positive: 'Thank you for trusting me with that. When you say there wouldn't be much point, have you had thoughts of ending your life? How? Any plans or preparations? Ever tried before? What keeps you going? I'm not going to leave you on your own with this — I'd like our mental health team to see you today.'

★ 'I think this is a psychogenic, or functional, seizure. It looks like an epileptic seizure, but it doesn't come from abnormal electrical activity in the brain.' / ★ 'What happened to you was real. You weren't putting it on, and you couldn't have stopped it.'

'So you think I faked it. That's what he said too.' → (pause) ★ 'No — I'm saying the opposite, and I can see why it might sound that way, so let me say it plainly. I believe what happened to you, and I don't think you had any control over it at all. This is a recognised condition with a name and a treatment. The only difference is the treatment isn't epilepsy tablets — it's working with someone on the stress that set it off. Take your time.'

★ 'In an epileptic seizure that makes all your limbs shake, you'd be unconscious — and you weren't.' / 'Afterwards you were completely clear-headed; after a true seizure people are usually confused for a while.' / 'It happened at the exact moment of a very stressful confrontation.'

'A true epileptic seizure — there's a type that can look a lot like this, so I'd like a brain wave test, an EEG… a heart rhythm problem — so I'll do a heart tracing… a low blood sugar or salt imbalance — bloods… and a panic attack — but you didn't feel you were going to die.' / 'I'm not going to start you on epilepsy medication, because it wouldn't help and could cause side effects.'

★ 'Please don't drive until you've been assessed — that applies after any blackout, whatever the cause.' / 'Can you write something for my boss?' → 'A certificate covering today and the time you need, stating you were seen after a collapse and are under investigation — yes. Anything about the allegation itself — no, that isn't a medical question. And anything I write about your health is yours; you decide what to share.'
pefe: Role-player: Jane, 25, retail, lives with partner, no PMHx. Answers 'aware' and 'shaking' separately — never spells out the contradiction. Flat and defensive, close to tears; defensive if you comment on the shoplifting either way ('why does everyone keep going on about that?'). ALWAYS delivers 'so you think I faked it — that's what he said too' whatever your wording; 'it's not a real seizure'/'nothing wrong with you' → goes cold: 'right, can I go then'. If never asked about self-harm, says nothing — the omission costs. Hidden agenda: losing the job and nobody believing her — 'nobody believes me about any of it' near the end. Jargon (psychogenic, functional, conversion, dissociative) → 'what does that mean?'

Features: bilateral jerking with retained awareness (the crux) · no tongue bite/incontinence/postictal confusion · 20–30 s · emotional trigger · full memory · further PNES features: asynchronous limb movements, side-to-side head shaking, waxing and waning, eyes closed resisting opening, ictal crying · frontal lobe seizure = classic mimic (preserved awareness, brief, no postictal) · definitive test video-EEG telemetry · treatment CBT/psychological therapy; no AEDs · bedside in every collapse: glucose + 12-lead ECG with QTc; then EUC, Ca, Mg, FBC, β-hCG

Variant 1 — angry ('first I'm a thief, now I put on a fit, I'm going home'): don't defend, re-state plainly — 'I am not saying you put it on; I'm saying the opposite'; offer to write it down; 'two more minutes?' · Variant 2 — risk positive: stop everything else, explore, same-day mental health — the seizure work-up continues but is no longer the priority · Variant 3 — findings shift (side-of-tongue bite, incontinence, 20 min confused): change track and say so — glucose, EUC + Ca/Mg, FBC, drug/alcohol/withdrawal history, CT brain, urgent neurology/EEG, driving advice

Examiner 'why not conversion disorder?' → 'psychogenic/functional non-epileptic seizure sits within DSM-5 functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder, with attacks or seizures) — not competing labels; but conversion disorder requires clinical findings demonstrating incompatibility, and I have no examination here; neuro examination and ideally video-EEG before formalising; functional seizure is the term I'd use with the patient' · 'a psychiatric diagnosis on a first presentation with no examination — safe?' → provisional; strongly suggestive history; video-EEG definitive; epileptic and psychogenic seizures coexist in a meaningful minority so a functional diagnosis doesn't stop the epilepsy work-up; would not start an AED or discharge without glucose and ECG

SA: driving — not until assessed; Austroads; Registrar of Motor Vehicles; neurology (RAH/FMC) for video-EEG; psychology via MHTP; Mental Health Triage 13 14 65; Lifeline 13 11 14; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 not needed
Words to avoid: 'not a real seizure' · 'nothing wrong' · 'all in your head' · 'pseudoseizure' · 'faking'

'It's not a real seizure' / 'there's nothing wrong with you' / 'pseudoseizure' to the patient ★
Recovering badly from 'so you think I faked it' — defending instead of denying explicitly and restating belief ★
Commenting on the shoplifting allegation, sympathetically or sceptically; skipping the confidentiality statement (you need it for the risk question)

setting: Emergency Department. Examination findings on a card after the history (~6 minutes): BP normal, ★ pulse 42 regular, T 36.5, CVS normal, neuro normal, BSL normal. Vitals may be deferred by the examiner to the card.
stem: Gary, 52, has presented after two episodes of falls. He is concerned about the reason for these falls.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Examination findings will be provided on screen or on a card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes, ~6 history. Vitals · WIPE · ★ name and answer his concern ('what if nobody's there?') · ★ reconfirm LOC despite the stem · witnessed · ★ seizure screen ×3 · duration, not first time, ★ 'describe each episode' (episode 2: seated on the couch, a thump in the chest, then out) · environment ×4 anyway · BEFORE ×4 — ★ no warning · AFTER ×3 (pale after the first — non-specific) · signpost → CNS → CVS: ★ palpitations → ★ 'fast or irregular? tap it out?' (he can't — the mark is asking; it's why you stay at bradyarrhythmia) → RS, GI, ★ meds/cessations (rate-slowing drugs), psychogenic last, travel/jaundice/thermal, PMHx, ★ FHx sudden death · ★ card: say '42, regular — a significant bradycardia, the key finding' aloud; ask for ECG + monitoring · ★ diagnose BRADYCARDIA, don't name a rhythm; rhythms and reversible causes as 'we don't know yet' · differentials across systems · admit, monitor, ECG, bloods, echo, cardiology · close his loop · ★ driving.

back.dx: Bradyarrhythmia causing cardiac syncope — pulse 42 regular; rhythm deliberately not named (sinus bradycardia, sinus node dysfunction, second/third-degree AV block, ischaemic conduction disease all compatible; if pushed: palpitations preceding syncope + resting 42 favour sinus node dysfunction with a tachy–brady pattern — but telemetry before saying so; measure the QT — pause-dependent torsades). Two witnessed blackouts (daughter), 1–2 min each, complete LOC, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, back to normal immediately, no injuries: episode 1 getting out of bed, looked very pale (non-specific — don't build vasovagal on it); ★ episode 2 sitting on the couch — 'a thump in my chest, one big heavy beat' — then out; ★ heart racing before the second (can't say fast vs irregular, can't tap it); ★ no warning either time. No chest pain/SOB/oedema, no meds and none stopped (drugs are the commonest reversible cause — beta blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin), no PMHx/FHx. Card: BP normal, ★ pulse 42 regular, T 36.5, CVS/neuro normal, BSL normal (hypoglycaemia excluded, <4.0 the adult threshold). To Gary: 'genuine blackouts, not trips — bradycardia, the heart beating more slowly than it should; normal 60–100, yours 42; too slow to push enough blood to the brain'; two things: no warning; a thump in the chest while seated (not standing up too quickly). Cause 'we don't know yet from a pulse alone': the natural pacemaker running slow; a block in the wiring; blood supply; medication, underactive thyroid, salt imbalance (the fixable ones) → ECG + monitoring over time. Differentials: seizure (no jerking/tongue/confusion), brain (no headache/focal/fever, normal neuro), PE (no travel/leg swelling/SOB), hypoglycaemia (excluded), vasovagal/orthostatic (no warning; seated), anxiety (no fast breathing; last resort). Plan: admit on a monitor, ECG, TSH, electrolytes, troponin, echo, cardiology; pacemaker if intrinsic. ★ Close his loop: 'you asked what happens if you're alone — that's exactly why I don't want you at home tonight; on a monitor we capture it and know what to fix'. 'Can I go home?' → no; ★ driving — not until assessed; no ladders/machinery/swimming alone.
plan: Vitals (may be deferred — 'he is stable at present') · WIPE · 'tell me more about the falls' → 'what if it happens when nobody's around?' → ★ 'I completely understand how concerning that must be. I'll do my best to find the cause today so we can prevent it. Is it alright if I ask some questions?'

★ 'Can you just confirm — did you lose consciousness, or were you aware of your surroundings?' → completely out · witnessed (daughter, both) · ★ 'jerky movements? bite your tongue? wet or soil yourself?' → no ×3

Duration (1–2 min) · first time? (twice) · ★ 'can you please describe each of the previous episodes for me?' → 1: getting out of bed, went down, very pale · 2: sitting on the couch, a thump in the chest — one big heavy beat — then out · environment anyway: hot/humid, emotion, position change, prolonged standing → no (the first was getting out of bed — orthostatic still live)

★ BEFORE: 'any warning at all — dizziness, sweating, nausea, blurred vision?' → 'none, that's what bothers me' (react) · meals/fluids · head injury · fever/rash · AFTER: confused or tired? (neither — back to normal) · injuries (none) · pale (after the first — take it, move on)

Signpost · CNS: headache, vision, speech, weakness, numbness → no · CVS: chest pain (no) · ★ 'any racing of your heart?' → yes, before the second → ★ 'describe that — beating fast, or irregularly? could you tap the rhythm out on the desk?' → 'I don't know', declines → 'that's fine' · SOB, leg swelling, cough → no

GI · alcohol (couple/week), drugs · ★ 'medications regularly, or recently stopped any?' → nothing · breathing fast/stress · travel, thermal intolerance, jaundice · PMHx · ★ FHx similar episodes or sudden death, especially young

★ Card, aloud: 'BP, temperature, CVS and neurological examination normal; glucose normal — hypoglycaemia excluded, threshold <4 in an adult; ★ but the pulse is 42 and regular, a significant bradycardia — I think that's the key finding. Could I have a 12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring?'

★ To Gary: genuine blackouts; bradycardia named at the right level; 60–100 vs 42; too slow to push blood to the brain · two things: no warning; the thump while seated · 'what's making it slow?' → ★ 'I can't tell you which one it is yet from a pulse alone' — pacemaker/wiring/blood supply/medication/thyroid/salts; ECG + monitoring will tell · differentials across systems

'Can I go home and see how it goes?' → no · admit on a monitor, ECG, bloods (thyroid, salts, heart enzymes), echo, cardiology; pacemaker if the heart is running too slowly on its own — works very well · ★ 'you asked what happens if you're on your own — that's exactly why I don't want you at home tonight' · ★ driving — not until assessed, national rules, notification · no ladders/machinery/swimming alone · summary · questions
ask: ★ 'I completely understand how concerning that must be. I'll do my best to find the cause today so we can prevent this happening again.' / ★ 'Can you just confirm for me — did you lose consciousness, or were you aware of your surroundings?'
'Did you have any jerky movements of your arms or legs? Did you bite your tongue? Did you wet or soil yourself?' / ★ 'Can you describe each of the previous episodes for me?'

★ 'Did you have any warning at all — did you know you were about to go down?' / 'When you came round, were you confused, or just tired?' / 'For the next questions, tell me whether you had it before this happened, after it, or not at all.'

★ 'Can you describe that racing — was it beating fast, or beating irregularly? Could you tap the rhythm out for me?' / ★ 'Do you take any medications regularly, or have you recently stopped any?' / 'Has anyone in your family died suddenly and unexpectedly, especially at a young age?'
★ 'His pulse is 42 and regular, which is a significant bradycardia — I think that's the key finding. Could I have a 12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring?'

★ 'You have a condition called bradycardia, which means your heart is beating more slowly than it should. A normal resting rate is 60 to 100; yours is 42.' / 'When the heart beats too slowly it can't push enough blood up to the brain, and that's why you blacked out.' / 'Two things fit: no warning at all — a simple faint almost always gives a few seconds of dizziness or sweating first — and the thump in your chest while you were sitting down, so it wasn't a matter of standing up too quickly.'

★ 'I can't tell you which one it is yet from a pulse alone — that's why I want a heart tracing and monitoring.' / 'It can be the heart's own natural pacemaker running slow; a block in the electrical wiring between the top and bottom chambers; a problem with the blood supply; or a medication, an underactive thyroid, or a salt imbalance — and those we can simply fix.'

'How do you know that?' (if you name a rhythm) — don't. Examiner 'bradycardia isn't a diagnosis': 'I'd call it a bradyarrhythmia causing cardiac syncope. A regular 42 is compatible with sinus bradycardia, sinus node dysfunction, second- or third-degree AV block, or ischaemic conduction disease, and he couldn't characterise the palpitations. If pressed, palpitations preceding syncope with a resting 42 would make me favour sinus node dysfunction with a tachy–brady pattern — but I'd want the ECG and telemetry before telling a patient that. I'd also measure the QT.'

★ 'You asked what happens if you're on your own — that's exactly why I want you here on a monitor tonight. If it happens again we capture it, and then we know precisely what to fix.' / 'If your heart is running too slowly on its own, the usual treatment is a pacemaker — a small device that stops it dropping below a safe rate — and it works very well.'

★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you — and no ladders, machinery, or swimming alone.' / Refuses admission: 'It's your decision and I won't keep you against your will — but you've blacked out twice with no warning and your heart is running at 42; my worry isn't another fall, it's a pause long enough that someone needs to be there with the equipment. Whatever you decide — no driving, no heights or machinery; ambulance if it happens again, chest pain or severe breathlessness. Can I ask what's making you want to leave?'

'What if nobody's there?' in the opening line (part of the stem) — raises it again in the last minute if never answered. Generic 'what happened?' gets 'I just went down, both times' — make them ask per episode.
