setting: Emergency Department. Mother on the way. An ECG has already been done — laminated tracing handed over for task 2. The examiner gives the QTc (0.54 s) ONLY if you ask for it. Vitals: BP normal, ★ pulse 50, RR and temperature normal.
stem: Lily, 15, brought in by ambulance after fainting at school. Her mother is on the way. She has had two previous similar episodes, and an ECG has already been done.
tasks: Take a history (5 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: 8 minutes: 5 history · ECG · explanation. Register 'pulse 50' at the vitals · speak to Lily, plainly, permission first · ★ confirm LOC · ★ seizure screen ×3 · duration, ★ each episode, ★ 'what were you doing?' → sitting, three times — no reflex/orthostatic explanation · context ×4 · ★ BEFORE — no warning (positive 1) · AFTER ×3 · sweep: CNS, CVS, GI, ★ all medications (acne, allergies, nausea, mood), alcohol/drugs, stress · ★ protect the last 30 s for FAMILY HISTORY — similar episodes (mum faints — positive 2), sudden death, drowning, cot death, congenital deafness · ★ ECG in seven steps aloud → step 7: 'examiner, could you tell me what the QTc is?' → 0.54 → commit · LQTS + three reasons · honest about 'could I die?' · differentials across systems · admit, monitor, K/Mg/Ca/TSH, paediatric cardiology, beta blocker, drugs to avoid · ★ ECG the mother and first-degree relatives · defer sport; no swimming alone.

back.dx: Congenital long QT syndrome: three syncopal episodes over months, each while seated doing nothing (class, home, class), ~1 min, complete LOC, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, ★ never any warning ('I'm fine, then I'm on the floor'), not confused after, not pale, no injury; everything else negative — no chest pain/palpitations/SOB, no medications (none for acne/allergies/nausea/mood), no alcohol/drugs, no stress, no PMHx; ★ mother used to faint when younger and still does sometimes; no sudden deaths, drownings, cot deaths or congenital deafness. Vitals: pulse 50 (bradycardia — note it). ECG in seven steps: rate ~50 (six large squares), regular, P before every QRS → sinus bradycardia, PR normal, QRS normal, ST no elevation/depression, T waves and QT → ★ 'examiner, could you tell me what the QTc is?' → 0.54 s = 540 ms — markedly prolonged (expect <~460 in a girl; >500 high risk) → sinus bradycardia with a significantly prolonged QTc — long QT syndrome. Never try to measure it silently on a laminated tracing (paper-folding unavailable, Bazett under time pressure unrealistic — candidates default to sinus bradycardia/sick sinus and fail; a correct differential does not rescue a wrong primary diagnosis). To Lily: 'after each beat the electrical system takes longer than it should to reset; sometimes it tips the heart into a fast, disorganised rhythm — the heart can't pump, blood doesn't reach the brain, you black out, then it settles, which is why you wake up fine'. Three reasons: the QT on the tracing; mum's fainting (a version runs in families); no warning (cause in the heart, not a simple faint). 'Could I die?' → honest: taken seriously, occasionally dangerous — hence not home; very treatable; finding it today is good news; a tablet (beta blocker) greatly reduces the chance; a list of medicines to avoid. Differentials across systems: other rhythms (too slow, block), muscle/valve, seizure, brain, glucose/salts, PE, reflex/orthostatic (seated, no warning), panic last. Plan: admit on a monitor, K/Mg/Ca/TSH/glucose, paediatric cardiology today, beta blocker likely, QT-prolonging drug list (antibiotics, antiemetics); ★ when mum arrives — with Lily's permission — mum needs an ECG today; screen parents and siblings; sport — defer to the specialists (type-dependent), hold competitive sport, no swimming (some forms triggered by exercise and swimming).

Examiner won't give it: 'The QT runs from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave, measured in lead II. At normal rates the QT should be less than half the RR — here the T wave extends beyond the halfway point, so it's prolonged. At a rate of 50 the raw QT overstates it, so it must be rate-corrected with Bazett — QT ÷ √RR. My assessment: the corrected QT is prolonged; with recurrent syncope without prodrome and a family history, long QT syndrome.'

★ 'After each beat, the electrical system takes longer than it should to reset — and that can tip the heart into a fast, disorganised rhythm, so blood doesn't reach the brain and you black out.' / ★ 'Three reasons: the QT measurement on your tracing, your mum's history of fainting, and the fact you faint with no warning.'

It is something we take seriously — occasionally that rhythm can be dangerous, and that's why I don't want you going home while we sort it out. back.dx: Aortic stenosis (commonest cause at 40: bicuspid valve) — exertional syncope with the triad: collapsed mid-rally chasing a ball, complete LOC 2–3 min, first ever, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, ★ no warning at all, warm day but drinking between games and had breakfast (the decoy), clear-headed on waking, looked washed out, grazed elbow; ★ chest pain while playing — left/central, radiating down the left arm and up the neck, heavy 'like a weight' (exertional angina — hold both ACS and AS; you haven't listened yet); ★ more puffed on court this season; no palpitations/oedema/PE features; non-smoker, 6–8 SD/week, no meds; cholesterol high-normal 3–4 years ago, BP normal, no diabetes, no known murmur/rheumatic fever, no FHx sudden death. Examination: no postural drop; pulse 84 regular (ask character — slow-rising/low volume/narrow pulse pressure); neuro normal; JVP not raised; ★ prominent but undisplaced LV impulse (pressure overload, concentric hypertrophy — say so), no thrill; S1 S2 normal; ★ murmur — aortic area (R 2nd ICS), systolic, radiating to the carotids, no separate carotid bruit; chest clear; abdomen normal; no oedema/calf tenderness; ECG, BSL normal (a normal ECG doesn't exclude structural disease → echo). 15-second diagnosis: 'the aortic valve is the gateway between your heart and the main blood tube carrying blood to your body — in your case that gateway has become narrowed'; two reasons: the trio with exercise, the murmur. Differentials by system: heart — MI/blocked artery (ECG normal, troponin), arrhythmia (no palpitations), HOCM, pericarditis, PE; brain — seizure, stroke, bleed, meningitis, SOL; chemistry — glucose, salts; simple — dehydration, heat, standing faint; drugs/alcohol/panic. Plan: admit on a monitor, bloods + serial ECGs (exclude MI), echo, cardiology today; valve replacement if tight — results very good; no tennis or heavy exertion; ★ no driving until cleared — SA notification, done together; return if recurrent, chest pain, SOB at rest; letter for the employer, social work. Hidden agenda: 'am I going to drop dead?' (a colleague's brother); 'will I lose my licence — I drive for work?'.

back.dx: Acute inferior STEMI, painless — diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Presyncope after three hours of walking (far more activity than usual), skipped breakfast (an apple), aware throughout, a few seconds, no jerking/incontinence, first time, ★ no warning, not confused, no injury, friend said 'washed out'; diabetes ~2 years on insulin, adherent (took it this morning, slightly offended at the question), no dose change, nothing new/herbal, usually eats and snacks properly, sugars in the 7s, 3-monthly reviews; ★ feet tingle at night, ★ early retinal changes at the last eye check (microvascular disease → painless ischaemia plausible); ★ 'no chest pain at all' (firm); no SOB/palpitations/oedema; non-smoker, occasional wine; BP and cholesterol 'a bit up'; father MI at 58; ★ drove herself here; husband at work. Bedside glucose 6.1 (Version B). ECG: rate ~70, regular sinus, PR normal, QRS narrow, axis normal, ★ ST elevation II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression aVL and I (reciprocal change = infarction, not pericarditis/early repolarisation), no Q waves, T upright; examine V1–V3 for posterior extension; ★ right-sided leads (V4R) before any nitrate → 'acute inferior STEMI — a time-critical emergency' (RCA ~80%; ST III > II favours RCA). Warning shot, then: 'your heart tracing shows you are having a heart attack right now'; 'no chest pain' → two-part explanation: diabetes damages the small vessels (blocks → heart attack) AND the nerves carrying pain from the heart → a silent heart attack; 'the tracing tells us more than how you feel'. 'Am I going to die?' → serious and very treatable; the safest thing is what we're doing now. Differential: hypoglycaemia (skipped breakfast, hours of walking — may still be part of it), hyperglycaemia/DKA, arrhythmia/valve, PE, TIA, seizure, electrolytes, dehydration, anaemia, medication — the tracing puts MI at the top. Action: ★ aspirin 300 mg chewed, IV access, monitor with a defibrillator available, oxygen only if SpO2 <93%, V4R before nitrates, ★ 000 to a PCI-capable centre, ECG transmitted ahead, stay with her; no party; ★ no driving today or until cleared (~2 weeks after successful PCI); call the husband; car stays.

(much more) · BP, cholesterol (a bit up), FHx (father MI 58) · ★ 'do you drive, and who's at home?' → drove herself; husband at work

★ ECG, one breath: 'rate ~70; regular sinus rhythm, P before every QRS; PR normal, no block; QRS narrow; axis normal; ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in aVL and I; no established Q waves; T upright. I'd examine V1–V3 for posterior extension and obtain right-sided leads, V4R, before any nitrate. Acute inferior STEMI — a time-critical emergency.' · 'which artery?' → RCA ~80% (III > II) · 'why no pain?' → autonomic neuropathy · 'first?' → aspirin 300 mg chewed + ambulance to PCI

★ Warning shot: 'I need to tell you something important, and I'd like you to hear all of it before you react. Your heart tracing shows that you are having a heart attack right now.' · 'not possible — no chest pain' → ★ two-part diabetes explanation · 'am I going to die?' → serious and very treatable; the safest thing is what we're doing

Differential named (hypo may still be part of it) — 'the tracing moves the heart attack to the top' · ★ chew this aspirin · ★ calling an ambulance to a hospital that can open the vessel; drip, monitor, stay with you, tracing sent ahead · 'the party? my car's outside' → no party; ★ no driving today or until cleared; car stays; 'is there someone I can call — your husband?' · summary · questions
ask: 'Thank you for coming in — your friends gave you good advice.' / ★ 'Could I please have a bedside blood glucose while we talk?' / 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?' / ★ 'Did you get any warning at all?'

★ 'Are you taking your insulin exactly as prescribed — and did you take it today? Has the dose been changed recently — and any new medicines, supplements, or herbal or traditional remedies? Do you take your mid-morning and mid-afternoon snacks? Do you get warning symptoms when you go low?'

'Any numbness, tingling or burning in your feet, or ulcers? Any blurring of vision — when was your last eye check? Any kidney problems? Do you get dizzy on standing, feel full very quickly after meals, or have bladder trouble?'
★ 'Any chest pain, tightness or heaviness — even a little?' / 'Have you done more physical activity than usual today?' / ★ 'Do you drive, and who's at home with you?'

★ 'Rate, rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS, axis, ST segments, T waves, Q waves.' / ★ 'ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in aVL — an acute inferior STEMI.' / ★ 'I would obtain right-sided leads, particularly V4R, before giving any nitrate.'

Examiner: 'which artery?' → 'Most often the right coronary artery — about 80% of inferior infarcts; the circumflex in the rest. ST elevation taller in III than II favours the RCA.' / 'why no chest pain?' → 'Diabetic autonomic neuropathy impairs the afferent pain pathway; painless infarction is well described in diabetes, in women and in older patients.'
★ 'I need to tell you something important, and I'd like you to hear all of it. Your heart tracing shows that you are having a heart attack right now — the medical name is a myocardial infarction.'

★ 'Diabetes does two separate things here. First, over years, it damages the small blood vessels that supply the heart muscle — if one suddenly blocks, that part of the muscle stops getting blood, and that is a heart attack. Second, the same diabetes damages the nerves that carry pain from the heart — so instead of chest pain, the only thing you felt was being unwell and about to fall. We call that a silent heart attack, and it's why the tracing tells us more than how you feel.' / 'This is serious, and it is also very treatable — the safest thing possible is what we're doing now.'

★ 'I'd like you to chew this aspirin. I'm calling an ambulance, and you'll go straight to a hospital that can open the blocked vessel — the sooner that's done, the more heart muscle we save. I'll stay with you, put a drip in, keep you on a monitor, and send your tracing ahead.'

★ 'I'm sorry — the party isn't possible tonight, and you must not drive: not today, and not until the specialist clears you. Your car can stay here safely. Is there someone I can call — your husband?' / Refuses the ambulance: 'Part of your heart muscle is losing its blood supply right now, and every minute counts. It must be an ambulance rather than your car because the most dangerous moments are the first hours, when the rhythm can go wrong suddenly — the paramedics carry the equipment to fix that. You can decline — I'll respect it — but I'd be failing you if I didn't say plainly that I think it would be a very dangerous choice. Can I call your husband before you decide?'
pefe: Role-player: Anita, 44, retail admin, married, two teenagers; insulin ~2 years, conscientious and mildly offended at any suggestion otherwise; BP/cholesterol 'a bit up'; father MI at 58; non-smoker; feet tingle at night and early retinal changes — only if asked directly; ★ 'no chest pain at all' — firm, repeated. Brisk and dismissive at first; pushes at 2 min 'it's just my sugar, isn't it? I skipped breakfast' (agree possible, keep going); disbelieves the diagnosis; frightened once explained; 'am I going to die?'; always finishes 'can I still go to the party? my car's outside — I'll drive myself to hospital'. Agree/hesitate/no ambulance = fail; no aspirin = fail

Examiner: capillary glucose 6.1 (Version B) · ECG: rate ~70, sinus, PR normal, narrow QRS, normal axis, ST elevation II/III/aVF, reciprocal depression aVL/I, no Q, T upright · Version A: ECG SR 78, no acute change; first-aider glucose at the centre 2.7 → hypoglycaemia (insulin, skipped breakfast, hours of walking) — ★ still give the differential (rhythm/artery, orthostatic, dehydration, TIA, seizure, infection, anaemia, salts, medication); eat now, bloods, review insulin/meal timing/snacks on active days — 'it's a hypo' with nothing else fails

Variant 3 — BP 82/54, pulse 46 after the ECG: RV involvement — lie flat, withhold nitrates, avoid morphine, right-sided leads, cautious IV saline bolus (preload-dependent RV), atropine 600 µg ready, transcutaneous pacing available, escalate — urgent reperfusion/cardiology · Variant 4 — rural SA >2 h from a cath lab: activate MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33/RFDS in parallel, transmit the ECG for remote cardiology, pre-hospital fibrinolysis with weight-adjusted tenecteplase within 30 min under the SA Health STEMI pathway after checking contraindications (recent stroke, bleeding, surgery, uncontrolled hypertension); angiography at 3–24 h, immediately if reperfusion fails

STEMI: new ST elevation ≥1 mm in two contiguous leads (V2–V3: ≥2 mm men ≥40, ≥2.5 men <40, ≥1.5 women) · inferior II/III/aVF, reciprocal I/aVL · RV V4R · posterior V7–V9 · ECG within 10 min · aspirin 300 mg chewed · ticagrelor 180 mg or clopidogrel 300–600 mg loading · GTN 300–600 µg SL — not in RV infarct, hypotension, bradycardia, PDE5 inhibitor 24–48 h · morphine 2.5–5 mg IV titrated · oxygen only if SpO2 <93% · primary PCI within 90 min FMC (120 if transfer) else fibrinolysis within 30 min VERIFY
Hypoglycaemia <4.0: 15 g fast carbohydrate, repeat at 15 min; unconscious — glucagon 1 mg IM or 50 mL 50% glucose IV · driving: ~2 weeks off after STEMI with successful PCI (private) VERIFY Austroads
SA: SA Health STEMI pathway; SA Ambulance 000; PCI centres RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 / RFDS; Registrar of Motor Vehicles

setting: Orthopaedic ward; you are the resident. Day 1 after TKR under spinal. Vitals in the stem (ask for them anyway, lying and standing). No examination required. Task 3 is investigations to the examiner. The one sentence the station is marked on: PE named first, CTPA named.
stem: John Whittaker, 60, had an elective total knee replacement yesterday morning under spinal anaesthetic. Overnight he walked to the ward toilet with a frame and was found on the floor by a nurse. He is back in bed, alert and talking. BP 118/74 lying, 104/66 standing; HR 104 regular; RR 20; SpO2 94% RA; T 36.9; BSL 6.2; GCS 15.
tasks: Take a focused history (approx. 6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient
Tell the examiner your investigations
time: 8 minutes: leave 2 for explanation + investigations. Vitals lying/standing — interpret aloud (tachycardic, borderline sats, postural drop) · WIPE, sit, open question, empathy · ★ true LOC (a fresh TKR gives every mechanical reason to fall) · last memory, duration, witnessed (no), first time · context: doing, standing long, pain, ★ micturition/defecation/straining, heat · ★ prodrome (none) · chest pain/palpitations · during: shaking, tongue, incontinence, pallor · after: confusion, how long · ★ 'did you hit your head?' · ★ full respiratory and calf screen despite negatives · CNS, GI, fever · ★ opioids/pregabalin, antihypertensive restarted, ★ VTE prophylaxis — which, missed doses · intake · VTE risk factors (previous VTE, cancer, travel, FHx clotting/sudden death), smoking, PMHx · ★ concerns · ★ PE named FIRST — 'guided by your situation as well as your symptoms' · vasovagal, peri-op MI, orthostatic/opioid/blood loss, rhythm/glucose/salts as differentials · check understanding · investigations tied to differentials — ★ CTPA, ★ no D-dimer · escalation, safety-net, summary.

back.dx: Pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise — provoked by post-operative immobilisation, day 1 after TKR (syncope occurs in ~1 in 7 PE presentations and suggests a central clot with RV strain). Complete LOC ('there's a gap', last memory reaching for the rail), unwitnessed, found a few minutes later, first ever; had just passed urine, not straining, not standing long, bathroom not hot, knee sore but no worse; ★ no warning; no chest pain/palpitations; nobody saw shaking; 'white as a sheet'; muddled ~1 min then himself; grazed elbow, shoulder took the impact, 'I don't think I hit my head' (if he clipped the sink and is on enoxaparin → CT head too); ★ entirely negative respiratory and calf screen — do NOT downgrade PE (that is the designed reaction); no CNS/GI/fever; oxycodone at midnight, paracetamol; ★ nightly abdominal injection, name unknown, ★ one dose missed on the day of surgery; perindopril restarted this morning; nil by mouth pre-op, eaten little; no previous VTE/cancer/travel/FHx; ex-smoker 20/day quit 10 y; BP tablet only. Vitals: HR 104, SpO2 94%, postural drop 118/74 → 104/66. To John, lead with the dangerous diagnosis: 'the thing I am most concerned about is a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood tubes of your lungs; the reason isn't your symptoms, it's your situation — major knee surgery yesterday, hardly able to move that leg; blood clots in the deep veins and a piece travels to the lungs; it can cause exactly this sort of blackout, sometimes with no chest symptoms at all; even though your breathing is fine I'm not prepared to leave that untested'. Then: vasovagal (pain, toilet, first stand after surgery — may well be it), peri-operative MI (days 0–3, can be quiet), orthostatic hypotension (surgical blood loss + opioids), rhythm, glucose, salts. 'But I feel fine' → 'a clot in the lung doesn't always announce itself — sometimes a blackout is the only thing it does; treatable, very treatable early; the scan takes twenty minutes'. Investigations tied to differentials: bedside — lying/standing obs, continuous sats and cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, BSL, oxygen to 94–98%, two large-bore cannulae; PE — ★ urgent CTPA after renal function and contrast allergy (V/Q if contrast contraindicated); ★ no D-dimer (raised in virtually everyone a day after surgery, wouldn't change management); MI — ECG + serial troponin; bleeding — FBE, coags, group and hold, wound and drains; metabolic — UEC (also for contrast), Ca, Mg; CXR (collapse/effusion/pneumothorax); CT head if head strike or persistent confusion; bedside echo for RV strain if hypotensive; discuss empirical anticoagulation with orthopaedics while awaiting the scan; bed rest, supervised mobilisation, mechanical prophylaxis; escalate to the registrar now; MET if he deteriorates; ★ 'press the buzzer before you get up'. Hidden agenda: home Friday — wife Margaret has early dementia; social work either way.
plan: 'May I have the vital signs — BP lying and standing, HR, RR, sats, temperature, blood sugar?' → interpret aloud: 'stable but tachycardic, borderline saturations, a postural drop — I'll keep monitoring running' · WIPE, hands washed, sits · 'tell me about it in your own words' · 'I'm so sorry — that must have been frightening; let's find out what's going on together'

★ 'Did you black out completely, or go down but stay aware?' → right out, a gap · last thing you remember (reaching for the rail) · how long, anyone with you (unwitnessed, found minutes later) · ever before (never)

Context: doing (just got there, passed urine) · standing a while · pain (sore, no worse) · ★ passing urine/opening bowels/straining · bathroom hot · ★ 'any warning — light-headed, sweaty, sick, ringing, vision closing in?' → none · chest pain/racing heart → no

During: anyone see it (no) · told you shook/stiffened, bit your tongue, wet yourself (nobody mentioned) · pale (white as a sheet) · after: confused/drowsy, how long (muddled a minute) · quickly yourself · ★ 'did you hurt yourself — did you hit your head?' → elbow, shoulder, doesn't think so (Variant 2: clipped the sink)

★ Systems, all of it, despite negatives: chest pain/tightness, SOB even on moving, cough/haemoptysis, calf pain/swelling/redness · headache, vision, speech, weakness, numbness · nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain/melaena · fever/sweats/rash → all no — do not downgrade PE

★ Medications: pain relief — anything strong (oxycodone, midnight), pregabalin · usual BP tablets restarted (perindopril this morning) · ★ 'a blood-thinning injection since the operation — which one, any doses missed?' → nightly abdominal injection, name unknown, one missed on the day of surgery · eating/drinking (little, NBM) · alcohol/substances

VTE risk and background: previous clot leg/lung, cancer, long flights/drives, FHx clotting or sudden death young, smoking (ex 20/day ×30 y, quit 10 y), PMHx (BP), ★ 'is there anything you've been particularly worried about?' → home Friday, wife unwell → acknowledge, promise to return, don't derail

★ Explain — PE FIRST: 'everything you've told me is reassuring, and I have to be guided by your situation as well as your symptoms; what concerns me most is a pulmonary embolism…' · 'but I feel fine — is it dangerous?' → answered · differentials: simple faint (pain/straining/first stand), quiet peri-op heart attack, low BP from blood loss + strong painkillers, rhythm/sugar/salts · 'does that make sense — what questions?' · Friday: can't promise; team told about Margaret; social work either way

★ To the examiner, each test tied to a differential: bedside obs lying/standing, monitoring, ECG, BSL, O2 to 94–98%, two large-bore cannulae · PE — ★ urgent CTPA after UEC and contrast allergy (V/Q if contraindicated); ★ no D-dimer and why · MI — ECG + serial troponin · bleeding — FBE, coags, G&H, wound/drains · metabolic — UEC, Ca, Mg · CXR · CT head if head strike/confusion · bedside echo for RV strain if hypotensive · empirical anticoagulation discussed with orthopaedics · bed rest, supervised mobilisation, mechanical prophylaxis · registrar now, MET if deteriorates · summary
ask: 'Before I begin, may I have the vital signs, including lying and standing blood pressure?' / 'I'm so sorry to hear that — let's find out what's happening together.' / ★ 'Did you black out completely, or did you go down but stay aware?'
'Did it happen while you were passing urine or opening your bowels, or straining? Was the bathroom hot?' / ★ 'Did you get any warning?' / ★ 'Did you hit your head?'

★ 'Have you had a blood-thinning injection since the operation — do you know which one, and have any doses been missed?' / 'What have they been giving you for pain — anything strong like morphine or oxycodone, or a nerve tablet such as pregabalin? Were your usual blood-pressure tablets restarted this morning?'

'Have you ever had a clot in the leg or the lung? Any cancer? Long flights or drives? Anyone in the family with clotting problems, or died suddenly and young?' / ★ 'Is there anything you have been particularly worried about?'

★ 'Everything you've told me is reassuring, and I want to be honest about where that leaves us. The thing I am most concerned about is a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood tubes of your lungs. The reason I am concerned is not your symptoms — it is your situation. You had major knee surgery yesterday and you have hardly been able to move that leg; when the legs stay still, blood can clot in the deep veins, and a piece can travel to the lungs. That can cause exactly this sort of blackout, sometimes with no chest symptoms at all. So even though your breathing is fine, I am not prepared to leave that untested.'

'But I feel fine — how can it be a clot?' → 'I know, and that's a good sign. But a clot in the lung doesn't always announce itself — sometimes a blackout is the only thing it does. It is treatable, and very treatable when we find it early, which is exactly what I'm trying to do. The scan takes about twenty minutes and we'll know today.'

'A simple faint — a vasovagal faint — is common when people are in pain, or straining on the toilet, or standing up for the first time after an operation, and that may well be what happened. Heart attacks are more common in the first few days after a big operation and can be surprisingly quiet, so I want to check that. Low blood pressure from blood loss during surgery, together with the strong painkillers, can also drop you when you stand.' / 'A simple faint is a diagnosis I can only make after ruling out the dangerous ones.'

★ 'For pulmonary embolism, which is my leading diagnosis: an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram, after checking renal function and contrast allergy — a V/Q scan if contrast is contraindicated.' / ★ 'I would not order a D-dimer, because it is elevated in virtually every patient a day after major surgery and would not change my management either way.'

'For myocardial infarction: the ECG plus serial troponin. For bleeding and anaemia: full blood examination, coagulation profile, group and hold, and inspection of the wound and drains. For metabolic causes: urea, electrolytes and creatinine — which I also need before contrast — plus calcium and magnesium. A chest X-ray; a CT head if he struck his head or remains confused; a bedside echo looking for right ventricular strain if he becomes hypotensive.' / 'I'd discuss empirical anticoagulation with the orthopaedic team while awaiting the scan, escalate to my registrar now, and call a MET if he deteriorates.'

'Am I still getting home Friday? My wife's not well' → 'Thank you for telling me — I can hear how much it matters. I can't promise, but I'll make sure the team knows about your wife and that social work is involved either way.' / ★ 'Please press the buzzer before you get up — do not walk to the toilet on your own.'
pefe: Role-player: John, 60, retired carpenter, cares for wife Margaret (early dementia); ex-smoker 20/day ×30 y, quit 10 y; two drinks Friday; perindopril restarted; paracetamol, oxycodone (midnight), nightly abdominal injection (name unknown, one missed on surgery day); NBM pre-op. Practical, embarrassed, minimising. One-sentence answers, doesn't help; open question gets the vignette. 'But I feel fine — how can it be a clot?' once. 'It's probably just a faint' → accepts cheerfully and marks you down. Wife raised only if asked about concerns, else last minute

Vitals: 118/74 lying → 104/66 standing · HR 104 reg · RR 20 · SpO2 94% RA · T 36.9 · BSL 6.2 · GCS 15 · no examination. ECG in PE: sinus tachycardia commonest; RV strain = TWI V1–V4, new RBBB; S1Q3T3 uncommon · syncope in ~1 in 7 PE presentations

Variant 1 — convincing vasovagal (straining, hot, sweaty and light-headed first): 'that does sound like a simple faint and may well be it — I still have to be careful, because after this operation a clot can look identical and it's the one cause I can't afford to be wrong about; treat the faint as likely and rule out the dangerous one at the same time' · Variant 2 — clipped the sink, on prophylaxis: CT head + CTPA; hold prophylaxis pending imaging; regular neuro obs; discuss with the surgical team — 'two things can be true at once'

Variant 3 — deteriorates (80/50, sats 86%, HR 130): high-risk PE until proven otherwise — MET call, sit up, high-flow O2, large-bore access, cautious fluids, registrar + ICU; bedside echo for RV dilatation; CTPA only if safe to travel; ★ systemic thrombolysis relatively contraindicated within 3 weeks of major surgery → catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy; unfractionated heparin infusion (short-acting, reversible) · Variant 4 — wound soaked, Hb 74: post-op bleeding — hold all anticoagulation, orthopaedic registrar urgently, cross-match, fluids, transfuse, reassess the wound; no blood thinner until the surgeon reviews

SA: MET call; orthopaedic registrar; ICU; regional site → MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if high-risk PE; social work for Margaret; ACAT/Country Health Connect for discharge planning
